    ]]>         The EU media connects Europe’s connectors – allow us to help https://euobserver.com/244439/media-connects-europes-connectors/ Fri, 23 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244439 Outlets such as EUobserver do more than report on European affairs. They provide a space where different perspectives meet, complex policy debates become accessible and stakeholders can better understand the choices shaping the continent. In doing so, they can help connect the communities that make the European project work. This is also the thinking behind our initiative to develop a media product dedicated to the business community.]]> Europe is a work in progress. Its future depends on the ability of people, institutions and businesses to work together across national borders and political divides.

    The European project is far from perfect, but it remains the strongest alternative to a continent defined by division and confrontation.

    Europe has advanced through dialogue, negotiation and compromise. Challenging established ideas is part of that process. So is recognising that criticism alone cannot deliver change. The task is to improve what we have built and find common ground on what comes next.

    That responsibility extends well beyond the EU institutions and the Brussels bubble.

    Businesses, civil society, universities, national governments, media and citizens all have a stake in Europe’s future. The single market and the euro, for example, are not merely institutional achievements. They are also the products of economic cooperation and the participation of businesses and citizens across the continent.

    Strengthening Europe’s competitiveness and prosperity should be understood in the same way: as a shared undertaking, not an agenda reserved for political and economic elites. A stronger Europe requires participation, initiative and a willingness to contribute. It cannot be built by those who remain on the sidelines.

    Europe needs more Connectors

    Construction usually brings to mind roads, bridges and buildings — the concrete structures that link cities, countries and communities. But Europe also relies on less visible infrastructure: the networks, institutions and platforms that bring people together, build trust and turn ideas into action.

    Media, civic organisations, universities and professional networks all play a role in this process. They connect perspectives, create opportunities for dialogue and help people identify shared interests across sectors and borders. They make cooperation possible where distance, competing priorities or a lack of understanding might otherwise stand in the way.

    These Connectors are essential to Europe’s ability to act collectively. They help businesses engage with policymakers, give citizens access to informed public debate and enable organisations to exchange knowledge and develop partnerships. Their value lies not only in the connections they create, but also in what those connections make possible.

    Pan-European media has a particular role to play. Outlets such as EUobserver do more than report on European affairs. They provide a space where different perspectives meet, complex policy debates become accessible and stakeholders can better understand the choices shaping the continent. In doing so, they can help connect the communities that make the European project work.

    This is also the thinking behind our initiative to develop a media product dedicated to the business community. The aim is to create opportunities for organisations to communicate their priorities, strengthen their visibility and engage with the people and ideas shaping Europe’s economic future.

    But the ambition goes beyond communication. It is about building relationships between businesses and the wider European ecosystem, encouraging the exchange of ideas and helping organisations find common ground around shared challenges and opportunities.

    A competitive and prosperous Europe needs more than sound policies and strong institutions. It needs people and organisations willing to connect, cooperate and contribute. Media can help bring them together.

    Europe is still under construction. Let’s connect its Connectors

    To explore how we can connect your organisation with the people and ideas shaping Europe, contact us at connector@euobserver.com.

      <description><p>Meta says share sale will support its “continued investment in AI infrastructure and personal superintelligence”, as<a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/live/2026/oct/26/ai-cloud-computing-companies-guppy-level-death-elon-musk-stock-markets-dollar-oil-bond-yieds-latest-news-updates?page=with%3Ablock-6adef8968f08a448dcaddf6f#block-6adef8968f08a448dcaddf6f"> Elon Musk warns some AI cloud computing firms face ‘guppy-level death’</a></p><p><strong>UK government borrowing costs are dropping this morning, a welcome sign ahead of Wednesday’s budget.</strong></p><p>The yield (or interest rate) on 10 and 30-year UK gilts have both dropped by around three basis points (0.03 of a percentage point) this morning.</p><p>Issuing loans to public financial institutions creates a financial asset that offsets the increase in outstanding government debt. If the investments that the PuFins make generate sufficient returns for the PuFins to repay their government loans, then long term debt sustainability is little affected.</p><p>Limited transparency and the risk that the PuFins may suffer impairments on their investments will probably make bond market investors skeptical of the extra gilt issuance. Chancellor Healey should avoid a big increase in gilt issuance to fund such intra-public sector lending.</p><p>Nebius, CoreWeave and Iren were slammed in premarket trading on Monday after SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk said more than 200 neoclouds are “going to see guppy-level death and consolidation.”</p><p>That’s the guppy fish – prone to suddenly dying in household fisk tanks – not the GBPJPY FX cross...In a post on X Musk said “debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers”.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/live/2026/oct/26/ai-cloud-computing-companies-guppy-level-death-elon-musk-stock-markets-dollar-oil-bond-yieds-latest-news-updates">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Republican senator faces critical re-election battle in state where president’s trade war has outraged voters </p><p>Donald Trump dropped some of the US’s tariffs on Canada on Friday to “better serve the public interest” the White House said, handing a win to Susan Collins, the embattled Republican senator for Maine, as she faces a tight re-election campaign that will help determine whether Democrats can flip control of Congress.</p><p>Collins announced that the exemptions would apply to nine agricultural products, including blueberries, potatoes, apples and seaweed.       <title>The young Americans choosing Y2K cars over shiny new SUVs: ‘I get so much crap from people’</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/23/y2k-used-cars-gen-z</link>
      <description><p>People under 35 are hunting for no-frills rides they can pay for in cash and fix themselves – defying expectations to take on steep loans</p><p>Jack Price joined the marines in fall 2021 knowing he would need a car to get around base and that he couldn’t afford a new one. A joyless, month-long search through dealer classifieds and Facebook Marketplace listings ended when his mother spotted a 2010 Volkswagen Jetta posted on her office listserv by a co-worker moving abroad. With just 60,000 miles (96,560km) on the meter, the car (a manual!) was mechanically sound, and the air conditioning, sunroof and Bluetooth radio worked too. At $6,000, it was a steal. Price paid in cash.</p><p>Five years on, the Jetta, which he called the Pewter Pebble, is still carting him from A to B in unassuming style. “I’ve completely driven it into the ground,” says the 30-year-old, who lives in Los Angeles. “All over bases, cross-country a couple times, not really lovingly. I get so much crap from people, but not people my age.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/23/y2k-used-cars-gen-z">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/oct/15/food-delivery-apps-cost-economy</link>
      <description><p>As Americans use apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats more habitually, they confront the guilt of paying extra fees for convenience</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/what-is-your-personal-recession-indicator">Tell us: what is your personal ‘recession indicator’?</a></p></li></ul><p>When it comes to food, Caroline Bauldree does not like to “deprive” herself of anything. She does not like to cook either, so that means a lot of food deliveries. “If I want sushi, I’m getting sushi,” said the 24-year-old nanny, who lives in Raleigh, North Carolina. “I’m definitely lazy in that regard.”</p><p>Bauldree got into the habit of near-daily DoorDashing back in college. “I could order whatever food from whatever restaurant and it showed up at my door – that’s the dream,” she said. “But then I just feel like crap about myself because I’m like, ‘wow, I’m a lazy piece of shit.’ Nine times out of 10, I feel bad about myself.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/oct/15/food-delivery-apps-cost-economy">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comMon, 26 Oct 2026 14:27:55 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[AI firm Anthropic begins countdown to IPO with prospectus filing]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/10/26/anthropic-begins-countdown-to-ipo-with-prospectus-filing/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/10/26/anthropic-begins-countdown-to-ipo-with-prospectus-filing/Mon, 26 Oct 2026 13:54:20 +0000Anthropic has fired the starting gun on one of the largest-ever initial public offerings, unveiling its pitch for a listing that is set to be the biggest test so far of investor appetite for the artificial intelligence boom.

The developer of Claude published its highly anticipated prospectus on Monday, detailing for the first time how it plans to sustain the exponential growth that propelled the company from a $183 billion (€163.5 billion) valuation just over a year ago to $965 billion in its last private funding round in May.

The group recently told backers that its third-quarter revenue had jumped nearly 50 per cent on the previous three months to $16.8 billion and that the company was profitable on an adjusted basis.

The nearly 240,000-word prospectus showed that in the first half of the year, Anthropic’s net loss was $81 billion, with more than $72 billion related to changes in the value of convertible notes as the company’s valuation increased.

The bulk of the remaining losses come from a near-$9 billion outlay on computing power and infrastructure.

The document also said that Anthropic plans to aggressively increase its spending in the years to come, with commitments totalling close to $800 billion over the coming decade.

Goldman Sachs was listed as having secured the coveted “lead left” role in Anthropic’s IPO.

Anthropic’s founders said AI could “raise productivity across every sector of the economy” but also warned its models “have become better able to circumvent” systems designed to make sure they act as intended. It added that it has documented cases where models “manipulate or subvert” monitoring.

The company also pointed to risks stemming from a small number of high-value clients that account for a large slice of its revenues. While it noted that “no single customer” represented more than 10 per cent of its revenue in the nine months to September, Anthropic said that a quarter over the period came from its “top five” clients.

The San Francisco-based group is pressing ahead with the IPO at a critical juncture for the AI industry, as a furious debate rages over the safety of the technology and concerns grow over whether the increasingly debt-fuelled investment boom will pay off.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 has fallen just over 7 per cent from a record high touched on October 6th.

In a sign of the more testing backdrop, existing Anthropic investors expect the company to seek a valuation of between $1.5 trillion and $1.75 trillion. In August, several of Anthropic’s backers had said they expected the group to list at a valuation of $2 trillion or more.

In its prospectus, the company’s founders said the advice they had received from multiple partners was: “Never let your company be worth a dollar more than it is actually worth.”

The publication of the prospectus puts Anthropic on track to list after the US midterm elections on November 3rd, in which the benefits and costs of the AI boom have emerged as a central issue for voters, but before the Thanksgiving holiday on November 26th.

Disclosing the prospectus is likely to ease the nerves of investors who feared that Anthropic’s window to go public was rapidly closing. It is rare for companies to list between the Thanksgiving holiday and the end of the year.

Anthropic has emerged from the shadow of arch-rival rival OpenAI this year, surpassing the creator of ChatGPT in revenues and traction with business customers.

Anthropic was founded in 2021 by a group of seven former OpenAI researchers and engineers after they became disillusioned with the approach to AI safety at Sam Altman’s AI lab.

Chief executive Dario Amodei and other AI leaders including Altman and Elon Musk have called for a slowdown in AI research to ensure the technology does not run catastrophically out of control.

Investment banks including Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs will fix Anthropic’s valuation following conversations with investors over the coming weeks.

Anthropic said it would issue five different classes of shares, including Class T shares that would give its long-term benefit trust the right to appoint the majority of its board and class F stock that would hand its seven founders 50.1 per cent of the voting power. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

]]>Imen Ben Youssef<![CDATA[Pilot fatigue risk badly managed in Ireland, says international survey]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/26/pilot-fatigue-risk-badly-managed-in-ireland-says-international-survey/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/26/pilot-fatigue-risk-badly-managed-in-ireland-says-international-survey/Mon, 26 Oct 2026 13:59:05 +0000Trade unionists want greater Government and regulatory oversight of pilot fatigue after a survey showing the Irish air travel industry performs poorly relative to the rest of Europe in managing the problem.

European safety rules limit the hours that pilots can fly and allow them to stand down if they feel fatigued.

But most Irish pilots say the issue is poorly managed here while a significant number say they do not report fatigue to their employers as they fear “punishment” or “reprisals”, according to a survey by trade union group, the European Cockpit Association.

The Irish Airline Pilots’ Association (Ialpa) called for greater oversight of the issue in the Republic, in response to the survey.

Capt Nicola Hughes, the trade union’s international director, said Minister for Transport, Darragh O’Brien, should appoint employment inspectors to ensure that airlines comply with the law and allow pilots to exercise their safety responsibilities without fear of punitive consequences.

The report, which does not name any Irish airline, shows that 71.5 per cent of Irish pilots say fatigue risk is “not well managed” or “mostly not well managed”.

In the last such survey in 2023, the number was 61.7 per cent.

“Ireland is at or near the bottom across a range of critical fatigue-management and reporting measures, and in several areas the position has deteriorated rather than improved,” said Hughes.

]]>Michal Krakowiak<![CDATA[Whiskey distilleries attract over one million visitors, industry group says]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/26/whiskey-distilleries-attract-over-one-million-visitors-industry-group-says/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/26/whiskey-distilleries-attract-over-one-million-visitors-industry-group-says/Mon, 26 Oct 2026 13:32:47 +0000More than one million people visited whiskey distilleries across Ireland for the second year running, according to the Irish Whiskey Association (IWA), with tourists from the United States representing the largest national cohort.

The number is up 30,000 on the previous year, the industry group said. The 1,040,00 visitors between June 2025 and June 2026 spent approximately €50 per person on average, up around 20 per cent “as more visitors choose premium distillery experiences”, the IWA said.

The Jameson Distillery in Dublin city centre remains the most popular whiskey visitor centres followed by the Old Bushmills Distillery in Co Antrim and the Teeling Whiskey Distillery, also in Dublin city centre, according to the IWA. The Midleton Distillery Experience in Co Cork and Leitrim’s Shed Distillery, where numbers jumped 20 per cent, were also popular with visitors.

“Distillery experiences and visitor centres have become an established part of Ireland’s tourism offering” the findings from its annual survey confirm, the association said, with numbers and spending outpacing general growth in the tourism sector.

“Distilleries are drawing people interested in Ireland’s heritage, culture and craftsmanship, as well as those seeking a tasting experience”, the IWA added, noting over a third of sightseers do not consume alcohol during their visit.

Irish people represented the second highest nationality among distillery visitors after Americans, followed by Britons, Germans and French.

“Reaching one million visitors for the second year in a row shows that Irish whiskey tourism has real staying power, and that is down to the innovation and resilience of our distilleries and visitor centres,” said Eoin Ó Catháin, director of the Irish Whiskey Association.

“Visitors are spending more and travelling further, bringing that value into rural communities across the island,” he said. “Since we launched the Irish Whiskey Way last November, it has given visitors a new way to discover our distilleries”.

“With continued support from Government, State agencies and our tourism partners, Irish Whiskey can play an even bigger role in growing tourism in every region of Ireland,” Ó Catháin said.

The IWA promotes an Irish Whiskey Way, a route of 28 distilleries open to visitors across Ireland, divided into five separate regions.

]]>ArtistGNDphotography<![CDATA[Meta plans $95bn stock offering to bankroll AI expansion]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/26/meta-plans-95bn-stock-offering-to-bankroll-ai-expansion/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/26/meta-plans-95bn-stock-offering-to-bankroll-ai-expansion/Mon, 26 Oct 2026 11:47:03 +0000Meta is planning to raise $95 Billion (€85 billion) in a stock offering to fuel its massive artificial intelligence infrastructure spending, backed by chipmakers Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom, who will act as cornerstone investors.

The parent of Instagram and WhatsApp last week reported a 26 per cent jump in sales in the third quarter, ahead of analysts’ estimates, and projected capital spending of up to $145 billion this year, as it warned investors it would need to raise “hundreds of billions of dollars” over several years to fund its bet on AI.

The news sent shares in Mark Zuckerberg’s social media group tumbling by 7 per cent on Thursday.

Meta kicked off that fundraising process on Monday with a plan to raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings. It also plans to raise a further $60 billion via an “at the market” programme.

“AI is creating significant opportunities for Meta across its core business and new products and services,” the Silicon Valley company said. “Meta’s AI investments are already generating tangible returns through increased engagement, improved advertising performance and increased monetisation.” – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

]]>Minh Connors<![CDATA[Half of consumers use Revolut app, with 6% indicating option as main banking account]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/26/half-of-consumers-use-revolut-app-with-6-indicating-option-as-main-banking-account/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/26/half-of-consumers-use-revolut-app-with-6-indicating-option-as-main-banking-account/Mon, 26 Oct 2026 00:01:00 +0000Almost half of consumers in the Republic now hold an account with online bank Revolut, the latest annual survey of banking practice and sentiment has found.

Revolut continues to grow strongly in the market here. Moreover, there is evidence that a growing number of consumers now see it as something more than a money transfer app.

The Consumer Sentiment Banking Survey for 2026 found that 48 per cent of consumers hold an account with Revolut, up from 43 per cent in 2025. While most still use it to transfer money, 6 per cent identified it as their main account, up from 3 per cent the previous year.

Revolut’s outage was a warning to us all

Tánaiste Simon Harris said the survey exposed a “striking gap” between savings and investment.

It found that 77 per cent of Irish consumers hold savings accounts, but only 3 per cent have an investment account.

“We are a nation of savers, but far too few people see investing as an option for them.”

Harris has plans to introduce a new investment account next year that will encourage consumers to switch from saving to investing. The scheme will have no minimum contribution and a tax-free threshold of €50,000.

One in five of all shoppers still pay for goods in cash, a figure that has stayed constant, the survey said.

However, the use of contactless smartphone as a payment method has risen sharply. Its use has increased from 27 per cent in 2025 to 35 per cent in 2025. The use of cards for contactless payments is falling.

There has been consistency in the habits of consumers with other financial products. Nearly all consumers hold a current account, while 77 per cent have a savings account and 25 per cent hold a mortgage account.

There has been a slight drop in the number of people who have credit cards, down from 37 per cent in 2025 to 35 per cent in 2026.

Credit unions also remain popular, with a third of all consumers holding an account. However, only 3 per cent of people said that their main banking account is with a credit union.

In new findings, one in five reported that they have used artificial intelligence (AI) to obtain information or advice on financial services. There are striking generational differences in attitudes, with younger consumers the primary users of AI.

]]>NejauPhoto<![CDATA[Jones Engineering eyes record €1.9bn turnover on back of data centre boom]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/26/jones-engineering-eyes-record-29bn-turnover-on-back-of-data-centre-boom/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/26/jones-engineering-eyes-record-29bn-turnover-on-back-of-data-centre-boom/Mon, 26 Oct 2026 06:00:00 +0000Dublin-headquartered Jones Engineering expects to achieve a record €1.9 billion turnover this year as it capitalises on the boom in data centre development.

According to its most recently filed accounts, the company generated a turnover of €1.6 billion in 2025, up from €1.28 billion the previous year.

Operating profits rose by 65 per cent to €170 million, giving the business a margin of 10.6 per cent.

“The results reflect the continued growth and diversification of the business, with international operations making an increasingly important contribution to overall performance,” it said.

The company, which specialises in building large-scale engineering projects for the tech and life sciences sectors, said the momentum had continued into 2026, “with turnover projected to exceed €1.9 billion, supported by a strong pipeline of work extending into 2027 and beyond”.

The company generates more than half of its revenue from overseas.

In the accounts, the directors note the company faces inflation pressures associated with macroeconomic conditions.

]]>KIRAN RIDLEY<![CDATA[Across-the-board pay rise will do little to help fill key public sector posts]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/26/across-the-board-pay-rise-will-do-little-to-help-fill-key-public-sector-posts/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/26/across-the-board-pay-rise-will-do-little-to-help-fill-key-public-sector-posts/Mon, 26 Oct 2026 05:38:00 +0000

Until the early 1970s, the Civil Service was a very traditional organisation that had changed little over time. There was limited movement between departments, and almost none between the public sector and the private sector.

Most people joined straight after school, there were few graduates, although many ambitious civil servants, like TK Whitaker, studied for a degree at night. Unless they were women who married [and who were effectively fired as a result], civil servants were likely to stay until they retired. Men progressed slowly through the ranks, based on seniority.

My first boss in the Department of Finance told me that when he joined it in the 1950s, he had calculated, based on the seniority rule and his colleagues’ ages, that he would spend most of his career as an assistant principal before, in the final three years before retirement, being promoted in rapid succession as a principal officer and then assistant secretary. In the event, he served as secretary general of the department for seven years.

Joining the EU meant quite a number of Irish civil servants left to work for the European Commission. The marriage bar ended in July 1973. Gradually, other reforms led to much more fluid movement across the public service.

The wider public service included graduate roles such as secondary teachers, doctors and local-authority engineers. While less than a third of public servants held third-level qualifications in 1970, those who did constituted more than half of the Irish graduate workforce.

All of this made public sector employment rather different from that in the private sector, with limited parallels in terms of pay. To a large extent, public and private sector employers were not competing to attract the same workers.

The advent of mass third level education in Ireland changed things. Few now enter the public sector straight from school. Primary teachers and nurses now have graduate qualifications. Today, three quarters of public sector workers have a third level qualification, but only constitute a third of graduate workers.

There is also greater choice, and substantial movement, between jobs in the public and private sectors. The security of a public sector job does not have the same allure when there is full employment. So the State as an employer needs to compete to attract and retain talent. That means the public sector must pay competitive rates, or some of the most able and ambitious teachers, civil servants, nurses or physiotherapists will seek better pay elsewhere.

Are public sector workers all as badly off as strikes might suggest? This is what the data says

In the run-up to the 2008 economic crash, average pay in the public sector had reached 50 per cent more than in the private sector – an excessive gap.

Following the collapse in the public finances, all public sector workers experienced painful cuts in pay. Over the subsequent decade, public service pay rose more slowly than the private sector. However, over the past few years the relationship has stabilised.

Public service workers are paid, on average, about 30 per cent more than the private sector, but this largely reflects their higher average qualifications.

The Government now needs to deliver a pay increase for public service workers, not because prices are higher but because most other workers are seeing their pay rise. Failure to keep pace with the private sector would see skilled employees leave.

The Department of Finance forecast that average pay across the economy will rise by around 4 per cent this year and next. The budget arithmetic provided for a 3 per cent public pay rise next year, so any higher pay deal will need additional funding.

The expected rise in private sector pay sets a guideline for any public sector pay agreement. If public sector workers are offered significantly more, that could push up taxes, and have knock-on effects on other pay. But if offered significantly less than their private sector counterparts, there could be an exodus of skilled staff for better pay elsewhere.

A public pay deal will be done – and here’s what it will look like

While this sounds fairly straightforward, things are, of course, more complex. Private sector pay deals are generally contingent on increased productivity. That, too, should be the case in the public sector.

Across-the-board pay increases in the public sector won’t address what’s needed to attract workers to some key areas where posts have been hard to fill – in the Naval Service, in special care, in some IT roles.

While a private employer would simply pay more, public pay agreements cannot easily handle such differentiation, but need to find a way to do so. The alternative of filling key roles by outsourcing to consultants is not an ideal one.

]]>Chris Maddaloni<![CDATA[With EU presidency, Ireland has chance to implement digital identity wallet by end of year ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/26/with-eu-presidency-ireland-has-chance-to-implement-digital-identity-wallet-by-end-of-year/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/26/with-eu-presidency-ireland-has-chance-to-implement-digital-identity-wallet-by-end-of-year/Mon, 26 Oct 2026 05:27:00 +0000The priorities for Ireland’s presidency of the Council of the EU have been wide in scope across various sections of society, different sectors within the economy, along with competing national or common interests.

Some of those will resolve in due course under the current term, while many will either stall or progress as it passes onto Lithuania and then Greece through 2027.

One long-standing objective and policy priority that falls directly during our watch is the provision for an EU Digital Identity Wallet for all citizens and businesses by December of this year.

This is part of the wider Digital Decade Policy Programme (DDPP), which is the EU’s framework for achieving digital transformation by the end of the decade.

It includes targets in relation to digital skills, digital infrastructure, the digitalisation of businesses, and access to digital public services.

That last (but not least) area essentially involves all key public services being available online with citizens’ digital identity and ability to access services working seamlessly throughout the EU.

The practical applications are complex but the “only once” principle applies throughout, where citizens should not be repeatedly asked by governments or multiple agencies for information already available.

With progress being made on all fronts to various degrees, this is now a defining period for Ireland to help push the digital public services agenda forward for citizens, businesses and State services. Interoperable data should flow freely enough to support everything from mortgage approvals to healthcare records and planning applications.

The main challenge is one that often falls on European or cross-border projects. It comes down to collective co-ordination and consensus. Twenty-seven member states, with as many starting points, governance structures, all building toward the same targets along separate paths that sometimes fail to intersect.

The issues to be resolved don’t solely lie within policy, legal or technological constraints. It is often social where the connectivity falls down. How do people, who each hold a piece of a public problem, find one another, build trust, and produce outcomes that outlast a ministerial photocall or presidential term? The EU and the Irish Government have invested heavily in the building blocks that are needed for this journey. The digital identity wallets, data spaces and cloud platforms already exist.

What is missing is the right people coming together from different corners, knowing how to assemble these blocks in the right way.

Practitioners who have the ability and mindset to move between a Brussels regulation and a rural county council’s operating reality, without treating the two as separate jobs.

Ireland’s role in this during its EU presidency is reflected in a new initiative that will gather the necessary stakeholders to generate those collective solutions for the next phase of Europe’s digital public services roadmap.

To break the roadblocks and unlock the capabilities that can advance these future services, we need to first go back though to an age-old practice. Before internet technology, quantum computing or artificial intelligence were even imagined, Ireland had meitheal.

This was among our oldest social networks and was based on reciprocity, trust and shared responsibilities. Its approach was replicated in similiar forms in different countries: Norway’s dugnad, Finland’s talkoot, Lithuania’s talka, Hungary’s kaláka and the Balkan moba.

Each European tradition reflects the same civic principle that complex problems can be solved when communities pool effort, skills and responsibility. It activated to do work that no single person or household could manage alone.

The main rule being that help given would be returned. This created a social infrastructure and self-enforcing system for dedicating skills exactly when and where they were needed. That practice and principle may be what is needed now to push forward on Ireland and Europe’s digital public services programme.

On November 19th and 20th, Ireland will hold the first Meitheal Digiteach that will bring policy makers, community groups, data designers, delivery practitioners, architects and engineers into the same room to work through the shared challenges, while looking to create practical solutions and connect the diverging tracks on the new Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) rails.

The gathering will not work like a regular conference with the usual panel discussions, keynote addresses and firesides or roundtables. This will be a hands-on exercise for participants with no hierarchy and no spectators.

It is due to be held at a fitting location within the Drogheda Civic Offices which, since its relatively recent refurbishment, now represents a suitable blend of heritage with modern design and functionality. The call is for like-minded citizens and groups to get involved in building the next level of digital public services.

I’d encourage all who have a role to play to join us, as Ireland’s meitheal provides a mechanism that can be passed on to the next custodians of the EU presidency and the subsequent phases of our shared digital public services programme.

Gar Mac Críosta is digital advisor strategy & architecture at the HSE, and co-founder of Meitheal Digiteach 2026

]]>Marc O'Sullivan<![CDATA[What my most embarrassing job interview taught me]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/26/what-my-most-embarrassing-job-interview-taught-me/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/26/what-my-most-embarrassing-job-interview-taught-me/Mon, 26 Oct 2026 05:24:00 +0000The other day, I was chatting with a friend about how we got into journalism when I suddenly remembered my most disastrously embarrassing job interview.

It happened years ago, not long after I arrived in London and spotted an ad for a deputy news magazine editor. The advert was highly detailed. Applicants had to send in an assessment of the publication outlining what worked and what did not, along with compelling cover story ideas.

Having recently edited a national news magazine in Australia, I was full of thoughts. But there was one question in the advert that stumped me. What was my preferred salary?

I asked two other journalists I knew in London, both men, for advice. Each told me to ask for what I had been paid in Sydney, plus more for the abysmal exchange rate and the cost of living in London, which I did.

To my delight, I got an interview. A team of people politely listened as I went on about their magazine, whose editor then took me off to a side room for a further chat. He loved my application, he said, but there was just one thing. How wedded was I to that salary I had mentioned? “Because it’s a lot more than what I’m paid.”

At the time, I was mortified. My face burned. What an idiot I had been to name such an outlandish figure. Why hadn’t I done a better job of researching the going rate for deputy magazine editors?

Today, though, I recall that moment fondly. Women are always being told they cement the gender pay gap by asking for too little in pay negotiations, and there was my younger self, gormlessly doing the opposite.

I also think of how much easier it would have been if that advert had simply listed the salary on offer. That way, I would have known if it was worth my while to apply and everyone else, inside and outside the magazine, would have had a better idea of whether their pay was fair, or if they should demand more. This is, of course, precisely why so many employers do not spell out salaries in public.

For similar reasons, job hunters are often asked to disclose their salary history, even though this is an excellent way to bake in the lower pay endured by so many women, ethnic minorities and others.

Workplace conflict is said to be costing Irish firms €239m annually. What can be done about it?

It’s tough to ask for £50,000 for a job, no matter how well qualified you are, if you have just revealed your last role paid £35,000, which it might have if you had been doing the same work at, say, a charity.

Women were told for years to just “lean in” and become savvier negotiators. Thankfully, this approach is fading as research shows the benefits of policies aimed at fixing the practice of negotiations, instead of fixing the women.

This is why the EU has brought in a directive requiring employers to do two things: tell job seekers about starting salaries or pay ranges, and stop asking them about their pay histories. A number of US states already have such measures, which can help to shrink a gender wage gap that averaged 11 per cent across OECD countries in 2023.

The deadline to put the EU directive into national law was June 2026, but unfortunately many countries have yet to get there. They include Germany, the bloc’s largest economy, where Indeed data shows that less than 15 per cent of job advertisements include explicit pay information. That number plunges for sectors such as banking and finance, which typically have far worse gender pay gaps.

No wonder thousands of women are supporting outfits such as Female X Finance, a five-year-old start-up that aims to help boost women’s careers in the financial industry. Its Dutch co-founders just published their second annual survey of the salaries – and bonuses – being paid in investment banking, M&A, private equity and other fields in the UK and the Netherlands.

HR bosses predict AI will not cause ‘significant reduction’ in employee numbers

How I wish this type of information, and those pay transparency laws, had been around when I answered that magazine advert all those years ago.

If you’re wondering, I never did get the job. It went to an insider, which is probably just as well. I’m sure they did a far better job than I would have done, but I would still like to know how much they were paid. – The Financial Times

It appears to be an uphill battle for Ireland to reach the heights of trilingualism, but Mavric is optimistic.

“For me, language is always linked to an identity, to a culture, and that’s why it’s so important to include language as the conditions for the European Union, for the European project. Languages, as part of our lives in Europe, are here to stay.”

]]><![CDATA[Trump is about to discover the political cost of inflation]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/23/trump-is-about-to-discover-the-political-cost-of-inflation/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/23/trump-is-about-to-discover-the-political-cost-of-inflation/Fri, 23 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000The great slayer of political careers – inflation – has come for Donald Trump.

The irony is that it won’t be the racist rhetoric, his role in the Capitol riots, or the self-sabotaging tariffs that remove the Teflon, but something entirely more mundane: gas prices.

They have averaged over $4 a gallon for a record 169 days, a timeline that runs concurrent with the Iran war. The average cost of gas in California, the most expensive state, has been over $6 since late September.

Car ownership is a necessity in many parts of the US, with motorists spending on average two-thirds more on fuel than their European counterparts. That’s why fuel costs are such a flashpoint.

The country’s 196,000 gas stations and their price billboards serve as a daily reminder of Trump’s failed war aims, a political burden he now carries into the midterm elections. Polls suggest he will lose big.

US and Israel draw up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after midterm elections

The latest Reuters/Ipsos survey indicates Trump’s approval rating has fallen to a record low of 31 per cent. It was 44 per cent at the same point in his first term.

More worrying for Trump’s avowedly pro-business administration is that more than two-thirds (68 per cent) of voters disapprove of his handling of the economy, including 37 per cent of republicans.

Asked which party they would vote ⁠for if the elections were held today, some ​47 per cent of registered voters chose Democrats, while 35 per cent chose republicans.

The 12-point advantage in favour of Democrats ​is the widest in the current election cycle and could, if translated into actual votes, see the Democrats seize control of both houses, the House of Representatives and the Senate.

What are the US midterms? A visual guide

This would hobble Trump’s presidency as Democrats would be in a position to block cabinet and judicial appointments while having subpoena powers to investigate the administration.

The top Democrat on the House oversight committee, Robert Garcia of California, says he will prioritise the examination of Trump’s family businesses, the Epstein files, immigration enforcement, corporate profiteering, and how US health secretary Robert Kennedy jnr has handled vaccines.

US inflation accelerated to 3.7 per cent (in annual terms) in September, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. This was faster than the annual growth in wages (3 per cent), meaning real wages are falling.

Trump’s big mistake has been to dismiss this marker or at least be insensitive to it, repeatedly telling voters that the economy is great and that they’ve never had it so good.

“We have the hottest country anywhere in the world,” he repeatedly says at rallies.

To be fair, the US economy is faring better than many had predicted in the wake of his sweeping “Liberation Day” tariffs in 2025. Unemployment has been at or below 4.5 per cent for 60 consecutive months, a postwar record. Consumer spending remains solid while business investment is being fuelled by the AI boom.

But Trump is falling into the same trap as his predecessor, Joe Biden, in talking up the macroeconomy when consumers and households are being screwed by the micro one: prices.

Jame Carville’s’s famous maxim, “It’s the economy, stupid”, might need to be refined to “It’s the price economy, stupid”, to highlight what matters most to voters in the 2020s.

The Irish Government has learned not to make political capital out of its turbocharged GDP numbers or its windfall taxes, as it only antagonises households in the grip of a price squeeze.

But Trump can’t help himself.

US inflation peaked at 9 per cent in June 2022 as the reopening of the economy after the pandemic led to a burst in price growth. A year later it had fallen to 3.1 per cent and by Trump’s election win in November 2024, it was down to 2.6 per cent. It had been expected to fall to the Federal Reserve’s target rate of 2 per cent by the end of 2025, paving the way for growth-affirming interest rate cuts.

But Trump destroyed that trajectory by imposing tariffs on imported goods. Inflation stopped falling and started to rise again, hitting 3 per cent in September 2025.

Even with the tariffs, US inflation would probably have slowed again this year if the US leader hadn’t gone to war with Iran, triggering a spike in global oil prices.

This has not just driven up petrol prices but also the cost of diesel, the fuel needed to transport everything.

The full ramifications of Trump’s war can be seen through the prism of producer prices, which surged by 6.3 per cent in September. This will translate into further consumer price inflation in the coming months.

High inflation is also resulting in upward pressure on interest rates, further anchoring household spending and Trump’s poll ratings.

Trump’s political shtick has always been to proclaim everything he touches gold. It won’t wash this time.

]]>Jacquelyn Martin<![CDATA[What limits apply to the new personal investment accounts? ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/25/what-limits-apply-to-the-new-personal-investment-accounts/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/25/what-limits-apply-to-the-new-personal-investment-accounts/Sun, 25 Oct 2026 10:00:00 +0000The Finance Bill published last week puts further detail on and provides legislative underpinning for the new personal investment accounts. So we are taking the chance this week to run through in a quick-fire style a series of recent readers’ questions on various aspects of the personal investment account scheme as providers start working on the shape of products that they will offer under the scheme.

As a non-resident Irish citizen but with a PPSN, can I invest in the proposed investment scheme?

BP

No, you cannot open an account unless you are over 18, resident in the State and hold a PPS number. The fact that you are an Irish citizen is irrelevant. And if someone opens an account and subsequently moves outside the State, they can no longer contribute to the account during any period when they are non-resident.

Money you would put in the investment scheme would be money you had likely already paid tax on (maybe at 52 per cent or 55 per cent if you are self employed). Why should this money be taxed again? It makes more sense to tax gain, not original contributions. It isn’t like you are getting a tax credit or deduction with your contributions. This investment scheme doesn’t make sense to me. You could actually lose money and yet still pay the 1 per cent tax.

AM

Taxing money you have already paid tax on is nothing new in Ireland or other jurisdictions – think VAT, excise on petrol and even customs duty on online shopping outside the EU. Or deposit interest retention tax (Dirt), capital gains tax and exit tax on savings and investments.

You are certainly correct that you could be taxed at 1 per cent on part of your fund even if it makes a loss in a given year, as long as its balance exceeds €50,000. That is the outcome of the Government decision to follow the Swedish model for such investments rather than the UK individual savings account model. I can only assume that was done (a) for simplicity and (b) to allow the Government set the tax rate at as low an advertised figure as possible.

Can I invest overseas in the new scheme?

RW

You can as long as it is through an investment account provider registered with Revenue for the purposes of providing these accounts. A register will be available as the scheme gets up and running. What investments they offer and in which markets remains to be seen.

My wife and I will have approx €60k to deposit in the investment scheme next July. Are we limited to a total of €12,000 deposited annually or could we both take out a separate plan to let us deposit €24,000 during the year?

BN

You are each limited to contributions of up to €12,000 in any tax year. You cannot hold a joint account but you can each hold an account, allowing you to invest €24,000 between you.

First-time buyers account for almost two-thirds of Irish mortgage transactions

Can I transfer my existing vanguard ETF to this investment account (new one) without any tax if it’s less than €12k threshold? Or should I sell this and transfer?

AP

This has cropped up a few times. The purpose of the new personal investment account is to encourage new investment by people of savings largely held in deposit accounts.

There is nothing to stop you moving money from an existing investment – such as your Vanguard ETF – to one of these new accounts as long as you stay within the contribution limits but each will be treated on a stand-alone basis so you will have to settle any tax due on the Vanguard investment before lodging the money to one of the new accounts.

In sum, no, you will not be able to avoid existing tax liabilities on an investment simply by transferring it to one of the personal investment accounts.

Am I reading the rules wrong, or could investors do the following: build up gains under the €50k limit and when nearing it, withdrawing some funds (free of CGT). Rinse and repeat, like making bread from a sourdough starter?

BL

As long as the balance of the account stays below €50,000, no tax is due. The account provider will be obliged to keep tabs on the account balance each day over the course of the year and if the balance exceeds it on any day, the account starts being liable for tax.

But as long as the particular investment is liquid enough, there is nothing to stop you withdrawing funds from the accounts on occasion as you approach the limit to avoid tax, although you obviously are limiting your potential investment gains.

Tech sell-off deepens, dents rate hike bets

Will dividend income within the personal investment account be tax free (up to €50k value), can you move existing investments to the new account without triggering a taxable event and finally will you be able to fully choose your own investments or will a fund manager do it for you?

OC

Dividend income on investments within the new personal investment account will be tax free subject, as you say, to the €50,000 tax free balance. Transfers from other investments will trigger any tax provisions attaching to those investments as stated above. You will be able to choose from the investment options offered by one or other fund provider. We don’t yet know how much flexibility that will offer though we do know that you will not be able to get interest in any uninvested cash held in your account.

Is there any age limit to the investment scheme? Myself and my wife plan to set up an account in each of my two kids’ names (ages 16 and 12). We want to fund this by the two of us giving them €3,000 each (€6,000 per child) as this is the limit of the small gift exemption. Is there anything preventing us from doing this and what, if any, tax liabilities apply?

GOC

There is an age limit and neither of your children will be eligible for at least a couple of years. No one under the age of 18 can hold one of these new accounts. You, as an adult, cannot open one in the name of your child and you cannot hold more than one account. However, you and your wife can each open an account in each individual’s name.

]]><![CDATA[Musk won his battle with Swedish union but it is still business as usual]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/big-tech/2026/10/25/musk-won-his-battle-with-swedish-union-but-it-is-still-business-as-usual/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/big-tech/2026/10/25/musk-won-his-battle-with-swedish-union-but-it-is-still-business-as-usual/Sun, 25 Oct 2026 08:00:00 +0000One of my bugbears about journalists – myself included – is that we tend to pile into stories when they first develop, explain why they matter, then forget about them and move on to the next new thing. But there is value in paying attention to how stories end.

Take, for example, the battle that broke out three years ago between Elon Musk and Sweden’s trade union movement. In 2023, a group of Tesla mechanics in Sweden went on strike over their employer’s refusal to sign a collective agreement with their union, IF Metall.

Other unions joined in. They halted postal deliveries, waste collection and the unloading of cars at ports.

The stakes were high. Musk did not want to set a precedent that he would recognise unions anywhere. And Sweden’s trade unions did not want to allow Tesla to undermine the country’s labour market model, in which government regulation takes a back seat and employers and unions negotiate the rules between themselves.

Journalists flocked to cover it. Musk called it “insane”. But how did it end?

Musk won. This summer, IF Metall announced that it was calling off the strike after more than 1,000 days because Tesla had bought out all the striking members.

“Without workers on strike, there is no strike,” said Veli-Pekka Säikkälä, the collective bargaining secretary at LO, the Swedish trade union confederation, in a statement at the time.

What does it mean that Musk was victorious? For the global labour movement – and indeed anyone with ambitions to curb the power of the tech titans of our age – it is hardly encouraging that even one of the strongest trade union movements in the world could not force Tesla to the table.

After all, the Swedish unions have high membership levels, deep pockets and a supportive institutional set-up, all things that elude unions in many other countries.

In the US, for example, trade unions thought they had secured a historic victory in 2022 when workers in an Amazon warehouse in Staten Island voted to form a union. But more than four years later, Amazon has still not even negotiated a contract.

But while the “Swedish model” could not break Musk, it does not seem as if Musk has broken the Swedish model either. Although trade union officials did worry that Tesla could be the thin end of the wedge, those I spoke to on a recent visit to Stockholm took some solace from the fact that they have continued to sign collective agreements with other companies, including with tech firms that will help to shape the future of the economy.

After a year of negotiations, for example, including a strike threat, video games company King (maker of Candy Crush) signed a collective agreement with Swedish unions last month.

“The Tesla strike is important because it’s an emblematic company in the green transition – at least it was,” German Bender of the think tank Arena Idé, who wrote a book on the conflict, tells me. “But the strike ended, the union lost, and the Swedish model hasn’t crumbled.”

What if the strike had gone the other way and Musk had been the one to lose? Entering into the Swedish way of doing things could have given him an insight into a very different type of trade unionism from the American style he knows and dislikes.

Although they have become known in recent years for their fight with Tesla, in fact, Sweden has the most pro-technology trade unionists I have come across.

Susan Schurman, professor of labour studies and employment relations at Rutgers University, says that Nordic unions in general understand that it is vital for employers to remain competitive in export-led economies.

“They don’t focus on restraining technology; they focus on: ‘How do we incorporate this in a way that will help our companies remain competitive and make sure our members get their fair share of the profits?’” she tells me. “American unions have not historically thought this way.”

Indeed, the Nordic region’s powerful unions have hardly held companies back on implementing the latest tech. Sweden has been called the Silicon Valley of Europe because of its high number of start-ups.

Meanwhile, the percentage of businesses that have adopted artificial intelligence is higher in Denmark, Finland and Sweden than any other country in the OECD’s database – and well in excess of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development average.

As one Swedish trade unionist put it to me: “We don’t fear new technology. We fear old technology.” A sentiment with which Musk – were he willing to listen – would probably agree. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

Yet, while equities recovered from their midsummer malaise, tech stocks came under significant renewed selling pressure in a volatile session on Friday. International investors give Ireland the thumbs up, ignoring corporate tax warnings

Once again, there is no one reason for the sell-off, which may yet prove to be short-lived. Factors also vary by region. In Europe, for example, France’s ongoing political uncertainty is heaping pressure on the country’s stocks.

At a higher level, the surge in global crude oil prices on Friday to their highest level since April is also causing significant anxiety. With the Trump administration threatening to ramp up strikes on Iran after next month’s midterm elections and Saudi Arabia being rattled by Houthi military activity in Yemen, there is a growing sense that energy prices could remain higher for longer, with long-term consequences for economic growth.

AI bubble? Nvidia is now bigger than Japan

Clary<![CDATA[‘Your best friend on the Cayman Islands is someone who owns a boat’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/25/your-best-friend-in-cayman-is-someone-who-owns-a-boat/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/25/your-best-friend-in-cayman-is-someone-who-owns-a-boat/Sun, 25 Oct 2026 05:58:00 +0000The Cayman Islands hold many attractions for young Irish professionals, especially those with legal or financial backgrounds. Apart from being a big centre for financial services, its sunny climate, world class beaches and tax-free status have seen a surge in Irish people spending time working there in recent decades.

Many move on after a few years, making some tidy money along the way, but for an increasing number of people, Cayman is becoming a more permanent home.

When the opportunity to work in Grand Cayman came for Pádraig Brosnan around 15 years ago, the young Wexford-born lawyer jumped at the chance. Like many, the newly-married Brosnan and his wife Anita, also a lawyer, saw Cayman as an opportunity to build a nest-egg while furthering their careers in a very different part of the world.

What was to have been a transitory experience has proved anything but as the couple are now raising their young family in Cayman and enjoying everything it has to offer.

“It was everything it was cracked up to be,” he says, recalling being picked up at the airport in a limo when the couple arrived. They were soon settled in accommodation at the edge of the famous Seven Mile Beach and felt that they had arrived in paradise.

“The picture you would have of the beaches, the boats and being out on the water –if you want that life, it’s there for you. I still remember that day we first arrived. There were three couples and a single woman on that flight coming to work here. All of us are still on the island, which I think says a lot.”

What brought them there was Maples Group, a Cayman-island founded law and professional services firm with offices in Dublin, among other global locations. Brosnan followed his boss to their newly-established Dublin office in 2006 having started his career at A&L Goodbody.

When the opportunity to set up an Irish funds desk in Cayman came up, the couple felt the timing was right to try something different, with Anita also securing a position at the firm.

Sun and sand of the Cayman Islands proved too powerful a lure for an accountant in cold and wet Cork

Brosnan is now a partner specialising in financial services law and leads the Maples Group’s Irish team in the Cayman Islands, which is the world’s largest investment funds hub. Working with big international asset managers and financial institutions, he advises on the launch, regulation, and ongoing operation of investment structures across multiple jurisdictions.

His practice also extends to advising fund administrators, depositaries, prime brokers, investment advisers, and boards on Irish regulatory and governance matters.

While Cayman is home, Brosnan’s role involves a lot of travel, especially to North America. “On one of my last trips, I was on the 92nd floor of a building overlooking the Hudson River in New York. It still astonishes me that I’m there helping these massive-named managers and global law firms helping them structure massive deals. I still get a massive thrill from that.”

On Cayman, the family has a busy life. “We have four kids under 12, two boys and two girls, so life is pretty full on at the moment. Thankfully, I’m only a four-minute drive from work which is very convenient. While the island is very small, I need to be out the door by 7am otherwise the traffic can get very heavy. I work until 6pm or later but I get home at lunchtime when I’m here.”

“The sun comes up around 6am and goes down early evening all year round. There are no seasons like we would be used to at home so that makes the time fly by. It gets very warm in the summer, and a lot of people go back to where they are from. Christmas time, the weather is at its best and a lot of people visit,” he explains.

While the climate is good, Cayman is still prone to hurricanes and tropical storms. “It was before our time here, but people still talk about Hurricane Ivan which hurt the island badly in 2004, causing huge damage,” he says.

Brosnan says that while the Cayman Islands was always prosperous relative to its neighbours, it is currently going through a Celtic Tiger boom with many new high-end hotels and private residences being built in recent years.

There is a well-established group of expat Irish on the island now, supporting a GAA club which fields multiple teams. Brosnan is active in the club, still playing Gaelic football, as well as soccer, and coaches junior teams. The family also enjoy life on the water. “Your best friend in Cayman is someone who owns a boat,” he says.

The family are well-settled now, and Brosnan says he cannot foresee a move back to Ireland anytime soon though he does not rule it out in the longer term. They make visits to Ireland twice a year typically.

“We’ve been away a long time at this stage, and you do miss friends and family, so we try to catch up with as many people as possible on these trips. WhatsApp is great but it’s not the same as sitting down and having a pint with someone.”

]]><![CDATA[Have Berkshire Hathaway investors really moved on from Warren Buffett?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/25/have-berkshire-hathaway-investors-really-moved-on-from-warren-buffett/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/25/have-berkshire-hathaway-investors-really-moved-on-from-warren-buffett/Sun, 25 Oct 2026 05:47:00 +0000Berkshire Hathaway shares have hit record highs, prompting a Bloomberg headline that investors have “moved on” from Warren Buffett (disclosure: I own shares in Berkshire).

But have they really?

Shares have certainly had a good run, hitting their first all-time high since May 2nd, 2025, the day before Buffett announced he was stepping down.

The rise has been rapid, with Berkshire going on a 10-day winning streak, its first since 2018. The gains came as nerves over the AI trade rattled semiconductor stocks, with Berkshire outperforming the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index by 22 percentage points in little over a fortnight.

That’s an impressive level of outperformance, but it doesn’t change the bigger picture. Since Buffett announced his impending departure 17 months ago, Berkshire shares have been essentially flat, whereas the S&P 500 advanced some 35 per cent.

The valuation story is similarly revealing. Immediately before Buffett’s announcement, Berkshire traded at about 1.8 times book value, well above its historical norm of roughly 1.4-1.5 times.

That looked generous even with Buffett still in charge. The subsequent sell-off wrung out that excess, with Berkshire trading at 1.55 times book value at the end of 2025. By March 2026 it had slipped further, to about 1.45, and it remains around that level today.

The recent rally, then, doesn’t so much suggest new-found confidence in Buffett’s successor, Greg Abel, as it does a flight to safety amid growing nerves over AI.

In fairness to Abel, nor do the figures amount to a vote of no confidence. However, if investors once paid a premium for Buffett himself, that premium is difficult to discern today.

]]>Dan Brouillette

   <description>Anlässlich des Nationalfeiertags sind am Montag auf dem Wiener Heldenplatz über 1.000 Rekrutinnen und Rekruten angelobt worden. <item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3446171/">
   <title>Studentenliste feiert Wahlsieg in Serbien</title>
   <description>Die Serbinnen und Serben haben am Sonntag ihren langjährigen Machthaber Aleksandar Vucic abgewählt. Die Studentenliste, die ihn herausgefordert hatte, erreichte laut unabhängigen Wahlbeobachtern eine absolute Mehrheit. Die Wahlbeteiligung war so hoch wie noch nie seit dem Zerfall Jugoslawiens im Jahr 1992. Vucic gestand noch vor der Verkündung erster Ergebnisse überraschend seine Niederlage ein. In Serbien herrschte vielerorts Jubelstimmung.</description>

Poland and Vietnam have upgraded their ties to a strategic partnership, pledging to deepen cooperation in trade and investment, security and defence, as well as education, science, technology and cultural exchanges.

“Vietnam and Poland share a success story in terms of development,” declared Prime Minister Donald Tusk at a joint press conference with his Vietnamese counterpart Lê Minh Hưng in Hanoi on Monday. “The time has come to turn our successes into joint actions that will open up more opportunities.”

The announcement comes amid a broader flurry of Polish diplomacy in Asia, with Tusk arriving in Hanoi following a visit to India and President Karol Nawrocki visiting the Philippines earlier this month. Poland also recently signed new strategic agreements with South Korea and Japan.

🇵🇱🤝🇻🇳 Polska i Wietnam wchodzą na poziom partnerstwa strategicznego!

✅ Podczas wizyty w Hanoi premier @donaldtusk oraz szef wietnamskiego rządu Lê Minh Hưng podjęli decyzję o podniesieniu wzajemnych relacji do rangi partnerstwa strategicznego, otwierając nowy rozdział we… pic.twitter.com/CCvHmc3eva

— Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 26, 2026

Tusk, who was making the first visit by a Polish prime minister to Vietnam in 16 years, pointed to the two countries’ rapid recent economic development.

“Within a single generation, Vietnam achieved middle-income status”, while “Poland recently joined the ranks of the world’s 20 largest economies”.

In fact, while Poland was forecast to join the world’s 20 largest economies last year, it eventually fell narrowly short. However, it is expected to soon overtake Switzerland, the current holder of 20th place.

Tusk said that, during his visit, he had often heard people say that “Poland is the Vietnam of Europe and Vietnam is the Poland of Asia”.

 

Last year, Hưng’s predecessor, Phạm Minh Chính, became the first Vietnamese prime minister in 15 years to visit Poland.

The two countries first established diplomatic relations in 1950, and both leaders emphasised Poland’s large Vietnamese community, which dates back to students arriving around that time.

Speaking on Monday, Hưng noted the two countries’ strong traditional ties, adding that Vietnam always remembers and is grateful for Polish support and assistance during his country’s struggle for independence and national reunification, reports the Vietnamese News Agency (VNA).

The Vietnamese are Poland's largest non-European migrant group.

Photographer Zula Rabikowska, through her images and interviews, offers an insight into their experiences, identities and the challenges they face https://t.co/tsRwHINapQ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 27, 2019

The new strategic partnership agreement signed by Tusk and Hưng pledges to “bring tangible benefits to both nations and contribute to peace, stability, cooperation and prosperity”.

It contains commitments to “maintain regular high-level contacts”, reduce non-tariff barriers to trade, and strengthen cooperation on defence, including trade in military equipment.

On Sunday, Poland’s deputy minister for state assets, Konrad Gołota, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that negotiations are already underway for Vietnam to buy Polish Krab howitzers and Rosomak armoured fighting vehicles, among other hardware.

Polish arms firm Mesko has announced the best financial results in its 100-year history.

Record revenues and profits were driven in large part by international demand for Mesko's flagship Piorun air-defence system, which has proved successful in Ukraine https://t.co/Dx1yY54qCP

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 16, 2026

Tusk, pointing to Poland’s current trade deficit with Vietnam, said that Warsaw’s “priority remains a better balance in trade”.

“The sectors in which the Vietnamese side is most interested, and in which we really have something to offer, are the arms industry, satellite and space cooperation, pharmaceuticals and food, especially dairy products,” he added.

Tusk also announced that the number of annual Polish-Vietnamese student exchanges would rise by 250% and noted that Poland’s national carrier, LOT, would resume direct Warsaw-Hanoi flights in the first quarter of 2027.

Poland is taking steps to attract more foreign students as universities face lower enrollment due to demographic decline.

Turkey, South Korea, Vietnam and Uzbekistan are among the countries with which the government is cultivating stronger academic ties https://t.co/r878KqS5OV

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 25, 2026

The Polish prime minister acknowledged differences between Poland and Vietnam’s approach to Russia’s war in Ukraine. Vietnam, which has long maintained close ties with Moscow, has avoided condemning the Russian invasion.

But he emphasised his belief that, “because of their history, wartime experience and international relations, both Vietnam and Poland can contribute a great deal to the peace process”.

Tusk’s trip to Vietnam follows a three-day visit to India, where he and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced a goal of doubling bilateral trade by 2030.

Poland and India's PMs have, after meeting in New Delhi, outlined aims to double bilateral trade by 2030 and expand cooperation in mining, shipbuilding, energy, space and defence technologies

Polish-Indian relations are "gaining speed", said @narendramodi https://t.co/iIVIkCXnvr

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 22, 2026

In April, Tusk visited South Korea, upgrading Poland’s relations with the country he described as Poland’s “most important ally after the United States”, and deepened Poland’s strategic partnership with Japan on the same tour.

Earlier this month, Tusk also announced plans to visit China before the end of the year. Meanwhile, President Nawrocki visited the Philippines this month as part of a bid to secure backing from Asian nations for Poland’s hoped-for membership in the G20.

]]> Two thirds of Poles support liberalising abortion law, finds new poll https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/26/two-thirds-of-poles-support-liberalising-abortion-law-finds-new-poll/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 10:55:05 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105996

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

Just over two thirds of Poles support liberalising the country’s abortion law, which is among the strictest in Europe, according to a new poll. However, most do not favour introducing abortion on demand, as protesters called for during demonstrations last week.

The findings come shortly after parliament approved legislation intended to ease access to abortion. But the measures face a potential veto from right-wing, opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki.

🔴 Sondaż dla @rzeczpospolita: Niemal 7 na 10 Polaków chce liberalizacji przepisów ws. aborcjihttps://t.co/f7mxwygIxz

— Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) October 25, 2026

In 2020, Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) outlawed abortions in cases where a severe defect is diagnosed in the foetus. That means pregnancies can now only be legally terminated in two cases: where they result from a crime (such as rape or incest) or if they threaten the mother’s life or health.

In a new poll by SW Research for Rzeczpospolita, a leading newspaper, a total of 67.2% of respondents said that they want to liberalise that law. However, only 37.7% favoured introducing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy.

Meanwhile, 29.5% preferred the softer option of returning to the situation from before the 2020 TK ruling – often referred to the “abortion compromise” in Poland – in which terminations were only available in three cases.

 

A further 16.2% supported maintaining the current abortion law; 6.0% wanted to make the rules even tougher (which would involve removing one or both justifications for abortion that currently exist); and 10.6% said they had no opinion.

The poll found that support for liberalisation of abortion was stronger among women (73.8%) than men (60.3%).

The latest findings are consistent with previous polling, which tends to show that a significant majority supports liberalising the abortion law but that there is not a majority in favour of abortion on demand (although some individual polls have narrowly found such a majority).

One member of Poland's likely new ruling coalition, The Left, says polls show a majority in favour of abortion on demand.

In fact, they do not. And this issue is likely to be one of the hardest for the incoming government to resolve, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/4Nze9wwEC3

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 20, 2023

The issue has caused significant political disputes in Poland, not only between the right-wing opposition and the more liberal ruling coalition, but also within the coalition itself.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and one of its partners, The Left (Lewica), favour introducing abortion on demand. However, more conservative elements of the government, especially the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), prefer a return to the pre-2020 “compromise”.

Much of the right-wing opposition, meanwhile, favours maintaining the status quo. However, some more moderate elements of the opposition have suggested it would be best to reverse the TK ruling and return to the “compromise”.

Protests took place in towns and cities around Poland on Thursday evening, demanding that the government fulfil its promise to liberalise the country’s strict abortion laws https://t.co/q7eK7mV9zr

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 23, 2026

In 2024, due to disputes within his coalition, Tusk declared that it was unlikely there would be any abortion reform during the current parliamentary term due to differences within his coalition.

However, last week the issue was revived, with the government’s majority in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, approving a bill that would reverse the 2020 TK ruling (but not introduce abortion on demand). It also passed another bill decriminalising providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions.

After both bills go through the upper-house Senate, which can suggest amendments but not block them, they will pass to President Nawrocki, who can sign them, veto them, or send them to the TK for assessment.

Given that Nawrocki is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has declared his opposition to abortion, and has vetoed a record number of government bills, it is widely expected that he will seek to block efforts to liberalise the abortion law.
