]]> Time is running out for Germany to pay Polish WWII victims the compensation they deserve [Opinion] https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/25/time-is-running-out-for-germany-to-pay-polish-wwii-victims-the-compensation-they-deserve-opinion/ Sun, 25 Oct 2026 14:10:55 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105968 Philipp Fritz There are 30,000-50,000 such survivors, but their number dwindles every week.]]>

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

By Philipp Fritz, Warsaw correspondent for Die Welt (which first published this article in German here)

Negotiations on compensation for the still-living victims of the German occupation of Poland have been going on for years. There are some 30,000 to 50,000 such survivors, but their number dwindles every week. Berlin should act now.

No “humanitarian gesture” has emerged. “The draft budget currently reflects the fact that no decision has been made,” said Josef Hinterseher, a German foreign office spokesman, at a press conference in late September.

He thereby confirmed what many observers had suspected: survivors of concentration camps, ghettos and death marches, former forced workers and participants in the Warsaw Uprising who are still living in Poland will not receive any compensation, one-off payment or monthly pension from the German government.

The German chancellor has announced that his country will offer support to surviving Polish victims of WW2 and will help strengthen Poland’s eastern border.

However, in both cases he did not provide details of what these measures will involve in practice https://t.co/gKX6142Alo

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2024

Just a few sentences later, Hinterseher moved onto the next subject – the fact that two Russian oligarchs were to be removed from the EU’s sanctions list. Or at least, that Berlin had not been successful in opposing this decision.

The fact that these two issues were dealt with publicly one after the other shows that the German government is quicker to reach a decision that makes Putin’s supporters’ lives easier than it is with victims of the Nazi terror. It is a declaration of moral bankruptcy.

Warsaw and Berlin have been negotiating compensation for the last remaining victims of the German occupation of Poland for years. There are between 30,000 and 50,000 of them – aged over 90, often living alone and in poor health. Their numbers are dwindling every week.

The fact that talks are taking place in Berlin ministries but without any decision being taken is met with sadness and fury in Poland.

 

Increasingly, Poles are getting the impression that, even if the Germans manage to put up memorials, they cannot offer survivors tangible help when it is asked for. It is a common view that in Berlin the descendants of the perpetrators are simply waiting for the victims to die so that this pesky issue will sort itself out.

Should that happen, those left behind will not forget, and the Germans will hardly be able to forgive themselves.

Warsaw is no longer demanding war reparations from Berlin. In December 2023, Donald Tusk’s government switched to talking about “making amends”.

Polish foreign minister @sikorskiradek has called on Germany to “think creatively” about compensating Poland for WWII.

On a visit to Berlin, he also said that the new government would "end the cold war" waged by the former ruling PiS party against Germany https://t.co/kZ62nUuqqO

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 31, 2024

This is not just splitting hairs. In so doing, Tusk put the ball in the German government’s court, giving it the chance to take action and, through a gesture recognising suffering and providing a relatively small sum of money, to offer people tangible help and do a service to the German-Polish relationship.

Former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz is reported to have offered Tusk a one-off payment in 2024, but Poland’s prime minister turned the sum down as insufficient. Instead, Polish diplomats are demanding monthly pensions.

In any case, we are talking about a few hundred million euro: a relatively small amount compared to the equivalent of €1.3 trillion that Poland’s former ruling national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party once demanded from Germany, and also in comparison to many other budget items – and yet still there is nothing about compensation in the budget planning.

Poland is seeking $1.3 trillion in war reparations from Germany, but Berlin says the issue was legally settled long ago.

Legal scholar @MPiatkowski1 examines the arguments of both sides, explains the legal context, and looks at what could come next https://t.co/xsKAY2TukS

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 9, 2022

Rumour has it that, in return for compensation, German foreign ministry officials are asking for a kind of Polish guarantee that in future there will be no more demands for reparations, or at least that at least the German gesture will receive good press in Poland.

If that is true, it would be thoroughly indecent, bringing to mind an image of a perpetrator trying to buy his victim’s silence. This reflects a belief in objectification, an ugly bureaucratic mentality stemming from a system in which “work” in a ghetto counts towards statutory pension contributions, but no one can bring themselves to pay compensation.

This issue can be resolved at the very top. Chancellor Friedrich Merz would have to work with the relevant ministries – the foreign office and finance ministry – to provide for compensation for the victims in the budget. This would be a belated but major and morally right gesture. If politics is too slow – time really is of the essence – then civil society should take it upon itself to show where it stands.

Donations for the still living victims of the German tyranny or a fund from which survivors would receive monthly payments can be created from within society. Business can also get involved. German corporations which were guilty of, for instance, exploiting forced labourers in occupied Poland, or those that emerged from them, such as BASF, Siemens, Volkswagen, BMW and Deutsche Bank, could contribute.

Poland covers almost all the costs of maintaining former Nazi-German camps on its territory. It has spent more on this than Germany has paid in compensation to Polish war victims

It's time for Germany to fund preservation of the sites, argues @W_Kononczuk https://t.co/08nf4c2jMz

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 25, 2026

Right now, since its state elections in September, Germany gives the impression of a country whose compass for right and wrong is broken.

As of 6 October, the state parliament of Sachsen-Anhalt has as its vice-president Hans-Thomas Tillschneider of the AfD, a man who wrote on X that “the Poles have been getting on my nerves for a long time now”. In Berlin, not only did the left-wing Die Linke celebrate their electoral success with Israel haters and antisemites, they even tolerate them in their ranks. It is shameful.

But now Germany, and particularly its government, has the opportunity to show that the rhetoric of responsibility for the victims is not merely empty words. That, contrary to a mood that does not support it, they are doing what is morally right. Time is running out, Germany – it’s your last chance.

Translated by Ben Koschalka

Katarzyna Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, the leader of a junior party in Poland’s ruling coalition, has announced her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party, the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), in protest over a parliamentary vote on Thursday.

Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) is set to remain in the government, thereby maintaining Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s parliamentary majority. However, the dispute has highlighted tensions within the ruling coalition just a year ahead of parliamentary elections at which it will seek another term.

Dwukadencyjność samorządów została utrzymana. Tak zdecydował dziś Sejm. Wygraliśmy! Zmiana, której chce 75% Polaków dojdzie do skutku!

Stało się to jednak pomimo głosów K15X. Koalicja, w tym niestety znaczna część posłów Polski 2050, stanęła przeciw ludziom, a za politykierskimi…

— Katarzyna Pełczyńska (@Kpelczynska) October 22, 2026

Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, who serves as minister for funds and regional policy, made her decision in the wake of an unusual voting result in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, on Thursday.

Another junior partner in the ruling coalition, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), had proposed a bill abolishing two-term limits for mayors. Those limits had been introduced in 2018 with the aim of reducing corruption and cronyism by preventing local officials from becoming entrenched in power.

However, PSL, which has a strong presence in local politics, argues that the limits prevent effective, popular mayors from being re-elected, thereby denying voters the right to decide who they want to represent them.

Although the government has a majority in the Sejm, the bill was narrowly defeated, with 213 votes in favour and 215 against, after 15 MPs from the ruling coalition joined with the right-wing opposition in voting against it.

How MPs from each parliamentary group voted on the bill (za = for, przeciw = against, wstrzymało się = abstained, nie głosowało = did not vote)

Pełczyńska-Nałęcz herself is not a member of parliament, so did not vote. Her party was split, with six MPs voting for the bill, three against, three abstaining, and three not voting at all.

Aftewards, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz made clear that she opposed the bill and celebrated the fact that it was blocked. She also announced her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party.

“The coalition, unfortunately including a significant portion of MPs from Poland 2050, stood against the people and in favour of backroom political deals,” she wrote. “I am leaving Donald Tusk’s government because values are more important to me than positions.”

“I am leaving the party in the hands of its founder, who stepped away but then returned,” she added, referring to Poland 2050’s founder, Szymon Hołownia. “I hope that he remembers what values he came to power in the name of.”

 

Pełczyńska-Nałęcz’s decision follows a year of turmoil for Poland 2050. In September 2025, Hołownia, who had led the party since founding it in 2021, announced that he was stepping down.

However, a first attempt to choose a new leader was invalidated in January after technical problems with voting. Hołownia then hinted that he may reverse course and seek to continue leading the party, though in the end that did not happen.

In February, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz was chosen as the new leader. That prompted her rival candidate, Paulina Hennig-Kloska, to quit the party, taking half of its MPs with her. They formed a new group called Centrum (Centre).

Both Poland 2050 and Centrum remain in the ruling coalition. However, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz has had an uneasy relationship with Tusk.

By Aleks Szczerbiak

Political scandals generate intense media attention and public outrage but rarely produce dramatic shifts in party support that they once did.

They are now more likely to affect electoral outcomes indirectly by demobilising softer, less committed voters and influencing turnout, particularly among supporters of the government disappointed by its apparent underperformance and broken election promises.

The hospital scandal

Two high-profile political scandals dominated the Polish news agenda for much of this summer. The first centred on irregularities at Warsaw’s Southern Hospital (Szpital Południowy) and involved a young and relatively inexperienced doctor, Dawid Kacprzyk.

In spite of his lack of a specialist qualification, Kacprzyk coordinated the hospital’s emergency department and reportedly earned a staggering 1.6 million złoty (€366,000) in the previous year alone. He also served as a Warsaw district councilor for the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO) grouping, Poland’s main governing party led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

Public outrage intensified following reports that the hospital had operated a dedicated “VIP path” or special lounge where ruling-party-linked politicians and their families were allowed faster access and medical examinations without the usual queues faced by ordinary patients.

Further claims emerged, including a whistleblower surgeon alleging that supervisory failures contributed to patient deaths and of improper private business activity in the hospital morgue.

Poland’s health minister has unveiled a set of reforms intended to “rebuild trust” in public hospitals following a series of reports about exorbitant pay for some doctors and that politically connected patients could skip queues and use a "VIP lounge" https://t.co/pidAHxohc4

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 8, 2026

For its part, KO insisted that the scandal was the personal misconduct of one former party member rather than a general problem affecting the entire healthcare system. They noted that Kacprzyk quickly resigned his council seat and hospital role, and that party-aligned Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski had dismissed the hospital board and two of his deputy mayors overseeing the city’s health services.

KO argued that no specific names of preferential VIP patients had been publicly confirmed, any irregularities were being fully investigated by prosecutors and independent bodies, and political and legal accountability would follow if ethical breaches or crimes were proven. The government also pledged systemic reforms including measures to curb excessive pay for doctors.

Nonetheless, the scandal struck a deep chord with the Polish public, triggering massive negative media and political fallout that aligned perfectly with the right-wing opposition’s narrative painting KO as part of a “Warsaw elite” that enjoys special privileges at the expense of ordinary citizens.

The cryptocurrency scandal

The second major summer scandal centred on allegations of financial impropriety and political entanglement involving Zondacrypto, once Poland’s largest crypto trading platform, that claimed over a million users but earlier this year collapsed abruptly after thousands of retail investors were unable to access their funds.

However, what began as a major financial scandal escalated into political warfare, providing the government with powerful ammunition to attack the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping, party-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, and the broader conservative political eco-system over payments and donations made by the crypto firm.

Prosecutors are investigating possible criminal offences relating to financing by Zondacrypto, a collapsed crypto firm, of organisations and individuals linked to the right-wing opposition, including the Polish version of US conservative conference CPAC https://t.co/swceV864nA

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 26, 2026

For example, Zondacrypto sponsored the 2025 Polish edition of the Conservative Political Action Committee (CPAC) conference attended by the then-presidential candidate Nawrocki, advertised heavily with conservative media outlets such as the TV Republika television network, and made donations to foundations linked to high-ranking PiS figures such as former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro.

The government also tried to entangle Nawrocki, who repeatedly vetoed its cryptocurrency regulation laws, into the scandal, arguing that he was protecting the shady interests of the industry and its political beneficiaries at the expense of ordinary Poles (the Tusk administration lacks the three-fifths parliamentary majority required to overturn a presidential veto).

For their part, PiS and the broader Polish right dismissed the government’s accusations as a smear campaign and sought to shift blame for the scandal onto the Tusk administration for inadequate oversight to protect investors. Figures on the right, including those connected to foundations that received money, framed these dealings as legitimate sponsorships common across the media and other organisations.

The president of the Polish Olympic Committee has been detained as part of a criminal investigation into Zondacrypto, a crypto firm that collapsed earlier this year and was a major sponsor of Poland's Olympic team https://t.co/QPG7ejAImD

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 27, 2026

PiS rejected claims that the party or associated groups received funds from the firm and defended Nawrocki’s vetoes as necessary against flawed legislation.

Nonetheless, opinion polls found that most respondents linked the scandal to PiS and the right-wing opposition, providing the government with numerous attack lines to force them onto the defensive.

The diminishing impact of scandals

It is worth recalling how an earlier era of post-communist politics scandals possessed much greater transformative, system-altering capacity and could act as catalysts for the restructuring of the electoral landscape.

For example, at the beginning of the 2000s, the so-called “Rywin scandal” was widely seen as a decisive factor in the near-destruction as a political force of the previously powerful, and then-governing, communist-successor Democratic Left Alliance (SLD). The scandal erupted in late 2002 when film producer Lew Rywin allegedly solicited a large bribe from the Agora media group, publisher of the influential liberal-left Gazeta Wyborcza newspaper, in exchange for media legislation changes while claiming to act on behalf of a “group holding power” (grupa trzymająca władzę) linked to the ruling party.

A high-profile parliamentary investigative commission, sustained media focus, and a series of follow-on scandals and accumulation of allegations of deep-seated influence peddling by post-communist networks created a powerful narrative of systemic bribery and corruption, completely discrediting the SLD as a competent governing force.

Having won a substantial victory in the 2001 parliamentary election, securing 41% of the votes, its support collapsed to only 11% at the next 2005 poll. This helped clear the way for the rise of the KO (originally Civic Platform)-PiS duopoly that has structured the Polish party system ever since, thereby establishing a precedent that scandals were electorally fatal transgressions.

 

The contrast with the recent hospital and cryptocurrency scandals is instructive and illustrates a broader transformation in the relationship between political misconduct and electoral politics in Poland.

Whereas in the more fluid party system of the early post-communist period a cluster of major scandals or single-event shocks could rapidly destroy dominant parties and restructure competition, now – although they still generate intense, high-octane political and media outrage – such controversies appear to slide off the main political actors with remarkably little immediate consequence.

Indeed, neither of these recent scandals produced the dramatic shift in headline polling numbers that some observers, drawing on historical precedent, might have anticipated given the intensity of the media coverage.

Scandal-neutralising structural shifts

This change stems from three interlocking shifts in the structural dynamics of Poland’s political system. Taken together, they have substantially diminished the capacity of scandals to move headline poll numbers and trigger the kind of large-scale systemic realignments seen in an earlier era of post-communist politics.

Firstly, the sheer velocity of modern political communication prevents single-issue-based scandals from sustaining public focus. In the early 2000s, a major corruption scandal could dominate the news headlines for months through concentrated media attention. The Rywin scandal unfolded through prolonged televised parliamentary commission hearings, keeping the story alive and allowing public outrage to build into a sustained narrative that slowly drained the ruling party’s legitimacy.

Today, digital algorithms and the 24-hour news cycle ensure that a major story, whether about healthcare management or cryptocurrency, moves at a breathtaking pace and is overtaken rapidly as public attention moves onto the next domestic controversy, international development, or strategic counter-narrative.

Seven people have been charged in relation to alleged corruption in the issuing of Polish visas to foreign nationals

The scandal has engulfed the government since last week, but officials say the opposition is exaggerating the scale and nature of the case https://t.co/iHnIShb1pQ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2023

This hyper-accelerated news cycle means that even a high-profile case that generates intense short-term media coverage does not remain the dominant story for long enough to produce cumulative, system-level damage by limiting the time window in which a scandal can convert temporary disapproval into lasting shifts in voting intentions. Scandals thereby become a form of ambient “background noise” in Polish public life rather than a singular focal point for popular outrage.

Secondly, and perhaps most formidably, the protective shield of deep polarisation and socio-political division renders large segments of the electorate relatively impervious to allegations against “their” side. After 2005, the Polish party system crystallised around a durable “post-transition” socio-economic divide reinforced by cultural and geopolitical fault lines.

In this deeply fractured and highly polarised landscape, with large segments of the electorate embedded within hostile camps, when a scandal like the hospital crisis or cryptocurrency controversy breaks, voters interpret allegations levelled against “their” party through a tribal filter as a politically motivated hit job or the work of hostile media.

So even severe scandals are shaped by, and largely confirm, existing political loyalties and rarely trigger cross-camp voter defections. This is a sharp contrast with the early 2000s, when the party system was still fluid and electoral volatility high.

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026

Thirdly, the parties themselves have become far more professional at message discipline and crisis management. Today’s parties are centralised media machines staffed by sophisticated public relations strategists who view a scandal not as a moral crisis but a communication problem requiring aggressive damage containment.

Rather than allowing a controversy to fester, they immediately launch counterattacks, accusing their opponents of far greater historical or concurrent corruption, and ruthlessly enforce internal party discipline and message conformity.

They also deploy well-rehearsed crisis management playbooks including: personnel sanctions; framing the problem as local or individual responsibility, or residual rather than systemic failure; ordering visible audits, investigations, or reforms to demonstrate “taking action”; and co-ordinated messaging that seeks to close the story quickly and shift the focus back onto the other side’s weaknesses or broader policy issues.

Differential mobilisation, not voter persuasion

Yet while polarisation and professional crisis management allow parties to survive the immediate news cycle, this does not mean that scandals have become irrelevant. Rather, their effects are more subtle and delayed through the “slow-burn” mechanism of differential turnout by selectively demobilising specific voter segments.

Although in a highly polarised polity the most committed hard-core partisans are relatively immune to negative information about “their” side, soft or conditional supporters may become disillusioned, or simply less motivated, when repeated scandals reinforce a narrative of self-interest or incompetence.

The net result is a gradual, cumulative, asymmetric demobilisation of one camp that does not fully register in standard inter-election voting intention surveys, which generally show expressed party preferences among those willing to answer but not necessarily the intensity of that preference or the probability that a respondent will actually turn out to vote.

In Poland’s deeply polarised political landscape, the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027, is unlikely to be determined by persuading voters to cross the ideological divide. Rather differential levels of electoral turnout and mobilisation are likely to be the key, specifically: whichever side’s core base is more motivated to – and peripheral, less ideologically committed “softer” supporters are demotivated from – showing up on polling day.

Young Poles are bucking the international trend by turning out at a higher rate than the oldest voters in recent elections.

We spoke with experts and young voters to find out more about the growing frustrations that are driving this political engagement https://t.co/y1JpYYmbjb

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2025

And in a context where the election is likely to be closely fought, and relatively small differences in participation rates could prove decisive, although they may not produce dramatic changes in headline party polling preferences, scandals can still play a significant role. However, we are only likely to see the full impact of any such scandals when voters eventually go to the polls and actual turnout patterns are revealed.

Given the general disillusionment with the current government and growing narrative of its underperformance and failure to deliver on its electoral promises, scandals are more likely to contribute to the demobilisation of the governing camp. It is anyway inherently more difficult for incumbent parties to mobilise their disillusioned supporters to turn out and vote than it is for motivated oppositions to rally their base to oust them.

Indeed, revealed voter preferences in the summer 2025 presidential election – when Nawrocki won an unexpected victory over Trzaskowski, the ruling party-backed favourite – and more recently the severe setback for KO in the Kraków mayoral by-election, suggest that government supporters are already showing greater reluctance to vote.

So, while their effects are routinely neutralised by fast-moving news, tribal shielding and professional spin, scandals still matter in Polish politics, although the battleground has shifted from voter persuasion to differential mobilisation.

A Polish soldier who accidentally shot a Syrian refugee who had entered Poland over the border from Belarus has been acquitted of negligent use of a weapon. The Syrian man had been seeking 50,000 zloty (€11,500) in compensation from the soldier.

The verdict was welcomed by defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, whose ministry had supported the soldier’s legal defence.

❗Podporucznik Wojska Polskiego został dziś uniewinniony przez Wojskowy Sąd Garnizonowy w Warszawie. Nie udowodniono mu żadnych zaniedbań w czasie służby na granicy z Białorusią. W listopadzie 2023 r. przypadkowo postrzelił on migranta.

Od początku zapewniliśmy mu pomoc prawną… pic.twitter.com/RS2p2WsQ7Z

— Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) October 21, 2026

The incident in question took place in November 2023 in Poland’s northeastern Podlasie province. The soldier, named only as Adam Ł. under Polish privacy law and who holds the rank of second lieutenant, had only recently received his first posting to the border, reports legal news service Prawo.pl.

Since 2021, Belarus has been encouraging, assisting and in some cases coercing tens of thousands of migrants, mainly from Asia and Africa, to try to cross into Poland. Among those who make it over the border, most head westwards to Germany, while some have sought to claim international protection in Poland.

In response, Poland has posted thousands of soldiers to the border, where they provide support to the border guard and police. Officers have at times faced violence from migrants trying to cross. In one case, in June 2023, a Polish soldier died after being stabbed.

Poland has named a Moroccan man, Mohamed Addamrou, as the suspect in the 2024 murder of a Polish soldier, Mateusz Sitek, who was fatally stabbed while trying to stop a group of migrants from forcing their way through the border from Belarus to Poland https://t.co/mw8JuOPwcE

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 10, 2026

A few months after that tragedy, Adam Ł. took part in an operation to apprehend a group of migrants who had crossed from Belarus and were around 2 kilometres from the border.

After the soldiers called on the migrants to stop, one of them, a 23-year-old Syrian man, began to flee. As Adam Ł. chased him, the soldier slipped and fell, resulting in his gun, a PM-98 Glauberyt submachine gun, accidentally discharging two rounds.

One bullet hit the Syrian man in the back, close to his spine. The soldier immediately began providing him with first aid, before the Syrian was taken to hospital. He was discharged a few weeks later and, in May 2024, was granted asylum in Poland.

 

Initially, when it appeared possible that the Syrian could suffer partial paralysis, military prosecutors considered charging Adam Ł. with negligent use of a weapon resulting in serious injury, a crime carrying a prison sentence of up to eight years.

In the end, that was downgraded to a lower charge of negligent use of a weapon causing impairment or a health disorder, which is punishable by up to three years in prison.

The defence ministry provided the soldier with legal counsel from a special team set up in 2024 to defend military personnel. They advised him not to plead guilty.

Eventually, prosecutors asked only that the court impose an indemnity of 2,000 zloty on Adam Ł., to be paid to the Syrian. The Syrian’s lawyer, meanwhile, sought 50,000 zloty for his client.

The president has signed into law new rules removing criminal liability from officers who use firearms while serving on the border.

The measures were passed in response to a surge in aggression from some migrants seeking to cross the border from Belarus https://t.co/sBMaoYhoCw

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 16, 2024

In a ruling announced on Wednesday, a military court in Warsaw fully acquitted Adam Ł. Judge Michał Żak said that it remained unclear how the incident unfolded. He also pointed to expert evidence commissioned by the court that found the soldier’s gun could have had defects that caused it to fire when it hit the ground.

Those doubts, and a lack of convincing evidence to support the prosecutor’s version of events, meant the charge of negligence could not be proven, found Żak. The verdict can still be appealed. The Syrian’s lawyer said they would wait for the judge’s full written justification before deciding whether to appeal.

Kosiniak-Kamysz, meanwhile, welcomed the ruling in a social media post. “From the very beginning, we provided him with legal assistance,” wrote the defence minister. “A soldier who carries out his duties cannot be left alone, even in a difficult situation.”

In May this year, another soldier was acquitted over an incident in which he fired shots towards a group of migrants who had illegally crossed the Belarussian border. The judge found that, in fact, the soldier had been fulfilling his obligation to defend the Polish border.

A Polish soldier who fired shots towards migrants who had illegally crossed the border from Belarus has been acquitted of abusing his powers and threatening the lives of others

The military judge found he had been fulfilling his duty to protect the border https://t.co/ugxq5tkdFV

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 27, 2026

In 2024, Poland’s government introduced a new law making it easier for soldiers and other uniformed officers serving at the border to use firearms. They now no longer face criminal liability for employing their weapons in certain cases.

Since then, the government has also further strengthened physical border barriers and banned asylum claims by migrants who cross irregularly from Belarus.

That has been followed by a significant drop in attempted crossings by migrants from Belarus: in the first half of this year, only 250 attempts were recorded, down from 15,500 in the same period of 2025 – a 98% drop. Poland also now claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending those who do manage to cross.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the decision “suicidal”, saying that it harms Ukraine by making it harder for the country’s friends to support it. Foreign minister Radosław Sikorski announced that the local official responsible for pushing through the commemorations in Lviv has been banned from entering Poland.

Decyzja Lwowskiej Rady Obwodowej, by 2027 rok był rokiem UPA i Szuchewycza, jest nieakceptowalna. Taka decyzja nie buduje wzajemnego zaufania między narodami, lecz wzmacnia podziały. Konieczne jest odcięcie się władz Ukrainy od tego stanowiska.

On Tuesday, the Lviv regional council adopted resolutions proclaiming 2027 the year of the UPA, of Shukhevych, and of Oleh Olzhych, a poet and leading figure in the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN).

Sviatoslav Sheremeta, chair of the region’s committee on culture, said the decisions will pave the way for “large-scale events” to commemorate the UPA, Shukhevych and Olzhych. “This is our history, our heroes, and we must duly honour their memory,” he added, quoted by local news service Sokal Voice.

The OUN was a nationalist organisation that sought Ukrainian independence. The UPA, a partisan formation, emerged in 1942 from a more radical faction of the OUN, with Shukhevych serving as its military commander.

While the UPA is still remembered positively by some in Ukraine for its role in fighting against Moscow-imposed Soviet rule, in Poland it is associated with the Volhynia massacres, in which the UPA led the slaughter of around 100,000 Poles, mostly women and children.

 

Poland has previously condemned official commemorations in Ukraine of Shukhevych and other figures associated with the UPA. And the resolutions adopted by the Lviv region on Tuesday likewise prompted a swift response from Warsaw.

“Glorifying the UPA and criminal figures is contrary to European values ​​and the strategic and good-neighbourly nature of relations between Poland and Ukraine,” foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór told news website Wirtualna Polska.

“Shukhevych is a criminal stained with the blood of thousands of innocent victims, people who were murdered simply because they were Poles,” he added, also noting that the UPA’s victims included Jews, Czechs, Armenians and Ukrainians themselves.

Wewiór warned that, while the Ukrainian and Polish governments have recently made progress towards reconciliation over historical issues, “irresponsible local activists are damaging these relations by honouring people clearly responsible for crimes and collaborating with the Nazis”.

Wirtualna Polska reports that Sheremeta was previously banned from entry in 2017, under Poland’s former government, for his actions in blocking the exhumation and commemoration of Polish massacre victims buried in Ukraine.

Podpisałem wniosek o wpisanie na listę osób niepożądanych w RP radnego obwodu lwowskiego S. Szeremeta, rekonstruktora Galizien Waffen-SS, autora pomysłu ustanowienia 2027 rokiem R.Szuchewycza, dowódcy UPA, który wydawał rozkazy wysiedlania i mordowania Polaków.…

— Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) October 21, 2026

Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) also condemned the resolutions. It called Shukhevych “an architect of the genocide in Volhynia” as well as the “co-founder of collaborationist units operating alongside Germany”.

It quoted an order issued by Shukhevych in which he wrote: “Cut them down to the last man. Burn villages inhabited exclusively by Poles; in mixed villages, eliminate only the Polish population.”

However, the IPN noted that Olzhych – whom Lviv is also honouring next year – was the head of a group that condemned the crimes committed by the more radical faction of the OUN.

The Lviv Regional Council has designated 2027 in the Lviv region as the Year of Roman Shukhevych, an architect of the genocide in Volhynia, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), and Oleh Olzhych, a leader of the OUN-M.

Among those being commemorated, Roman Shukhevych stands out as… pic.twitter.com/Bge2muwjHz

— Institute of National Remembrance (@ipngovpl_eng) October 21, 2026

Polish leaders have previously warned that the honouring of the UPA and figures associated with it would harm Ukraine’s chances of joining the European Union. Poland, like all other member states, can veto accession.

However, there have also been recent signs of progress on issues of historical memory. Last year, in a diplomatic breakthrough, Ukraine lifted a ban on exhuming the remains of Volhynia massacre victims on its territory.

But this year, President Volodymyr Zelensky triggered a diplomatic crisis when he approved the naming of a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”.

The government’s majority in parliament has approved two bills that would liberalise Poland’s strict abortion laws. One would reverse the 2020 constitutional court ruling introducing a near-total ban on abortion; the other would decriminalise providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions.

However, it appears likely that both measures will be vetoed by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition. His chief of staff reiterated on Tuesday that Nawrocki “supports the protection of life from conception to natural death”.

Mamy to! Sejm przyjął dwa projekty: dekryminalizujący pomocnictwo w aborcji i przywracający aborcyjny kompromis.
To niezbędne minimum i pierwszy krok.
Jesteśmy to winni kobietom. pic.twitter.com/1yLyfuFCQC

— Aleksandra LEO (@AleksandraLeo) October 20, 2026

When Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, took power in December 2023 from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, it pledged to soften abortion laws.

However, since then, it has failed to do so, largely due to disputes between more conservative and liberal elements within the coalition. But now, a year ahead of parliamentary elections, that has changed, with the more powerful lower-house Sejm pushing through two abortion bills on Tuesday.

One would once again allow abortions to be carried out in cases where a severe foetal abnormality is diagnosed. That would reverse a ruling by the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in 2020 outlawing such abortions, which the TK found contravened various constitutional principles, including the right to life.

That judgement, which went into force in January 2021, means that abortion is currently only allowed in two cases: when a pregnancy results from a crime (such as rape or incest) or when it threatens the mother’s life or health. In Europe, only Malta has a stricter abortion law.

The ruling was issued when the TK was stacked with PiS-appointed judges – including three who had been illegitimately appointed – and regarded as being under the control of the then-ruling party. It prompted the largest protests Poland has witnessed since the communist era.

 

In the Sejm vote on Tuesday, 233 MPs were in favour of the new bill, with 203 opposed. Support came from parties in Tusk’s coalition, as well as the small left-wing Together (Razem).

Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and The Left (Lewica), one of its coalition partners, have previously expressed support for an even greater liberalisation of the law, allowing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. However, all of their MPs voted in favour of the compromise option on the table.

Meanwhile, five MPs from the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), the most conservative element of the coalition, joined with the right-wing and far-right opposition in voting against the bill.

How MPs from each parliamentary caucus voted on the bill to allow abortions when a severe foetal abnormality is diagnosed (za = for, przeciw = against, wstrzymało się = abstained, nie głosowało = did not vote)

In a separate vote, the Sejm also approved a bill that would decriminalise the act of helping a woman obtain an unlawful abortion. Currently, that is an offence that carries a prison sentence of up to three years.

A previous attempt to pass such a bill was defeated in 2024, after most PSL MPs joined with the opposition to block it. That prompted Tusk to declare that abortion reform would be impossible during the current parliamentary term.

However, on Tuesday, 217 MPs voted in favour and 213 against, meaning the bill was approved. A total of 27 MPs failed to attend the vote, including 10 from PiS, among them party leader Jarosław Kaczyński. If they had participated, the bill would likely have been rejected.

All MPs from KO, The Left and Razem voted in favour of the bill, as did almost all from the centrist Poland 2050. However, 14 PSL MPs joined with the opposition in voting against it, including PSL’s leader, deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.

How MPs from each parliamentary caucus voted on the bill to decriminalise abortion assistance (za = for, przeciw = against, wstrzymało się = abstained, nie głosowało = did not vote)

Both the bills approved by the Sejm now pass to the upper-house Senate, which can propose amendments but not block the passage of legislation. Tusk’s coalition has an even larger majority in the Senate than the Sejm.

Once final versions of the bills are approved by parliament, they pass to the president, who can sign them into law, veto them, or ask the TK to assess whether they comply with the constitution.

Given that Nawrocki is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of government bills, and has declared his opposition to abortion, it appears very unlikely that he will sign either bill into law.

President Nawrocki joined thousands of people on the National March of Life, Poland’s largest annual anti-abortion event, which is held under the patronage of the Catholic church https://t.co/8BQEVUoMZn

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 20, 2026

Speaking to broadcaster Polsat on Tuesday evening after the Sejm votes, the president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, said that Nawrocki would wait to see what the legislation looked like by the time it reached him.

However, Bogucki noted that, “during his campaign, the president said he supported the protection of life from conception to natural death”. Bogucki also pointed to the fact that the TK, even before PiS was in power, had been “very clear” on “protection of life”.

He also suggested that abortion was now suddenly back on the table because Tusk wants to “rehash ideological issues in order to cover up his incompetence in matters he should actually be dealing with”.

.@BoguckiZbigniew o stanowisku prezydenta ws. aborcji ⬇️

🗨️ Pan prezydent w tej kampanii mówił, że jest za ochroną życia od poczęcia do naturalnej śmierci@GoscWydarzen 🎙️ @mtejchmanhttps://t.co/ZJ4gKAPywM

— PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) October 20, 2026

A further complication is the fact that the TK is currently in crisis. The government does not recognise any of its rulings (including the 2020 abortion ruling) due to the continued presence of judges illegitimately appointed under PiS.

Meanwhile, Nawrocki and the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, have refused to accept five new TK judges appointed by the Sejm this year.

Opinion polling has consistently shown that a majority of Poles want to liberalise the abortion law.

Leading figures from Poland’s ruling coalition have hit back at US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth over his recent remarks downplaying the contribution of America’s allies during the war in Afghanistan.

The speaker of parliament, Włodzimierz Czarzasty, called the comments “scandalous”, while Prime Minister Donald Tusk read out a message sent to him by a Polish army medic who was serving in Afghanistan when the last of 44 Polish soldiers who died there was declared dead.

💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️

Chciałbym, żeby te słowa dotarły do naszych sojuszników, żeby już nigdy więcej nikt nie lekceważył wysiłku naszych żołnierzy. pic.twitter.com/gGJkh4Gnft

— Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 20, 2026

The controversy stemmed from a speech the US defence secretary gave to US military cadets in Tennessee on Saturday. Hegseth referred to his time serving as a US Army officer in Afghanistan, where he recalled that the International Security Assistance Force (ISAF) headquarters had flags from over 50 countries.

“Except,” Hegseth said, “there were maybe five [countries] that contributed. It was actually closer to one or two that actually, by the end, were involved in kinetic operations. In fact, the patch ‘ISAF’ – we joked that it meant ‘I Saw Americans Fighting.'”

The comments earned quick reproach from Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski, who aimed a message at Hegseth on social media, saying: “Tell that to the families of 44 Polish soldiers who died securing the tough Ghazni province.”

Tell that, Mr @SecWar, to the families of 44 Polish soldiers who died securing the tough Ghazni province. https://t.co/vm4TM0sMJO

— Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) October 18, 2026

On Tuesday, the remarks earned even stronger reproach from Czarzasty, who is the speaker of the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, and the leader of The Left (Lewica), one of the groups that forms Poland’s ruling coalition.

At a press conference, Czarzasty said that Hegseth’s “scandalous” comments are “harmful to the families of Polish soldiers and to Polish national pride”.

He also criticised President Karol Nawrocki – an opponent of the government and conservative ally of Donald Trump – for not condemning Hegseth’s remarks.

It is “an insult to Polish soldiers” that Nawrocki, who serves as commander-in-chief, “is unable to stand up for their dignity and the dignity of those who died”, declared Czarzasty.

To skandaliczne, że prezydent Polski boi się potępić polityków amerykańskich za brak szacunku do polskich żołnierzy, którzy zginęli w Afganistanie. pic.twitter.com/uyv54yDvrI

— Włodzimierz Czarzasty 📚📖 (@wlodekczarzasty) October 20, 2026

Later on Tuesday, Tusk read out to his cabinet a text message he said he had received from a former military medic, whom he did not name.

“Please stand up for soldiers, I beg you,” wrote the medic. “During my tour in Afghanistan, we confirmed the death of the last Polish casualty, a platoon sergeant whose wife was pregnant in Poland at the time.”

“I received a medal from the Americans for helping them, for treating Americans. I didn’t have to do that. We treated them with our own Polish medicines,” they added.

Tusk then added his own remarks, stating: “I would like these words to reach our allies. So that no one will ever again downplay the efforts of our soldiers. Wherever our allies, including our closest ally, the Americans, have needed our participation, Polish soldiers stood shoulder to shoulder with them.”

Tusk also referenced Nawrocki’s silence on the matter. “Frankly, I was also counting on the president speaking out on this matter. But it seems I miscalculated.”

 

Tusk is the first European head of government to directly criticise Hegseth’s remarks, although a spokesperson for British Prime Minister Andy Burnham did say on Monday that it was “wrong to diminish the role” of British personnel, 457 of whom died in Afghanistan.

Of the 3,621 coalition deaths during the war in Afghanistan, around two thirds were Americans (2,461). The rest came from 31 different countries, with Poland’s 44 fatalities the seventh most of any nation.

Hegseth’s remarks are not the first time that the Trump administration has caused anger in Poland by downplaying allies’ role in Afghanistan. In January, Trump himself suggested that other countries had “stayed a little back, a little off the front lines”.

That prompted General Roman Polko, who commanded Poland’s GROM special forces unit in Iraq and Afghanistan, to call the US president “a coward who has never been on the front lines”.

The former commander of Poland's special forces in Iraq and Afghanistan has condemned Donald Trump for questioning the contribution of America's allies

"This is the cynicism of a coward who hasn’t been on the front lines himself," said General @PolkoRoman https://t.co/kElkAO5qX4

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 23, 2026

The Polish government has also clashed with the US on other issues. In January, Tusk joined other European leaders in calling for Greenland’s sovereignty to be respected, following Trump’s calls for the island to be brought under US control.

The following month, Tusk declared that Poland would not be a “vassal” of the US and suggested that Nawrocki wanted Poland to be too subservient to Washington. Czarzasty has twice this year clashed with the US ambassador over critical remarks he made towards Trump.

However, at the same time, the Polish government has sought to maintain positive relations with Washington, given the United States’ role as Poland’s most important security partner. In June, Poland formally requested that the US establish a new permanent military base on its territory.

Hegseth himself has praised Poland, calling it a “model ally” last year. The US State Department this month also announced that it was pushing for Poland to be allowed to join the G20 “as soon as possible”, pointing to its “growing leadership position in the international arena”.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Mon, 26 Oct 2026 14:25:21 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Anthropic reveals $80bn loss as AI giant files for blockbuster IPO https://www.cityam.com/anthropic-reveals-80bn-loss-as-ai-giant-files-for-blockbuster-ipo/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 14:03:56 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2471421

Anthropic has revealed an $80.7bn (£60bn) first-half loss as the AI giant filed for a blockbuster US stock market listing that could value the company at up to $2 trillion. The Claude developer published its long-awaited IPO prospectus with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, offering investors their first detailed look at its [...]]]>

Anthropic has revealed an $80.7bn (£60bn) first-half loss as the AI giant filed for a blockbuster US stock market listing that could value the company at up to $2 trillion.

The Claude developer published its long-awaited IPO prospectus with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, offering investors their first detailed look at its finances ahead of what could become one of the largest flotations in history.

Revenue surged to $16.3bn in the six months to June, up from $1.1bn a year earlier, as businesses ramped up spending on its AI models and coding tools.

However, the company reported a net loss of $80.7bn over the same period, including around $72bn in non-cash accounting adjustments linked to convertible debt and other financing instruments. It lost $42bn in 2025.

Anthropic also spent $9bn on AI infrastructure in the first half of 2026, compared with $7.3bn across the whole of last year, underlining the mounting costs of developing and operating advanced AI models.

The company has committed hundreds of billions of dollars to computing infrastructure in the coming years, including cloud agreements with Amazon and Google.

Anthropic targets record-breaking valuation

The San Francisco-based company plans to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley leading the offering.

Its market debut could come as early as November, although the company has yet to confirm a listing date or offer price.

Investment bankers have reportedly targeted a valuation of between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion, although recent market volatility has raised questions about investor appetite for richly valued AI companies.

The listing would provide Anthropic with access to public capital markets as it competes with OpenAI and Google to develop increasingly powerful models.

Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI executives Dario and Daniela Amodei, Anthropic has built a substantial enterprise business through its Claude chatbot and coding products.

Its prospectus also highlighted the risks associated with developing advanced AI, including potentially harmful model behaviour and an increasingly complex regulatory environment.

The company has faced scrutiny over its safety practices in recent months after former researcher Jacob Coxon accused Anthropic and OpenAI of “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence”.

The IPO comes amid growing investor concern over whether the enormous sums being invested in AI infrastructure will deliver sufficient returns.

Jared Carmel, co-founder of Manhattan Venture Partners, an early Anthropic investor, said a $2 trillion valuation was not unreasonable given the company’s rapid revenue growth.

“The market isn’t pricing a chatbot. It’s pricing an infrastructure layer for how every business is going to run”, he said.

]]> 2471421Saskia Koopman Saskia Koopman Revolut founder accused of hatching a ‘scheme’ to avoid fees in superyacht row https://www.cityam.com/revolut-founder-accused-of-hatching-a-scheme-to-avoid-fees-in-superyacht-row/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 13:51:51 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2471363

The billionaire founder of Revolut has been accused of hatching a “scheme” to avoid paying brokerage fees in a row over a superyacht said to cost €350m. In new legal filings, seen by City AM, Nik Storonsky is accused by a luxury superyacht broker of “secretly negotiating” to buy the vessel “behind the back” of [...]]]>

The billionaire founder of Revolut has been accused of hatching a “scheme” to avoid paying brokerage fees in a row over a superyacht said to cost €350m.

In new legal filings, seen by City AM, Nik Storonsky is accused by a luxury superyacht broker of “secretly negotiating” to buy the vessel “behind the back” of the company.

Cecil Wright & Partners (CWP) claims the fintech chief sidelined the company by entering direct talks with the yacht’s owner, even while an aide was actively liaising with brokers.

The firm accuses Storonsky’s representative, Alexander Chapchaev, of stringing the firm along with calls to discuss “next steps” while a direct deal was being hammered out behind the scenes.

In the new filing, which labelled Storonsky’s defence as “lengthy and repetitive”, CWP alleges the Revolut founder’s camp continued “pretending to the claimant that the defendant was not secretly negotiating… behind the Claimant’s back” as part of a “scheme to try to cut the Claimant out of the deal”.

Storonsky has argued he never indicated he wanted CWP to negotiate on his behalf and maintained he was free to strike a deal directly. 

Revolut boss found superyacht’s ex-owner on ChatGPT

The superyacht, which is named Nixie, was originally commissioned by Canadian billionaire and former professional ice hockey player Patrick Dovigi, before being sold to a Brazilian individual. The buyer was arrested for alleged fraud in 2025 leading to the yacht’s ownership reverting back to Dovigi.

When Storonsky purchased the yacht directly from Dovigi, the broker argued it was cut out of the standard five per cent commission rate for a vessel of that scale. CWP estimates Storonsky paid €350m for the yacht, which means its fees would equate to €17.5m (£15m). Storonsky’s defence says the sum paid is confidential.

Storonsky’s defence contends that no brokerage contract existed and said CWP explicitly told him in writing that “commissions are always paid by the seller”.

When Dovigi insisted the broker show written proof that Storonsky had hired them and would cover their fee, CWP agreed but never asked Storonsky to sign anything, the bank boss’s lawyers said. The broker said Storonsky had already struck a deal with the seller before such a stage was reached.

Storonsky’s legal team also argues CWP acted for the seller and marketed the vessel to rival buyers. 

Filings claim the Revolut boss identified Dovigi via ChatGPT and secured his direct contact through a mutual acquaintance without CWP’s help.

Storonsky’s family office declined to comment. 

A spokesperson for Cecil Wright & Partners said: “We stand by our account of the events leading to Mr Storonsky’s purchase of Nixie and look forward to presenting the evidence in court.”

]]> 2471363Samuel Norman Samuel Norman Financial advisers feel the effects of Reeves’ final tax raid as Healey’s Budget looms https://www.cityam.com/financial-advisers-feel-the-effects-of-reeves-final-tax-raid-as-healeys-budget-looms/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 13:31:57 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2471388

Financial advisers are feeling the effects of Rachel Reeves’ final Budget, as families brace for billions of pounds of tax rises regardless of what chancellor John Healey announces at the despatch box later this week. From April next year, the sweeping shake up to the tax system announced by Reeves in 2025 will come into [...]]]>

Financial advisers are feeling the effects of Rachel Reeves’ final Budget, as families brace for billions of pounds of tax rises regardless of what chancellor John Healey announces at the despatch box later this week.

From April next year, the sweeping shake up to the tax system announced by Reeves in 2025 will come into force. Financial advice firms say they have been hit by a deluge of requests and inquiries as Brits scramble to prepare.

Two thirds of firms said they had seen an increase in enquiries over inheritance tax (IHT) and estate planning, according to the Personal Investment Management & Financial Advice Association (PIMFA).

Under Reeves’ overhaul of IHT, pensions will be pulled into the tax’s scope, meaning families who inherit unspent pots will be required to pay tax on them. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), estimates it to raise £1.5bn annually by 2030.

Advisers have previously warned the change, coupled with frozen tax thresholds, will subject ordinary working families to the death duty, despite not considering themselves wealthy.

Richard Paddle, director at Isio wealth planning, said: “The decision…has already fundamentally changed how many people need to think about passing wealth to future generations.

“What was previously a relatively straightforward approach to retirement planning has therefore become considerably more complex.”

Pension taxation

Elsewhere, firms have been hit by an influx of questions surrounding pension taxation, with nearly 60 per cent reporting an increase, according to the survey.

In her final Budget, Reeves capped salary sacrifice contributions and extended the freeze on national insurance and income tax thresholds, which is expected to generate £7bn annually, leaving many workers questioning how to avoid being pulled into higher bands.

While advisers have noted they have not seen the “panicked rush” to withdraw tax-free cash that took place last year following “unfounded leaks”, many are still worried about how their savings could further be impacted.

Healey’s Budget has heightened concerns on taxation, following reports he will implement Reeves’ plan to shield low-income retirees from paying income tax on the state pension as it is set to rise above the £12,570 allowance threshold in the 2027/28 tax year, costing taxpayers £200m per year.

Tom Selby, director of public policy at AJ Bell, said: “While details remain thin on the ground, there is a danger in attempting to fulfil his predecessor Rachel Reeves’ promise not to apply income tax to those who only receive state pension income, Healey creates a mess of complexity, odd incentives and obvious unfairness in the tax system. 

“Those who have saved could understandably argue their diligent behaviour has effectively been punished.”

The cash ISA ceiling will also be cut from £20,000 to £12,000 for under 65s. Nearly 50 per cent of firms confirmed that clients have increased or maxed out their ISA contributions in a bid to beat the 2027 shakeup, while all taxpayers will experience a two percentage point rise to income tax.

Healey’s headache

Healey is facing a fiscal headache in his Budget, as he looks to raise revenue to offset the blow of rising interest rates and defence spending.

He is expected to slam the banking sector with a wave of hikes as his main-revenue raiser, but family businesses have also found themselves in the firing line.

The Chancellor is reportedly considering proposals to levy income tax when business owners hand down to their children, potentially almost doubling the bill.

Under current rules, transfers can be structured in a way that allows them to attract capital gains tax (CGT) which is charged at a lower rate, but Healey is debating a shake-up in a bid to increase revenue in his maiden Autumn Budget.

]]> 2471388Maisie Grice Maisie Grice Sheikh Mansour doubles down on Manchester City with £100m injection despite legal row https://www.cityam.com/sheikh-mansour-doubles-down-on-manchester-city-with-100m-injection-despite-legal-row/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 13:28:14 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2471417

Sheikh Mansour has reaffirmed his commitment to City Football Group despite Manchester City’s ongoing legal battle with the Premier League by investing a further £100m. Filings at Companies House show that 11,327,163 new shares in CFG were allotted on 14 October, raising the nine-figure sum. A spokesperson for CFG confirmed to City AM that the [...]]]>

Sheikh Mansour has reaffirmed his commitment to City Football Group despite Manchester City’s ongoing legal battle with the Premier League by investing a further £100m.

Filings at Companies House show that 11,327,163 new shares in CFG were allotted on 14 October, raising the nine-figure sum. A spokesperson for CFG confirmed to City AM that the shares were bought by Sheikh Mansour’s Newton Investment and Development, marginally increasing his majority holding.

The transaction came two weeks after the Premier League announced that Manchester City had been found guilty of more than 100 counts of breaking financial rules in order to increase their spending power, helping them to become England’s dominant team. 

City chiefs have appealed the verdict, which they said “contains clear material errors of law, principle and fact and is unsafe”. If upheld, they could be relegated, fined and Sheikh Mansour forced to sell the crown jewel in the CFG network.

Describing the cash injection as “equity from our largest shareholder”, a City Football Group spokesperson added: “The proceeds will be used for normal corporate purposes against our strategic plans, funding planned investments into the City Football Group.”

City Football Group valued at just under £6bn

CFG is football’s biggest multi-club ownership group, with mostly majority holdings in 10 teams across Europe, North and South America, Asia and Australia. They include New York City, Melbourne City, Palermo, Girona, Troyes, Montevideo City Torque and Bahia.

Following the share issue, Abu Dhabi royal Sheikh Mansour owns around 81 per cent of CFG, with US private equity firm Silver Lake holding most of the remainder. The transaction implies a valuation of CFG of £5.9bn.

CFG and Manchester City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak said earlier this year that CFG would fetch “$10bn [£7.3bn] minimum” if sold on the open market. He added that there was no desire to sell, calling the organisations “jewels”.

That valuation could be affected by City’s fight with the Premier League, however. The Independent Football Regulator has powers to force owners found guilty of wrongdoing to divest by a certain deadline, after which the IFR can take the matter out of owners’ hands.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has been forced to insist he will not apply any pressure to the Premier League or IFR over City’s treatment, having previously admitted he would be concerned to see Sheikh Mansour sell up given Abu Dhabi’s investment in the wider Manchester area.

]]> 2471417Frank Dalleres Frank Dalleres The Big Bang transformed the City of London – 40 years on, can it happen again? https://www.cityam.com/the-big-bang-transformed-the-city-of-london-40-years-on-can-it-happen-again/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 13:15:14 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2471288

The City of London was changed forever by a sweeping package of deregulation in 1986, known as the Big Bang. Forty years on – and facing existential threats – can the Square Mile reinvent itself again? When Alasdair Haynes left work as a young options trader on Friday 24th October 1986, he didn’t know what [...]]]>

The City of London was changed forever by a sweeping package of deregulation in 1986, known as the Big Bang. Forty years on – and facing existential threats – can the Square Mile reinvent itself again?

When Alasdair Haynes left work as a young options trader on Friday 24th October 1986, he didn’t know what world would await him when he returned on Monday morning.

For months technicians had been wiring up futuristic-looking machines in offices around the Square Mile. Haynes’s bosses had been running practice sessions on new electronic trading systems and briefing staff as best they could in preparation for the sweeping change ahead. The reality, he says, was more drastic than anyone could have imagined.

“Everybody thought on Friday that there would be a few people off the [stock exchange] trading floor working in offices, and everybody else would come in. But we came in and the trading floor was practically a desert,” Haynes, who went on to found challenger stock exchange Aquis, tells City AM. 

“Everybody else had gone off on Friday, never to come back ever again. It was a mind-blowing experience.”

On that Monday, 27th October 1986, the sudden deregulation of financial markets known as the Big Bang took effect, transforming the City of London and catapulting Britain’s financial industry into the modern age. 

The bustle and life of the London Stock Exchange floor were swapped for the screen-based Stock Exchange Automated Quotation system. Strict rules dividing work between brokers – who bought and sold shares on behalf of clients – and jobbers – who made markets and held shares – were ditched. Fixed commissions were abolished, allowing transaction fees to be negotiated freely, as were rules prohibiting international firms from owning London’s stockbrokers.

International firms piled into the City and consolidated London’s fractured broking market. Americans arrived in droves – and with them came their hard-charging, cut-throat ways of working. The City’s clubby and cosy ways were changed forever. 

“In the morning of the old days at the London Stock Exchange, you used to walk around the boxes around the edge of the exchange, and talk to everybody and find out what they thought about the market,” Haynes says. 

“You’d meet people after work in the Arbitrager or Greens, or go out to lunch. All that changed, literally as if somebody turned a light switch off.”

Speaking at the Lord Mayor’s banquet two weeks after the changes took effect, even Margaret Thatcher acknowledged her reforms were a death knell to a certain way of life.

“The new technology does have a disadvantage: the people who are making deals need never meet,” she said. “You can’t look a computer in the eye and shake its hand to close a bargain.”

The train timetables shifted too to accommodate the earlier starts and longer hours of new international arrivals coming in from the home counties, Sir Philip Augar writes in his book the Death of Gentlemanly Capitalism.

The result though was a sudden rise in jobs in Britain’s financial services sector. In early 1986, the City employed around 1m people. By 1990 that had swelled to 1.18m, according to government figures.

The deregulation drive, ushered in by Thatcher and Chancellor Nigel Lawson, triggered an explosion of activity in the Square Mile and thrust London back to the forefront of global finance. A string of huge privatisations of state-owned utilities added to a sudden influx of investment and jobs in the Square Mile.

While the day itself delivered a shot in the arm, London’s markets had been internationalising for years prior thanks to the rise of the Eurodollar market – the global banking market for dollar deposits held in banks outside the United States – and the abolition of exchange controls in 1979, which ended strict limits on moving money in and out of the country.

Duncan Weldon, the financial historian and author of Two Hundred Years of Muddling Through, argues those changes were just as significant as the sudden overhaul on that Monday in October 1986.

“The City was in this sort of funk from the 1920s, all the way up to the 1950s. And then in the 50s, ’60s and ’70s you see this rebirth in international finance in London in debt markets, because of the Eurodollar market,” he says. 

Dropping exchange controls in 1979 too was “just as big a deal as the changes to the market structure in the mid-80s”, he adds.

Big Bang 2.0?

Politicians have for years nostalgically invoked the Big Bang to pledge another wave of quick and transformative deregulation. Jeremy Hunt, Rishi Sunak, Liz Truss and Kwasi Kwarteng all promised various forms of Big Bang 2.0, claiming that slackened solvency buffers for insurance firms and an overhaul of listing rules would thrust London back to the centre of global finance.

But Weldon says the reality is more complex.

“Rhetorically, the idea of the Big Bang, and the idea there are some regulatory levers you can pull and it will turbocharge your financial sector, is clearly a very appealing one to policy makers,” he adds.

“But it helps to put this in a longer context. It wasn’t just that the policy unit in Number 10, and Nigel Lawson as Chancellor, did these reforms and it turbocharged the financial sector in London.”

Weldon’s warnings point to the challenge now facing the City as it is battered by a wave of foreign takeovers and a historic dearth of initial public offerings. While there have been signs of life for London’s listing market in recent weeks, a slew of reforms made to the rules governing UK capital markets have so far failed to yield a meaningful uptick in deals.

Changes to the buffers of insurance firms and calls for pension funds to pump more cash into domestic equities are also yet to shift the dial on domestic investment.

Policymakers and regulators point to a retreat of domestic capital as among the primary reasons for London’s market malaise. Just four per cent of the domestic stock market is now held by UK pension funds, down from 39 per cent around 20 years ago, according to think tank New Financial. Like the rebirth of the City in the 1980s, that trend has been decades in the marking.

Steven Fine, boss of City investment bank Peel Hunt, says: “The problem we’ve got is that the IPO Market hasn’t come back, and the bigger problem we’ve got is the almost complete lack of domestic demand and the hollowing out of the domestic asset management industry.

“That I think is something that is more in need of [another] Big Bang than regulatory change for listed companies.”

Few are looking at the Budget on Wednesday as a moment likely to deliver solutions and reignite the City’s animal spirits. Banks are set to be hit with higher taxes despite warnings from international bosses that such a move will force them to reallocate capital away from the UK. While a capital gains tax hike has been ruled out, the City’s calls for an end to stamp duty on shares and tax breaks for domestic investment from pension funds look set to be unheeded.

Is another Big Bang possible? Not in Haynes’s view. Rather than search for another deregulatory transformation to revive the Square Mile’s former glory, he says policymakers should learn from the principles that inspired it.

“There’s no magic wand, but the Big Bang wasn’t a magic wand. It was thought through for a long time beforehand” he says.

“It was about many things which a strong, powerful government at the time was able to push through. And that is what we need today. It’s not Big Bang 2.0 – you can’t electronify something again. But what you can do is take the same principles to make it work better.”

]]> 2471288Charlie Conchie Charlie Conchie Tech bosses warn Chancellor UK risks surrendering to foreign AI giants https://www.cityam.com/tech-bosses-warn-chancellor-uk-risks-surrendering-to-foreign-ai-giants/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 11:54:46 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2471325

Britain risks becoming dangerously dependent on foreign tech giants unless the government develops a comprehensive strategy for its own AI, industry leaders have warned the Chancellor ahead of his Budget on Wednesday. UKAI, which represents more than 270 AI businesses, has urged John Healey to commit substantial funding to a national sovereign AI strategy, warning [...]]]>

Britain risks becoming dangerously dependent on foreign tech giants unless the government develops a comprehensive strategy for its own AI, industry leaders have warned the Chancellor ahead of his Budget on Wednesday.

UKAI, which represents more than 270 AI businesses, has urged John Healey to commit substantial funding to a national sovereign AI strategy, warning that the country could become a “vassal state” reliant on overseas powers for critical technology.

The warning comes just days after the Treasury unveiled more than £600m in AI investment, including additional funding for British startups and domestic chip design.

However, the trade body argued that successive funding announcements had failed to address the broader problem of Britain’s dependence on foreign companies for the AI models, computing infrastructure and services underpinning its economy.

“The UK has some of the world’s best AI companies, yet no Sovereign AI strategy to help them thrive”, said Tim Flagg, UKAI’s chief executive.

“The AI Opportunities Action Plan, the Sovereign AI Fund and the AI Hardware Plan are all welcome steps, but nothing joins them together. On their own, they are building blocks. Joined up as a strategy, they would be transformative”.

He warned that without immediate action, Britain risked becoming a “vassal state, dependent on countries that control the AI infrastructure our economy increasingly relies on”.

Pressure builds over Britain’s AI dependence

The warning follows major disruptions from a recent Google Cloud outage, which UKAI said affected banks, businesses and courts, proving the risks of relying on a small number of overseas providers.

It also comes amid growing concern over Britain’s exposure to geopolitical tensions and the dominance of American tech companies in the global AI market.

Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at cybersecurity firm Check Point, said the government needed to move beyond individual funding commitments.

“Without a dedicated sovereign plan in place, the UK will continue to be at the mercy of overseas tech firms, subjected to damaging outages and major cyber security scares”, she said.

“Piecemeal funding announcements are tactical at best, and we need a detailed strategy about how the country will build and design a new wave of AI tools to support critical national infrastructure”.

Wilson argued that developing domestic AI capabilities should also form part of Britain’s defence spending plans, especially as cyber threats from hostile states intensify.

The calls follow a warning from the government’s Council for Science and Technology that Britain risks becoming a “high-value AI customer” rather than a producer of critical technology unless ministers strengthen domestic capabilities.

The government has already established a £500m Sovereign AI Fund to help British startups scale, with the Treasury announcing a further £60m for the programme on Saturday.

Another £60m will support research and procurement of British AI technology, while £18m has been earmarked for a new advanced chip-design academy.

The wider package includes £165m for a national AI biosecurity initiative, backed by OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind, alongside £130m for AI-powered cybersecurity projects.

Healey said the investment would help deliver a “distinctively British approach to AI” that protects national interests while supporting economic growth.

AI minister Kanishka Narayan also acknowledged the risks of overseas dependence, warning that Britain could not “afford to rely entirely on technology built overseas”.

However, UKAI wants the government to bring its existing initiatives together under a single strategy, backed by dedicated funding and changes to public procurement that would give British AI companies greater access to government contracts.

Flagg said Britain had the entrepreneurs, research and talent to compete but that these remained “fragmented and disconnected”.

“The government can change that by uniting and championing British AI businesses and reforming public procurement, so that taxpayer money builds British growth and British jobs”, he said. “Next week’s Budget is the moment to act”.

The finance boss of Plus500 has said a US listing is “always on the table” as the fintech firm turns to North America for its next phase of growth.

Elad Even-Chen, chief financial officer at Plus500, told City AM: “We always keep assessing all the opportunities. It’s our duty as a public company.” 

“It’s something that is always on the table, but in order for us to say it’s the right thing… it needs to come also with substance of a bit more and greater kind of level of performance,” he said.

Even-Chen tied the listing considerations to the group’s medium-term targets around revenue for the US. He said in the next three to four years the US will “be at least the level of 30 to 35 per cent” of the group total.

The fintech boss said it would be able to “consider” a US listing “properly” when a “considerable” amount of revenue and profit was driven from the region.

The pedestrianisation of Oxford Street is the most radical project to hit the West End in decades. The greening of Oxford Street, with plenty of opportunity for people to sit down and relax are both a large part of the plans. What Khan is describing is a vision of a public realm where it is anticipated that people will enjoy the new space, stay longer and spend more.

Here is the thing many people miss: Oxford Street is no longer just a shopping street. The Mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, sees a wider prize. “Revitalising Oxford Street will help to super-charge regeneration, boosting jobs and economic growth in the capital and beyond,” he said. This first phase is deliberately temporary, so that real-time feedback can be gathered from residents, accessibility groups, businesses and workers. Today, Oxford Street begins to find out.
