The department for science, innovation and technology, created in 2023, was dismantled. Rishi Sunak had set it up to develop the UK’s scientific, research and technological outputs: in essence to put the future under one ministerial portfolio.

Burnham reversed that approach, returning digital policy to the department for culture, media and sport (where it had never really set comfortably); hiving off artificial intelligence to a small “taskforce” in the Cabinet Office; and merging science and innovation with business and trade in a sprawling, baggy department for business, innovation, science and trade. The disappearance of a department dedicated to technology, research and innovation was mourned by many in the sector who warned that policy would be less coordinated and less high-profile. It was criticised by techUK, the Startup Coalition, Baroness Lane-Fox, Lord Vaizey of Didcot, the Institute for Government, the president of the Royal Society, Solarwinds, Tom Loosemore of Public Digital and Matt Clifford, Chair of the Advanced Research and Invention Agency. Meanwhile former cabinet minister Liam Byrne was incandescent. The government accepted 16 of its recommendations, partially accepted 18 and rejected 13.

There was another decision which must have provoked dissenting voices behind closed doors in Whitehall. Luke Pollard, minister for defence readiness and Industry, revealed in response to a written parliamentary question that the repair and recovery version of the Boxer armoured fighting vehicle was “no longer being pursued” (which is how the MoD says “cancelled”).

This potentially makes it much more difficult to retrieve stricken Boxers in combat. It is crude cost reduction and no-one in uniform is likely to have advised this course of action. But the government has chosen other priorities.

If we had paid careful attention, we could have foreseen this disinclination to listen. Burnham presents himself as a fanatically reasonable everyman, living in a world in which good people have ideals and bad people have ideology. But his first speech as Labour leader was significant. Burnham wants consensus and problem-solving, but he already knows what he wants to do. Labour represents “unity at the service of people”. A good tax system isn’t just about raising revenue, it’s about encouraging the behaviours (working, saving, investing) that create a prosperous economy, writes Harry Bell

With the UK’s public finances up for scrutiny at the Autumn Budget, it seems the main remedy to Healey’s diminishing fiscal headroom is one that is tried, but not necessarily true: taxing the rich. However, before we look for more ways to tax wealth, we need to make sure we aren’t discouraging people from creating it in the first place. 

If we want a prosperous economy, we need people to work, save, invest, build businesses and take risks. People understand the need to pay tax, but there needs to be a reward for playing an active and productive role in boosting the country, rather than a penalty. Tax policy doesn’t just raise revenue, it changes behaviour. The government needs to think much harder about what behaviours they are encouraging, particularly when it comes to individual, isolated taxes. 

Pensions are a good example. People need to be encouraged to save for their retirement, especially when there is evidence that many aren’t saving enough. In fact, our latest research shows that one in six (16 per cent) mass-affluent Brits have either completely or temporarily stopped contributing to their pension, while nine per cent don’t have one at all. Continually changing the rules will make people question whether pensions will still be attractive in 20 or 30 years, which is a terrible long-term strategy. 

A case study: Capital Gains Tax

Capital Gains Tax (CGT) also shows why behaviour matters. A future increase might initially bring disposals forward and create a bump in tax receipts, but what happens afterwards? People can simply choose not to sell. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) specifically recognises both bringing disposals forward and “locking in” gains by delaying disposals, potentially even until death, as behavioural responses to capital taxes. The economy will not benefit from a tax system where the tax-efficient decision is simply to do nothing.

The same goes for entrepreneurs, and the government needs to be encouraging people to take risks, build businesses and employ people. Business Asset Disposal Relief (BADR) has already become less generous, with the applicable CGT rate rising to 18 per cent from April 2026. A significant increase in CGT without appropriate consideration of BADR could seriously damage the incentive to build, and ultimately sell, a business.

The government should also address some of the strange tax traps in place, and resist the urge to introduce anymore, or push people into higher bands. The loss of the personal allowance above £100,000 means someone can face a very high effective marginal rate over a relatively narrow band of earnings, while the High Income Child Benefit Charge creates another taper for families. People should be incentivised to work hard, progress and reap some of the rewards, rather than trying to fall under arbitrary points where earning the next pound suddenly becomes far less worthwhile. 

More broadly, the tax system is so complicated and intertwined that changing one thing can have consequences elsewhere. CGT interacts with inheritance tax, pensions and estate planning, for example. The Treasury needs to look at the system as a whole and the ripple effect that could occur due to a singular change, rather than treating taxpayers as passive entries on a spreadsheet.

It’s widely understood that a good tax system raises revenue, but it should also encourage the behaviours that create a prosperous economy: working, saving, investing and building businesses, and ultimately, reaping the rewards of doing all those things. 

Harry Bell is director of financial planning at Raymond James

Tomorrow, we mark 40 years since that defining moment that delivered prosperity across the UK in the decades following.

On Wednesday, the Chancellor will deliver his first Budget, which if speculation is to be believed would put at risk the success we as a country have achieved since 1986, by levying higher taxes on banks. In an era increasingly defined by an absolute necessity to deliver growth, this would be the complete and utter wrong move.

Proponents of the measure argue that higher sector taxes have merits on grounds of fairness. Banks have done well due to macroeconomic factors and they must pay their share when people are struggling.

But financial and professional services already contribute 12 per cent of the UK’s taxes, enough to fund our entire defence Budget, with change to spare. That revenue has helped the Labour government deliver their priorities including removing the two-child benefit cap, cutting VAT on energy bills, and capping bus fares at £2.

And it cannot be fair that banks, which already face higher taxes than their competitors in Amsterdam and Frankfurt – and nearly 20 per cent more than our closest competitor as a financial centre, New York – are expected to shoulder an even greater burden.

Should the Chancellor announce this damaging step, the effects will not only be felt in the City of London, but in every town and city in the UK. Our own analysis shows that the financial and professional services sector employs 2.5m people, two thirds of which are outside of London – and in every Parliamentary constituency.

Such is the importance of London’s success to the rest of the country that firms in the sector with headquarters in the capital directly support 370,000 jobs outside of it. Greater Manchester, which the Prime Minister wants to form into the UK’s second political and economic centre, hosts 59,000 of these jobs.

For international banks, capital is mobile, and in an increasingly competitive world we cannot simply assume that businesses will tolerate an ever-rising tax burden. For domestic banks higher taxes mean less lending to SME’s who form a bedrock of our growth. According to a survey of industry executives by the trade association UK Finance, the “accumulation of individually manageable pressures has, over time, weakened the case for locating additional activity in the UK.”

The City of London Corporation has consistently argued that growth must be at the heart of economic policy. Financial and professional services are not simply another source of tax revenue; they are an engine of investment, productivity and opportunity. When firms thrive, they finance businesses, support innovation and help channel capital into the infrastructure and industries on which the UK’s future prosperity depends. Government should be looking to expand this contribution, instead it risks diminishing it.

The Chancellor must equip the Office for Investment: Financial Services, with the resource necessary to convert investor interest into jobs and investment. Attracting international capital is the key that will make the country thrive.

We must also abolish stamp duty on shares. If we want more firms to list in the UK, we need to make our capital markets more attractive to investors. Removing this tax would help strengthen the case for UK listings, supporting a wider ecosystem of high-paying jobs in legal, advisory and accounting services, while giving British businesses better access to the capital they need to grow.

And instead of piling on additional taxes, we must simplify our regulatory regime. Overlapping reporting requirements create unnecessary burdens for businesses. A more streamlined approach would reduce these costs and improve the UK’s competitiveness by allowing firms to focus on what they do best: creating jobs, backing British businesses and driving economic growth.

It was welcome to see the International Monetary Fund upgrade its UK growth forecast for 2026 to 1.3 per cent last week, while praising the government’s decisive action to reduce the deficit and urging it to stay the course. This is progress we must build on, not put at risk. Forty years after the Big Bang helped transform London’s financial markets, the Chancellor has an opportunity to strengthen the conditions for investment and growth for decades to come. We should not risk harming the goose that lays the golden egg.

Chris Hayward is policy chairman at the City of London Corporation

Britain’s space industry is the definition of good growth in every postcode, but too many start-ups are forced to seek foreign buyers when they want to scale, says James Lockyer

Andy Burnham has been desperate to turn back the clock lately. The mood music from the PM has been renationalise, regulate, back to the 1970s we go – like the backslapping at Labour’s conference for saving British Steel. At this rate, the Chancellor will probably be handing out free whippets for all at the Budget thisweek.

Take steel in particular, which is by any definition a sunset industry. It employs roughly 35,000 people and gets more than its fair share of airtime. But we hear much, much less about a forward-looking “sunrise” sector which has created more than 55,000 jobs and contributes much more to UK plc. The UK space sector – which is my area of expertise – would kill for the media steel gets, and it has a great story to tell.

The problem for space is that it doesn’t “look” like an industry, like the pictures of molten steel and foundries you see on the TV.  In the space world, the rockets get the TV pictures but most of the industry is satellites, the equipment that talks to them, and what people do with the data. Most Britons use space daily without a thought for the industry behind it.

What’s going wrong with our space industry is symptomatic of a wider national malaise, though, for all the Chancellor’s noises this week about supporting “sheer bloody-minded entrepreneurs”.  Britain is good at starting space companies but bad at keeping them. Glasgow builds more small satellites than any other European city, and Guildford more or less invented the modern small satellite. Yet the UK ranks third in the world for the number of space investments and 17th for the size of each deal.

Catch-22

The reason is a massive catch-22. A space company must prove its product works in orbit before customers or investors will commit, and it needs money to get up there. But the average UK Space Agency grant was under £100,000 in 2023/24, which does not buy a rocket seat. Compare that with the US which offers grants of up to $60m per company, matched by private money, while we throw small changes at our brightest prospects.

So what happens is inevitable. Surrey Satellite Technology, which pioneered the small satellite, was sold to Airbus for around £40m in 2009. Over in Finland though, ICEYE, a company founded by two university students, has been backed by Finnish state and pension funds through every round of funding since 2018. It is now valued at more than €10bn. In September, the UK published a Space Strategy which promises more than £7.8bn to 2030, but much of it repackages earlier pledges. Most of it is going on defence too, rather than backing start-ups.

So what do we need to do to keep and nurture home grown successes? Number one, pay for the first flight of promising start-ups, matched by private money and reserve launch slots for British payloads. Then create a fund, with pension money alongside, to back the winners later before they get snapped up. Funding flights without later-stage money merely hands proven technology to foreign buyers. Finally, put a senior minister in charge, with a real budget, to give it more Whitehall clout.

Given the PM’s regional focus, these jobs would also land outside London. Once satellite television is stripped out, manufacturing makes up almost 40 per cent of genuine space employment. Places like Glasgow, Leicester and Cornwall stand to gain, which is precisely the “good growth in every postcode” the Prime Minister promised. Space is a Cinderella industry, but it is time that changed. The PM should take his eyes off the sunset and admire the sunrise instead, and next week’s Budget would be a good place to start.

James Lockyer is a technology analyst and space specialist at investment bank Peel Hunt

John Healey faces several tests in delivering a Budget that keeps the UK economy on course to grow. Mauricio Alencar looks at the questions he will have to answer at the despatch box.

Investors are heading into the upcoming Budget with a lot of unknowns. John Healey faces a test in balancing expectations between different groups – businesses, traders, backbenchers and voters –  and fulfilling a promise to provide “breathing space” to each. 

On the one hand, voters want the Chancellor to support them through a gruelling winter as energy prices set to spike in the coming months. Businesses, who feel bruised after the last two budgets, expect Healey to help rein in their swollen cost bases. Traders are sceptical of a seemingly voracious desire for the government to spend more. And ministers and backbenchers expected Rachel Reeves’ successor to sound a little more Labour. 

But he is delivering a fiscal statement, which may not contain many radical measures, against an economic backdrop that has not been benign to the Treasury over the past two years – even if some green shoots in GDP growth may be starting to emerge. 

Healey has to answer to major impending economic tests on the disjointed jobs market, spiralling inflation and complicated public finances on Wednesday. Should he find solutions to reverse sluggish growth patterns in the UK economy and provide clarity on his fiscal agenda, he could triumph in the near-impossible task of winning over the three key interest groups. 

Healey’s jobs problem

The Chancellor has inherited a problem that is at least partially of the Labour government’s own making. 

With youth unemployment surpassing 16 per cent for the first time in 11 years and hundreds of thousands more people being put out of work since mid-2024, Healey has the challenge of reversing a worrying trend in the jobs market. Taxes and new employment regulations have been blamed by multiple business groups for a rapid deterioration in the jobs market. 

Should he deliver on a faster drop in the unemployment rate than is currently expected, he could benefit from a £40bn windfall in public finances, according to EY. 

As top UK banks cite AI as a reason for slashing headcount, the effort to strengthen the jobs market comes at a tough time. Economists have widely noted that official data did not show enough strong evidence of the technology replacing jobs although Boston Consulting Group director Raoul Ruparel, who was once a special adviser to Theresa May, said a recent fall in payroll data for some young people’s jobs across services industries suggests that there is cause for concern. 

Either way, sectors that rely on people working such as care and hospitality, have radically cut the number of work opportunities that are made available to job seekers. Healey’s support for businesses and workers will be judged on whether he manages to incentivise employers to put up more job offers. 

The pay problem

By several measures of living standards, a number of government ministers including Torsten Bell have claimed that people’s finances were improving over the last two years. 

In 2025, GDP per capita rose by 1.1 per cent after a difficult year of stagnation in 2020. In that year’s Spring Statement, Reeves insisted that growth in real household disposable income would make households up to £500 better off each year. The claims were heavily disputed by think tanks including the Resolution Foundation, who said measures that year would lead to the bottom half of the income distribution being £500 poorer by 2030. 

Since the Iran war, growth in living standards is under significant pressure. While, in real terms, pay has grown after a difficult period of high inflation around 2022 and 2023, those gains now look set to be eroded by a spike in prices.

Data for August showed that a rise in real terms pay increases was hanging off a cliff edge, leading economists at City firms to say it was “extremely likely” that workers on average would take a pay cut. 

A “breathing space” Budget may quickly come undone if Healey fails to provide some certainty that wages will continue to outpace the rate of consumer inflation.

Controlling debt

After a rapid rise in public debt levels after the pandemic, governments have promised to curb borrowing to ease the burden on public finances. 

As the OBR has repeatedly warned, those promises have not been delivered and public debt has continued to march on an upward path. The Office for National Statistics revealed last week it took just six years for gross debt to hit the £3 trillion mark from £2 trillion, having taken about 10 years to rise from £1 trillion. 

Labour officials have now stuck to quoting an International Monetary Fund report praising the UK government for its plans to narrow the deficit around 2031. Opponents have said that such a plan to limit borrowing would only come after an election, and the plans could be kicked even further into the future than that. 

The Chancellor may have a point to prove to the OBR – and therefore markets – that fiscal consolidation will continue and borrowing will not be loosened. 

The growth vision

The likes of Lord Jim O’Neill, the famed economist and ally of Andy Burnham, and Resolution Foundation researchers have suggested the UK economy may be undergoing a productivity boom. 

Results on output per hour have shown promising signs since 2024. On an annualised basis, the UK economy is on course to grow by nearly two per cent this year, far outpacing economists’ expectations. 

But beneath the headline figures, a dispute among analysts has broken out about what is driving the faster rise in GDP. 

While City forecasters surveyed by the Treasury broadly agree the UK economy will grow by between 1.1 and 1.4 per cent next year, there are vast differences in growth of business investment and domestic demand, which underpin consumption levels. 

The starkest difference in opinion comes in estimates for government consumption next year, which covers spending on goods and services such as health, education and defence. 

Last year, the Confederation of British Industry’s forecast, the industry group for the country’s biggest businesses, suggested that high levels of government spending would boost growth in 2026. 

If Healey wishes to provide a firm vision of how he can grow the pie, he may have to indicate just how far the state plans to contribute to a rise in GDP over the coming years.

The slow burn success of this playful malt has inspired a bevvy of rival brands to enter the category. But Monkey Shoulder’s fans are not drinking it because it’s a blended malt. For many it is just a cool, lifestyle brand discovers Tom Bruce-Gardyne.

That cheeky, fun-loving malt from William Grant & Sons, known as Monkey Shoulder, has undergone ‘a global brand relaunch’. 

The three little monkeys that sit on the shoulder of the bottle have been slightly enlarged, given ‘a premium antique-copper finish’, and moved from right to left! It’s the kind of thing that gets PR agencies fizzing with excitement.

For a whisky that doesn’t take itself too seriously, there’s a nice irony in how seriously they take things behind the scenes. “We put an enormous amount of care into the finer details of our packaging because it’s a new challenger brand that people are still discovering,” says Ifan Jenkins, Monkey Shoulder’s global brand MD. 

“Most people meet the brand for the first time through the packaging, which has to say why we’re special, and why we’re different. Packaging is probably the number one responsibility of any marketer – it’s the point of entry for every bar and every eCommerce site around the world.”

The story behind the brand

Launched in 2003, Monkey Shoulder is hardly new, but it is certainly younger than Chivas Regal or Johnnie Walker. For Ifan, “the three monkeys embody the three malts that we use, and link to a nice story of how we got our name.” This blended malt is from Speyside, “home to where the best single malts come from,” he claims. 

The name comes from the old days of floor maltings, when men turned the malt with shovels, flipping it over their shoulder. So, in a strapline yet to be used – it’s the repetitive strain injury you can drink.

As for moving the monkeys around the bottle, that is “because most people read from left to right,” he explains. “And on the backbar, you’re getting greater standout.”  That may be true, but rather more newsworthy is his claim that annual sales of Monkey Shoulder have doubled in the past six years to 800,000 cases.

If it was a slow burn at first, he sees similarities to William Grant’s Hendricks gin, where he used to work, and which he calls “the overnight success that took ten years.” 

Seeding such brands for the long-term requires no end of patience, and that’s something where this privately-owned company believes it has an edge over its publicly quoted rivals. 

Ifan is at pains to stress the importance of the bar trade. “Bartenders have always been a key part of the Monkey Shoulder brand story ever since we started,” he says. “Every year we do lots of training and hold competitions. We have our ‘ultimate bartender championship ’, and we run ‘Camp Monkey’ where we take fifty bartenders from some of the best bars on the planet.” 

In the on-trade, he talks of “three things coming together – great drinks, great people and great music.” 

The brand has been running its Studio Monkey Shoulder for three years to support grassroots music, and this summer it signed Fred again, the British producer, songwriter and DJ, to be its first ever creative partner. 

“We use the on-trade as a marketing lever,” admits Ifan. “We passionately believe in the power of bar advocacy.” 

And yet, if it’s selling 800,000 cases, there must be an awful lot pinging through the tills on the High Street. It is in all the major UK supermarkets at around £30 for a 70cl bottle, dropping to £25 on promotion. You wonder if some of the more edgy bars this whisky aspires to be in are put off by its presence in Asda and Tesco. 

Monkey Shoulder: Made for mixing

The team behind Monkey Shoulder has always pushed the idea of it being a whisky made for mixing. 

This is something of a holy grail for a category that often feels sidelined when it comes to cocktails – a market dominated by white spirits and those bright, neon, Instagram-able spritzes like Aperol. 

Scotch seems to suffer from a certain colour prejudice in how it’s served, and this was surely part of the inspiration for Chivas Crystal Gold, which was launched a year ago. 

Stripped of its amber hue, this almost clear spirit has been seeking to win over cocktail drinkers from premium vodka, gin and Cristalino tequila. Whether Crystal Gold will succeed remains to be seen.

With Monkey Shoulder, Ifan insists “consumers have no problem having it in great cocktails they were introduced to in a bar, or at a music festival or event.” 

For busy occasions, the brand has developed a line of kegged cocktails to provide “high quality drinks served at great pace,” he says. In the past, a fleet of cement mixer trucks were converted to pump out cocktails at live events.

With all this time and effort devoted to promoting the mixability of Monkey Shoulder, an obvious question arises. Why hasn’t William Grant’s launched a ready-to-serve version in a can? A 100ml Monkey Shoulder Old Fashioned feels like a no-brainer.   

“It’s partly prioritisation,” Ifan replies. “At the moment we’ve got enormous headroom for growth in what we’re doing. Numerous consumers around the world haven’t yet discovered Monkey Shoulder. We’re putting our energy into people discovering the brand in bars and on-line and in supermarkets.” 

He talks of building it “bar by bar, dram by dram,” and says: “We carefully take out time to make sure we’ve got the fundamentals in place when we launch into a new market. It’s about making sure we’re in the right bars.” As for the most exciting new markets, he immediately mentions India, where the partnership with Fred again kicks off in December.

More than just a blended malt

Monkey Shoulder may be the most popular blended malt, but that’s not why people buy it. 

Ifan believes its quality credentials from Speyside give new consumers reassurance, and that its provenance matters, however, he accepts that for many people it’s just a “cool, lifestyle brand.” 

He puts its success down to having “the right brand attitude, and always trying to do things differently.” Not having the baggage of a heritage whisky brand must also have helped.

    English football is one of the economy’s greatest successes, generating more than £9bn last season. Yet 94 per cent of clubs from the Premier League to National League are loss-making. 

    These issues have challenged English football for some time, and while the sport attracts substantial global interest, rising costs and uneven revenue distribution are creating severe financial challenges and a precipitous reliance on owner funding.  

    Even if a club is increasing revenue, growth needs to be supported by sufficient liquidity and credible contingency planning.     These additional costs are particularly felt by smaller clubs. Their supporters also inevitably feel the pinch in corresponding ticket price increases. Given the prospect of tax rises seems more likely by the day, fans may be squeezed even further, which could see a subsequent hit in gate revenue. If the Chancellor also goes after employers and businesses, clubs already struggling financially may face further pressures from both sides. 

    Image rights uncertainty

    The 2025 Budget announced the government’s intention to legislate that all image rights payments related to employment would be treated as taxable employment income from 6 April 2027.

    Uzbekistan is a pinnacle of the Silk Road but remains fairly undiscovered. Hannah Copeland went in search of childhood fantasies and got lost in vibrant bazaars

    My fascination with Central Asia began as a teenager when I read a historical romance novel about an Uzbek Princess and her travels along the Silk Road. The epic landscapes and sense of adventure made it a bucket list destination for me. Two decades later, I was finally making it a reality.

    Just getting to Uzbekistan is an experience, starting with the cultural jolt that is Uzbekistan Airways, which left me wondering if I’d boarded a plane to a parallel universe. Most of my fellow passengers appeared to be Uzbeks returning home with designer hauls from Istanbul airport, many of the women flashing their distinctive capped gold teeth (historically a symbol of status and beauty), and the men wearing traditional square ‘doppa’ hats. Others were decked out in Kazakh and Mongolian embroidered robes, leaving me well and truly the sore thumb as I headed to Tashkent, the capital of Uzbekistan.

    Like many sprawling Central Asian cities, Tashkent still has remnants of Eastern bloc influence, with concrete, brutalist architecture that couldn’t be described as beautiful, exactly, but is impressive nonetheless. A shallow earthquake right under the city in 1966 destroyed much of the historic centre, with Soviet planners rebuilding it to showcase state power.

    The Silk Road in style

    It’s a fascinating mix of old and new: imposing statues of bygone conquerors stand alongside mosques with intricate mosaic domes, wide boulevards and leafy parks, bustling bazaars, modern restaurants, and contemporary skyscrapers. Ancient Islamic history and grand artistic design clashes with a youthful vibe from the influx of students and young professionals.

    I was on a seven-day tour operated by Cox & Kings. Established in 1758, it is the world’s oldest travel company, and its tours include access to incredible on-the-ground experts and experiences. Mine included hotels, as well as local food and drink.

    Tashkent’s Old City is a dense maze of traditional clay houses and narrow lanes. I took the metro from the hotel, not because cars weren’t available, but because in Tashkent, public transport is high culture. Uzbek architects and Soviet authorities designed stations as ‘palaces of the people’, the system doubling as an underground art gallery, with marble-clad walls, murals of cosmonauts, and glass chandeliers hanging from the rafters.

    With blue mosaic domes, intricately carved Indian sandalwood doors and gold interiors, the Tillya Sheikh mosque is the city’s most commanding attraction. It’s also home to one of the world’s oldest Qur’ans, written in the 7th century. During my visit there was only a smattering of tourists, and some groups of local children flying colourful kites as part of the Eid celebrations.

    Everyday Uzbek life

    In the weeks before I arrived, 20,000 people gathered each morning to pray in the square. Most locals are curious, open, and fiercely proud of their heritage. In the nearby Abu Bakr Kaffal Shashi Mausoleum, a praying family told me the story of the Imam buried there, who was their great-great (many times over) grandfather.

    In contrast to the serenity of the square, Chorsu Bazaar introduced me to everyday Uzbek life. It is a vibrant spectacle that wallops the senses. One of the most iconic markets in Central Asia, traders have for centuries sold everything from silk Ikat kimonos to hearty local delicacies like plov (a fragrant and oily medley of rice, veg, meat and spices).

    I have to admit some of the bubbling pots and food displays were more alien than haute cuisine, but the smorgasbord of dishes I tried – including dill salad, quails eggs, pickles, mutton pie and lemon tea – was thankfully devoid of some of the slimier offerings I spotted (most notably Hisab, a huge sausage with intestinal casing resembling some sort of monster eel.) Pomegranate juice made fresh with a curious contraption, like an oversized lemon-squeezer, was both bitter and delicious.

    Madrasahs, mosques and minarets

    The ancient city of Bukhara, an hour-and-a-half’s internal flight away, took me deeper into this landlocked country. On the edge of the vast Kyzylkum Desert, it is one of the most complete examples of a medieval Islamic city. Like Tashkent, it has an urbanised part and a contrasting Old Town, where intriguing architectural attractions include madrasahs, mosques and minarets.

    These are relics of a time when the city was one of the main destinations on the Silk Road, when merchants travelled across the globe connecting East and West, exchanging goods, culture and ideas between Asia, the Middle East, and Europe.

    What struck me most was how I saw traces of Western European, Turkish, Persian, Central Asian, Russian and Chinese influence woven in the food, clothing and language.

    As a hoarder of cultural treasures, I was in heaven browsing stalls touting handmade carpets, silk embroidery (suzani), miniature paintings and ceramics. Every beautiful thing I bought came from small family businesses, and was a way to engage with local artists and learn about traditions passed through generations.

    Cox & Kings take guests off the traditional tourist routes, and one curiosity in Bukhara was an opulent, bizarre tearoom called the Retro Saloon Timur. The venue is hidden down a winding back street so tucked away it would evade even the most inquisitive tourist. It serves teas and homemade jams, but what stays with you are the surroundings: every centimetre of wall space is covered by a mix of paintings, from desert scenes to tasteful nudes and grand military portraiture.

    High speed Afrosiyob train

    Gaudy golden ornaments adorn every other orifice: mannequins in elaborate historical costumes grace corners and a mix of Russian and Central Asian music provides a backdrop to AI-generated princes and princesses on TV screens. I’m not quite sure whether owner Irina Sharipova’s intention was ironic tackiness or serious cultural commentary, but either way, it was huge fun: charming and memorable.

    A particularly special evening was spent on the rooftop of Minorai Kalon Boutique Hotel, where I dined al fresco on lamb stew and rosemary potatoes, a mixture of local salads, dill sour cream and pickles, homemade bread and soups. The restaurant overlooks a skyline dominated by a moonlit Po-i-Kalyan mosque and minaret as the call to prayer rings out across the city.

    The next day, I took the high-speed Afrosiyob train to Samarkand, the ultimate destination on any Uzbek itinerary and a city that has held profound wonder for me since those geeky childhood bookworm days, owing to its mystique and Silk Road history.

    The train service was clean, efficient, and modern. You even get a snack of ice cream with raspberries included with the ticket. Over the two-hour journey, I listened to a playlist of Central Asian music while watching the Uzbek countryside zoom past, imagining how caravans of traders once made this expedition on foot or camel.

    Pre-cursor to the Taj Mahal

    One of the oldest cities in the world, celebrated for its unparalleled beauty and historical significance, Samarkand has been a cultural crossroads for thousands of years. This is largely due to geography: its fertile, water-rich location was the junction where Central Asia’s impassable mountains and harsh deserts forced trade routes from China, India, and Persia to converge.

    The central Registan Square holds a trio of madrasahs, or historic Islamic places of study, with the Ulugh Beg, Sher-Dor, and Tilya-Kori each boasting wonderful decorative mosaic frontages. Just a short walk from the Registan is the Bibi-Khanym Mosque, considered by many to be a precursor to the Taj Mahal, which was built some 200 years later (Turco-Mongol conqueror Timur commissioned the building for his wife in the 15th century).

    Before I left, I asked our guide Bobur if he could take me to morning prayer at a small mosque near our hotel. It was worth the early rise to see the city at dawn, hear the Imam chant and witness men, young and old, at their daily ritual of worship in the shadow of the minaret. When they noticed me watching they gestured to the women’s section of the temple, a simple but beautiful room with a rug to pray on, where chinks of morning light seep through a carved wooden door and make an intricate pattern beside the Qur’an. I found it profoundly moving and felt a strong connection to the quiet and welcoming spirit of the place.

    There are few places on earth that feed my childlike imagination and conjure such excitement as Central Asia. I have never been anywhere with such a fusion of ancient cultures and landscapes. The trip whetted my appetite not only to explore the region more fully, but to delve deeper into the country, a destination many avoid in favour of tickbox express tours that can’t possibly do the ‘Stans’ justice. Uzbekistan is both enduring and alive – I’m so grateful to have explored before mass tourism arrives.

    Amendments to Fifa’s Disciplinary Code from January 2027 have attracted attention, but most of the changes have already been binding for almost six months.

    The May 2026 edition of the Code introduced changes affecting clubs, players, agents and their advisers, while January will introduce further changes around domestic enforcement.

    The immediate exposure

    Deadlines are one of the most important changes. Time limits now expire at midnight Eastern Standard Time on the final day rather than midnight Central European Time – in effect, six hours later than before.

    A deadline falling on a weekend or US federal holiday rolls forward to the next working day, and Zurich public holidays no longer count. The risk is miscalculation: parties must now track a foreign time zone and the US holiday calendar.

    The year-end pause no longer protects internal appeals. While most time limits remain paused between 20 December and 5 January, appeals under article 60 are excluded.

    Take a club that receives the reasons for a decision on 19 December. Previously, the clock stopped the following day. Now the three-day window to announce an appeal runs on through the festive period.

    A legal team away until 5 January could return to find the decision final, regardless of its merits, although there is some flexibility with extensions available in certain circumstances.

    Decisions, appeals and sanctions

    A single judge of the Disciplinary Committee may now decide any matter under the Code. A panel must now decide discrimination and match manipulation cases, unless the case is “deemed urgent”.

    Doping cases no longer fall within that guarantee. They go directly to the Appeal Committee, removing one internal stage.

    Internal appeals also carry greater cost risk. Proceedings before the Disciplinary Committee generally remain free, but before the Appeal Committee costs fall on the sanctioned party.

    Where no sanction is imposed, costs are allocated according to the degree of success rather than automatically borne by Fifa.

    For players or officials who admit to a discrimination offence, up to half their sanction may be converted into Fifa-approved educational, communication and training initiatives.

    A team that leaves the field in protest at a refereeing decision, as we saw at in the Africa Cup of Nations final this year, now forfeits the match, with no replay.

    Agents: creditors, sharper risk

    Article 21, which sanctions failure to comply with decisions, now names football agents and match agents among the creditors it protects.

    This gives an agent holding a Fifa or CAS decision over unpaid sums, such as commission, access to Fifa’s enforcement machinery.

    In practice, this means that an agent with an unpaid award can ask Fifa’s Disciplinary Committee to act, potentially resulting in a club being barred from registering new players until it pays. During a transfer window, this creates significant leverage.

    The same provision runs the other way: an agent who ignores a decision against him risks suspension of the licence he trades on.

    What changes in January 2027?

    The January 2027 edition, approved by the Bureau of the Fifa Council in June 2026, concerns decisions of national dispute resolution chambers (NDRCs) recognised under Fifa’s regulations.

    Where a member association fails to enforce a final and binding decision of a recognised NDRC within 60 days, Fifa’s Disciplinary Committee becomes automatically competent to enforce it against the club or individual concerned. From January, Fifa can act directly where an association fails to do so.

    A player who wins before his national chamber but remains unpaid can, after 60 days, take the matter to Fifa, which may impose a registration ban.

    Important questions remain, including when the 60 days begin, how finality will be proved and whether the new route applies to decisions that became final before 1 January 2027.

    Fifa’s disciplinary decisions are not routinely published, and appeals can take considerable time to produce a published award. The rules are live now, and the guidance on how they work may take a few years to emerge.

    Nilo Effori is a sports lawyer and a partner at Brandsmiths.

Mon, 19 Oct 2026 04:13:59 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.10 Researchers tracked the passwords 154 people used online for an average of 147 days and found them logging into 26 websites with fewer than 10 unique passwords — roughly 60 percent were reused outright or built from pieces of passwords they were already using elsewhere https://siliconcanals.com/d-researchers-tracked-the-passwords-154-people-used-online-for-an-average-of-147-days-and-found-them-logging-into-26-websites-with-fewer-than-10-unique-passwords-roughly-60-percent-were-reused/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:30:40 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109740

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

]]> A telemarketer refused to keep his webcam on for nine hours a day while working from home and was fired the next day — a Dutch court ruled the demand invaded his privacy and ordered his employer to pay him roughly €75,000 https://siliconcanals.com/d-a-telemarketer-refused-to-keep-his-webcam-on-for-nine-hours-a-day-while-working-from-home-and-was-fired-the-next-day-a-dutch-court-ruled-the-demand-invaded-his-privacy-and-ordered-his-employ/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:15:27 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109737

A Dutch court sided with a worker who refused constant video surveillance, forcing his employer to pay damages—a warning shot across the evolving battle over remote work monitoring.]]>

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

How common all-day camera rules are

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

]]> Agility’s 284-pound Digit 5 runs for 90 minutes and recharges in nine, a 10-to-1 work-to-charge ratio the company says can deliver more than 20 productive hours a day, with early customer access planned for the first half of 2027 https://siliconcanals.com/n-agilitys-284-pound-digit-5-runs-for-90-minutes-and-recharges-in-nine-a-10-to-1-work-to-charge-ratio-the-company-says-can-deliver-more-than-20-productive-hours-a-day-with-early-customer-access/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 19:00:38 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109721

Agility says Digit 5 is engineered for unfenced work near people; its runtime, charging and daily-productivity figures remain manufacturer specifications ahead of planned 2027 customer access.]]>

Correction, 1 October 2026: An earlier version miscounted the number of charge cycles in a 24-hour day and said early access was more than a year away. The idealised 90-to-9-minute ratio implies about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging; early access is planned for the first half of 2027.

Agility Robotics has unveiled Digit 5, the fifth generation of its bipedal warehouse robot, and the headline change is the safety cage — specifically, its absence. Earlier Digit models, like most industrial robots, operated inside fenced cells to keep people out of reach. Digit 5 is designed to work in the open, using sensors and a separate safety controller that can make it stop, back away or drop into a seated position when a person gets close, according to the company’s hardware rundown from The Robot Report.

The robot stands 5 feet 11 inches tall and weighs 284 pounds, roughly the mass of two adult humans packed into a torso, legs and a pair of articulated arms. That weight matters less as a curiosity than as context for what follows: a machine that heavy needs a battery system that can be recharged fast enough to stay useful across a full shift, and Agility has built its pitch to investors and warehouse customers around exactly that number.

The 90-minute run, nine-minute charge math

Digit 5 runs for about 90 minutes on a charge and returns to full power in roughly 9 minutes, a figure Agility frames as a 10-to-1 run-to-charge ratio, up from the 2-to-1 ratio it says the previous Digit 4 managed, per the company’s own announcement. In practical terms, that means a robot could in theory swap onto a charger for the length of a coffee break and be back on the floor before a human coworker finishes one.

The idealised arithmetic gives each 99-minute cycle 90 minutes of runtime and nine minutes of charging. Repeating that ratio across 24 hours yields about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging before allowing for maintenance, handoffs or faults. That is the basis for the company’s more conservative claim that Digit 5 can deliver more than 20 productive hours in a 24-hour day.

What a 20-hour day actually means

Agility is measuring two things and projecting a third. The 90-minute runtime and 9-minute recharge are specifications the company attaches to Digit 5’s battery hardware. The “more than 20 productive hours” figure is a company calculation built from those two hardware numbers, assuming charging cycles that fit cleanly around a robot’s task queue — no downtime, faults or maintenance stops of the kind that show up in real operations. Agility has not published an independent customer-floor validation of a Digit 5 working day yet.

Independent reporting on the launch has generally repeated the 20-hour figure as Agility’s claim rather than as a verified outcome. IEEE Spectrum’s Evan Ackerman, reviewing Digit 5, raised a broader doubt about Agility’s underlying assumption that the robot can function as what he called “a more or less effortless drop-in replacement for human labor,” noting he was not sure that had happened yet with any robot, anywhere. The one field metric that has been independently reported involves the previous generation, not Digit 5: at a GXO logistics facility, Digit 4 reportedly 98% accuracy sorting totes over more than 100,000 units, a real operational number — though it speaks to picking accuracy, a separate metric from hours worked per day.

Heavier lifts, taller reach than the last generation

Alongside the battery changes, Agility increased what Digit 5 can physically do. The robot can repeatedly lift loads of up to 50 pounds, which the company describes as a 40 percent jump over Digit 4’s payload, and it can reach items up to 7.2 feet high, up from about 5.5 feet on the previous version, according to Forbes’ coverage of the launch. Both changes target the same use case Agility has pursued since the original Digit: moving totes, boxes and cases between conveyors, shelving and pallets in warehouses and distribution centers, work currently done by human “pickers” and “stockers.”

How Digit 5 compares with Boston Dynamics’ Atlas

Agility is not the only company chasing this category, and the comparison is not entirely favorable to Digit 5 on paper. Boston Dynamics’ electric Atlas, per the same Forbes report, is rated to carry up to 66 pounds, reach 7.5 feet and run for about four hours on a hot-swappable battery pack that can be physically pulled and replaced rather than recharged in place. On payload and reach, Atlas currently claims an edge. Digit 5’s advantage is charging speed and, by extension, uptime: a fixed nine-minute recharge cycle is a different operational model than swapping battery packs, and it is the piece Agility is betting its productivity math on.

Orders, a SPAC, and a company still losing money

The timing of the announcement lines up with a corporate transition. Agility disclosed more than $300 million in multi-year customer orders for Digit 5, a figure the company itself qualifies as subject to unspecified contractual milestones being met, and it disclosed the number days after filing paperwork for a SPAC merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a deal valued at roughly $2.5 billion. Regulatory filings tied to that merger show a company still far from commercial scale: Agility net sales and losses came to $1.78 million in 2025, up from $310,000 in 2024, against an operating loss of $140.2 million that roughly doubled year over year, and an auditor’s note flagging “substantial doubt” about its ability to continue as a going concern absent further financing.

That financial picture is the backdrop against which the hardware claims should be read; it doesn’t make them false. A company preparing to go public via SPAC has a direct financial incentive to publish its most favorable operating math right before that listing, and the $300 million order figure and 20-hour productivity claim are doing real work in that narrative, alongside more grounded facts, like Amazon’s $1.05 million purchase of five Digit units — a completed transaction, not a pipeline projection.

What 2027 actually promises customers

Agility says early customer access to Digit 5 is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with general availability, aimed at manufacturing, warehouse and distribution operators, following by the end of that year. The company also plans to extend sales into the European Union and United Kingdom alongside its existing North American base, pending regulatory approval in those markets. Those dates put Digit 5’s actual commercial debut several months out from this week’s unveiling, and every performance figure attached to the robot right now, from its 90-minute runtime to its 20-hour workday, is a specification and a projection. Still, this has not yet been measured on a customer floor.

]]> At 19, an Estonian borrowed €5,000 from his family and recruited Tallinn taxi drivers face-to-face for an app he had built because the city’s taxis were unreliable; twelve years later the company took €2.27 billion in revenue in more than 50 countries and posted its first annual profit — €920,000, a margin of four hundredths of one percent https://siliconcanals.com/n-at-19-an-estonian-borrowed-e5000-from-his-family-and-recruited-tallinn-taxi-drivers-face-to-face-for-an-app-he-had-built-because-the-citys-taxis-were-unreliable-twelve-years-later-the-company-took/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 14:00:26 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109712

An Estonian founder’s company posted its first annual net profit in 2025: €920,000 on €2.27 billion in revenue.]]>

Markus Villig was 19 in 2013, fresh out of high school in Tallinn, and frustrated with how hard it was to get a reliable taxi in his own city. He borrowed €5,000 from his family to build a first version of an app, then did the unglamorous part himself: walking up to taxi drivers on the street in Tallinn and persuading them, one at a time, to sign up. The company launched as Taxify and rebranded as Bolt in March 2019, taking the name from the electric scooter service it had just launched, a signal, as the company put it at the time, that it saw the future of urban transport as electric and intended to be far more than a taxi app. Existing users didn’t have to do anything; the new name and logo simply appeared the next time they opened the app.

From a taxi app to a five-line business

What Bolt actually is today looks very different from what Villig built in 2013. Ride-hailing still accounts for the large majority of its revenue, 82 percent in 2024, according to figures reported in public company profiles of Bolt, but the company has spent the years since methodically bolting on new verticals, largely by copying its own playbook of arriving in a category cheaper and faster than the incumbent. Bolt Food launched in Tallinn in August 2019 and now operates in more than 80 cities across 20 countries with over 30,000 partner restaurants. Micromobility came earlier, e-scooters in Paris from September 2018 and e-bikes from mid-2020, and by early 2023 had grown into roughly 250,000 shared vehicles across 260 cities in 25 countries. Bolt Drive, a car-sharing service, launched in Tallinn in May 2021 and has since spread to Latvia, Lithuania, Germany, Poland, Czechia and Portugal. Bolt Market, a grocery-delivery arm launched the same year, has partnered with the robotics company Starship Technologies on autonomous sidewalk delivery in parts of the Baltics.

A decade of growth without a profit

None of that expansion was cheap, and for most of Bolt’s history it wasn’t profitable either. The company pushed early and aggressively into markets Uber had mostly ignored or arrived in late, establishing itself in South Africa, Kenya and Nigeria as early as 2016, and it now operates in more than 850 cities across over 50 countries spanning Europe, Africa, Asia and Latin America, with more recent entries into Dubai (December 2024) and the Toronto area (February 2025).

Investors funded that land grab at increasing valuations: Bolt crossed $1 billion, and unicorn status, in May 2018 after a $175 million round led by Daimler, according to TechCrunch’s coverage, then climbed to $2 billion by March 2021, $4.75 billion five months later, and $8.4 billion by January 2022.

Revenue kept climbing through all of it. Profit didn’t.

As recently as 2024, the company’s operating loss was €87.7 million even as revenue grew, a pattern common among ride-hailing and delivery platforms still spending to win market share rather than to defend one already won.

Who was willing to fund a decade of losses

Villig’s own €5,000 loan covered exactly one prototype. Everything after that came from investors willing to bet that Bolt’s low-cost, fast-mover approach would eventually outlast better-funded rivals in the markets it entered. The largest of those rounds closed in January 2022: $709 million, co-led by Sequoia Capital and Fidelity Management and Research, with Whale Rock, D1, G Squared and several other funds also participating, valuing the company at $8.4 billion, according to TechCrunch’s coverage of the round.

Bolt said at the time the money would go toward opening more of the small, city-centre “dark stores” that supply its 15-minute grocery delivery service, and toward pushing further into new geographic markets, the same expansion strategy that had defined the company since Villig first stood on a Tallinn street corner recruiting drivers by hand. That January 2022 round is the most recent outside capital the company has raised at scale; the 2025 results suggest it hasn’t needed another one since.

The first profit, and how thin it was

That changed with the 2025 financial year. According to Bolt’s own results, reported in coverage from Trade with Estonia, the company took €2.27 billion in revenue across more than 50 countries, a 14 percent increase on the year before, and posted its first-ever annual net profit: €920,000. Set against €2.27 billion in revenue, that works out to a margin of roughly four hundredths of one percent, the kind of number that is technically profitable and not much more. Operating profit told a similar story of a company just crossing the line, at €19.5 million, reversed from the prior year’s €87.7 million loss. Villig described the underlying business as having reached a $14 billion gross merchandise value run-rate with two consecutive years of positive cash flow, arguably the more meaningful signal for a company at Bolt’s stage than the net income line itself.

What a four-hundredths-of-a-percent margin actually means

A margin that thin is not really a statement about profitability so much as a statement about intent. The accounts do not reveal whether Bolt targeted that result or whether it could sustain growth without further external financing. They show a small net profit and positive operating cash flow for the year, not permanent financial independence. It hasn’t settled every question that scale raises, either.

In November 2024, a UK employment tribunal ruled that Bolt’s drivers qualify as workers rather than independent contractors — a ruling on status only, with compensation still to be set at a separate hearing. Leigh Day, the law firm representing roughly 15,000 drivers in the claim, estimates the compensation owed could exceed £200 million, or upwards of £15,000 per driver on average, according to Leigh Day’s own statement. Whether a margin this thin holds, thickens, or gets eaten by exactly that kind of regulatory ruling as Bolt pushes into new cities, verticals and eventually autonomous vehicles is the open question its 2025 results don’t settle either way.

]]> A country of fewer than 1.4 million people has produced ten billion-dollar startups — about 7 for every million residents, more than three times the US rate — and the first of them was a voice-call app a handful of engineers built in Tallinn in 2003. https://siliconcanals.com/n-a-country-of-fewer-than-1-4-million-people-has-produced-ten-billion-dollar-startups-about-7-for-every-million-residents-more-than-three-times-the-us-rate/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 10:00:24 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109711

Estonia ranks second in the cited per-capita tally—and first in the EU—with about 7.1 startups that have reached a billion-dollar valuation per million residents.]]>

Correction, 1 October 2026: The original excerpt called Estonia the world leader, although the cited per-capita tally places it second behind Liechtenstein. The article also misstated the Tiger Leap school-internet rollout; first-party history says all schools were connected by 2001.

Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

That per-capita figure is a calculation built on CB Insights’ data, not a ranking CB Insights itself publishes, and it is worth reading as a proxy for the ecosystem’s density rather than a formal league table.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. Its goal was blunt: wire the country’s schools for computers and the internet as a deliberate act of catching up. It worked faster than almost anyone expected.

The rollout was rapid but not instantaneous. Education Estonia says all schools had computers by 2000 and all were connected to the internet by 2001. Two decades later, in 2014, the government extended the same instinct outward with e-Residency, a digital identity scheme that lets people anywhere in the world register and run an Estonian company online, without granting them any right to actually live there. Neither programme produced a unicorn by itself. What they produced was a population that treated computers as ordinary tools a generation before most of Europe did, and a legal and administrative system built to let a small number of people start companies with very little friction.

The one that started it

The first of the ten billion-dollar companies was Skype, built in Tallinn in 2003. Its founders, the Swede Niklas Zennström and the Dane Janus Friis, co-founded the company with three Estonian engineers, Ahti Heinla, Priit Kasesalu and Jaan Tallinn, who built the software behind what was then an unusually good way to make free voice calls over the internet. eBay bought the company two years later for a reported $2.6 billion in upfront cash and stock (total consideration including later earn-outs was reported as high as $4.1 billion).

Skype itself has since been folded into Microsoft and no longer exists as a standalone business, but it left something behind in Tallinn that the other nine companies on the list arguably needed first: a generation of engineers and early employees who had already helped build something that scaled to hundreds of millions of users, and who knew, from direct experience, that it could be done from Estonia rather than London or Silicon Valley.

Why the count kept growing

The clearest example of that inheritance is Wise. Its co-founder Taavet Hinrikus was Skype’s first employee; his eventual co-founder, Kristo Käärmann, worked at Deloitte in London. Both were Estonians living abroad with an ordinary, irritating problem: Hinrikus was paid in euros but lived in the UK, and Käärmann was paid in pounds but had a mortgage back in Estonia in euros. According to the company’s own account of its founding, on Wise’s own history page, the two of them started by simply swapping money directly with each other every month, at the real mid-market exchange rate, to avoid their banks’ fees and markups. They launched TransferWise, later renamed Wise, in 2011, and it went public in London a decade later, making both founders Estonia’s first tech billionaires.

That pattern, alumni from one successful company seeding the next, is common in tech clusters generally, but it is unusually visible in a country as small as Estonia, where the total pool of experienced software engineers was never large to begin with, and where a handful of Skype veterans and their networks touch a disproportionate share of what came after. It wasn’t only talent that recirculated. The ecosystem underneath those ten companies is larger and more active than the unicorn count alone suggests. A per-capita unicorn count says nothing about how many of those companies are still worth a billion dollars today, still headquartered in Estonia, or profitable. The part of Vinted’s model that isn’t obvious from the outside is that listing and selling on the platform costs a seller nothing. Underneath the fee structure sits a harder problem: getting a stranger’s old jumper from a seller’s flat to a buyer’s front door, cheaply and reliably, across dozens of countries. An hour disappears into the phone and the honest inventory afterwards runs to three items: a man cutting marble, somebody’s strong opinion about interest rates, a dog on a skateboard.

None of it is retained in any way worth having. The hour still lands like work.

That mismatch, between the feeling of effort and the absence of anything learned, has a reasonable research explanation behind it, and willpower barely features in it.

A feed is a run of cold starts

Reading a book is one long continuous job. The brain loads a setting, a cast, an argument, and then keeps using that same setup for as long as the reading lasts.

A feed offers nothing of the kind.

Each post arrives with its own subject, tone, format and rules, which means the machinery of attention has to reconfigure itself before any of the content can be processed.

A feed adds another recurring job: a verdict. Each item has to be sized up for whether it is true, whether it is funny, whether it is aimed at anyone in particular. That call gets made before the thing can be dismissed, and then made again at the next one, and the one after that.

Psychologists have taken that reconfiguration apart. In a paper published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans described two stages: goal shifting, meaning the decision to do this now instead of that, and rule activation, meaning the swap of mental instructions from the old job to the new one. Both stages take time. A single switch might cost only a few tenths of a second. That sounds trivial until you count the switches inside an hour of scrolling.

Their experiments used arithmetic and shape-sorting rather than phones, so applying the finding to a feed is an inference, not a measurement.

The part that stays behind

Switching also leaves something on the floor. Sophie Leroy, now a professor at the University of Washington Bothell, coined the term attention residue in a 2009 paper in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, after experiments in which people were pulled off one task and pushed onto another. Performance on the second task dropped, because a slice of their attention was still parked on the first, and the effect was sharpest when the first task had been left unfinished.

Scrolling has the shape of that setup. Post after post is dropped mid-thought and replaced by the next one, which looks a great deal like the unfinished condition Leroy identified as the costly one. Her participants were working through lab tasks, though. The parallel to a phone is drawn by analogy, and nobody has run the experiment there.

Forty-seven seconds

Gloria Mark, a professor of informatics at the University of California, Irvine, has been logging how long people stay on a single screen since 2004. Back then the average was about two and a half minutes. In an interview with the University of California, she put the recent figure at roughly 47 seconds, with a median of 40, meaning half of all observed stretches were shorter than that.

That number needs handling with care. It is assembled from separate studies across two decades, not one group of people followed the whole way, and what it measures is screen behaviour. People still read long books. They just do it somewhere other than a browser tab.

Why a book behaves differently

Does the medium itself change how much gets understood? Pablo Delgado of the University of Valencia and three co-authors pooled 54 studies covering more than 171,000 participants in a meta-analysis for Educational Research Review, and found a consistent, modest advantage for paper. The gap widened when reading was timed instead of self-paced, held for informational texts but not narrative ones, and grew across the years studied, an unhelpful trend for anyone expecting digital natives to close it.

Pooling dozens of experiments makes that result sturdier than any single study, though the effect itself stays small.

Maryanne Wolf, who studies the reading brain at UCLA, argues in an op-ed for the Guardian that skimming squeezes out the slower processes that make reading useful: drawing inferences, making analogies, testing whether a claim is true, stepping into another person’s point of view. Move the eye fast enough and there is no room left for any of it.

Fatigue needs its own explanation, and it comes from a separate strand of Mark’s research.

In a study presented at the 2008 CHI conference, Mark, working with Daniela Gudith and Ulrich Klocke, interrupted people mid-task and measured what happened. The interrupted group finished faster, with no drop in quality, which was the surprise. They also reported more stress, more frustration, more time pressure and more effort.

Compensation, in other words.

The brain appears to cover the cost of fragmentation by spending harder. Mark’s participants were working rather than scrolling, and the equivalent test has not been run on a feed, so the link is suggestive rather than established. Even so, the flatness and irritability at the end of a long scroll, the vague sense of having been mugged, match what those participants described.

Which puts the whole exercise in a different light. An hour on a feed involves several hundred small decisions made at speed, each one demanding a quick ruling on what the thing is and whether it matters. The content was the least of it. The deciding was the job.

Nobody sends an invoice for that. The tiredness is the receipt.
