A pair of speakers, two years old, is up for sale online. When no music is playing, they give off an annoying static noise, and the listing does not say so.

A buyer’s message ends with a pointed question: “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” In one of the experiments built around that exact question, 85 percent of sellers mentioned the noise, and fewer buyers than that expected their seller to mention a problem.

Shira Garber and three colleagues staged a string of these secondhand sales online across five main studies and a pilot, added a second pilot that surveyed people about what drives negotiators, and reported the results in an open-access paper in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin this July. Buyers, they found, often underestimated how honest sellers would be. Sellers also reported more concern with being honest, fair and kind, and less concern with the money, than buyers credited them with.

How often did sellers come clean?

In each of the five main studies, some participants played sellers of a secondhand device with a defect they had been told about: an iPod whose battery drained fast, an electric scooter with a faulty battery, the speakers with the static. The rest played buyers, who could earn bonuses for accurately predicting how honest sellers would be.

In the first four studies, a seller counted as honest only if a reply named the defect. Staying quiet counted as dishonest, and so did a dodge like a battery that “isn’t brand new.”

The first pilot set the pattern. Of 76 online workers playing sellers, 63.2 percent picked a truthful opening message over one describing the iPod as being in excellent condition. Of 85 observers given the same information, 43.5 percent predicted the truthful one.

In Study 1, the 176 sellers wrote their own replies to “What can you tell me about it?” and “Anything else?” Of those sellers, 51.7 percent disclosed the battery problem, while the 270 buyers guessed, on average, that 43.2 percent would. With the scooter and a direct question in Study 2, three quarters of sellers disclosed the fault.

The rate swung with the setup. One cause, a direct question, got its own test; other swings the researchers could not fully explain. Until the last study, the exchanges were also largely scripted, with sellers answering pre-written buyer messages rather than a live counterpart.

The way the question is asked

Study 3, with 483 participants, gave half the sellers the pointed “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” and half the open “What can you tell me about them?” Buyers here were not told about the static, which is closer to how a real listing works.

The direct question made sellers more likely to mention the noise. Buyers’ predictions did not move with it.

The gap between expected and actual honesty was statistically significant under the direct question and not under the open one, so even inside this paper it did not show up everywhere. Of several possible reasons Study 1 still found a gap with open questions, the authors single out one: sellers there had two chances to come clean, and concealing twice may weigh more on a seller’s conscience than concealing once.

A few minutes of small talk

Study 5 was the only one that paired people live. It matched 422 participants into 211 buyer-seller pairs on an online platform, and some pairs first spent three minutes chatting about something they had enjoyed recently or how they unwind after a busy day.

Across the study, buyers rated their seller’s likely honesty at 6.56 on a ten-point scale, while coders scored the sellers’ actual replies at 7.51. Among pairs who chatted first, that difference was no longer statistically significant. Sellers’ scores did not differ significantly between the two conditions. The chat raised buyers’ expectations of honesty instead.

Study 4 tried a different nudge on 358 participants. Some buyers were asked about the seller’s moral concerns before predicting, others afterward. Thinking about the seller’s conscience first raised buyers’ expectations, and the gap was nearly halved.

It did not close. The authors suggest one reason: 85 percent of sellers in that study disclosed, a rate higher than in the matching condition of Study 3 for reasons they say are not readily apparent.

Study 2 measured three motives, adding the pull of money to the two that Study 1 had tracked. The 214 management undergraduates who took part rated, on a seven-point scale, how much the seller had been weighing being decent, feeling guilty, and getting the best price. The sellers still cared about the money. They cared about it less, and about their own decency more, than the buyers pictured.

The paper’s explanation leans on moral typecasting, the idea that people tend to see others as either doers or feelers, rarely both. A seller holds the object and the information, so, the authors argue, a buyer casts them as a doer, and the competitive setting makes that doer look like someone chasing an advantage rather than guarding a clean conscience. In the abstract’s words: “While sellers tended to be honest because of moral identity concerns, buyers expected them to be driven primarily by self-interest.”

Two duller explanations get a hearing too, and the authors say their own mechanism is not the only one. Poor forecasting in general, they point out, gives no reason to expect guesses to run low rather than high. Plain caution, a buyer bracing for the worst to avoid a loss, gets mixed treatment: the Study 4 discussion offers it as a possible added force, while the general discussion says it cannot explain the results, because in the first pilot observers with nothing at stake still underestimated the sellers.

Their mediation analyses deserve a lighter touch than the abstract’s sentence suggests. Buyers and sellers answered parallel versions of the motive questions rather than the same ones, and the authors say the results should be “cautiously interpreted” for that reason. Sellers rated their motives after choosing whether to disclose, which leaves room for a flattering story told afterward, though the authors argue buyers’ parallel ratings may reduce that concern. And in Study 1, the measure of anticipated guilt and related feelings showed no significant difference between buyers and sellers.

Small stakes, narrow scope

The stakes stayed small. Most bonuses were paid by lottery, and a seller in Study 1 had a five percent chance of earning at most $7. The authors grant that low stakes may keep self-interest from fully switching on, while citing earlier work that finds self-interest at work even when stakes are small.

The honesty studied was one kind: telling a buyer about a defect the seller knew. Misrepresenting a bottom price or inventing urgency, both named by the authors, were outside the design. They describe the findings as “based primarily on Western participant samples,” and the sales were one-off exchanges between strangers, chosen to keep reputation largely out of play. Ongoing work relationships and repeat customers sit outside what was measured.

Suspicion is sometimes the sensible response, and the paper says so. A buyer facing a salesperson expected to use persuasion tactics, or shopping where one side knows far more than the other, as with used cars, has good reason for care. The paper does not argue for trusting everyone. It asks for work on when doubting a counterpart’s honesty hurts a negotiator and when it protects one.

Every finding in this piece comes from the published text and tables of one paper, read by an editorial desk that reports on research and does not train negotiators; the supplementary files the paper points to could not be opened. The studies compared predictions with replies across hundreds of people, which says something about buyers and sellers like the ones studied, taken as groups, and cannot tell anyone whether the particular seller in their inbox is being straight with them. For a purchase that matters, sensible safeguards include an independent inspection, a written description of the item’s condition, and the buyer protection some platforms offer.

This paper did not measure what the gap costs. The authors’ illustration is a used car that looks too good to be true, and a buyer who distrusts the seller, walks away, and settles for something worse. Examining what the honesty gap does to the outcomes of negotiations is what they call an important next step; they also call for testing the idea where far more money is at stake.

The last time I was properly lost, I was standing at a petrol station somewhere north of Chiang Rai with a dead phone, a warm bottle of water and a dog who clearly ran the place. My bus had left without me. I had four hours to wait, nothing to do and no way to tell anyone about it.

It was the calmest I had been in about eighteen months.

Sometimes you find yourself in the middle of nowhere, and sometimes, in the middle of nowhere, you find yourself.

Yes, it is the sort of line that ends up engraved on a bracelet and screwed to somebody’s kitchen wall. Both of which have happened, it turns out. I went looking for whoever wrote it and found nothing, only evidence that it has been circulating since at least 2014 with no author attached. Anonymous, then. It holds up better than most things sold at a craft market.

Nowhere is mostly an absence of audience

Here is what I think the line is really about. Nowhere has very little to do with distance. It is any situation where nobody knows your job title.

In a city you are surrounded by people who already have a version of you loaded. The neighbour who thinks you are the loud one. The old colleague who still introduces you by the thing you did in 2019. You end up performing that version without noticing, because it is easier than correcting everybody.

Take the audience away and something odd happens. For a day or two you feel faintly useless, because nobody needs anything from you. Then the noise drops. You start hearing your own opinions, which are less impressive and a good deal more honest than the ones you say out loud.

That is the whole mechanism. No mysticism required.

The year my diary went blank

I lost my business, restaurants, during the pandemic. The deal was agreed over a phone call while I sat on a plastic chair in a dining room with the lights off, and it was the least bad option available to me at the time.

For years my day had been decided for me by suppliers, staff rotas and the seven o’clock rush. Then it was not. I woke up on a Tuesday with an empty calendar and genuinely no idea what a Tuesday was for.

I would love to tell you this was peaceful. I reorganised the same cupboard twice. I developed strong opinions about a neighbour’s parking. I rang people I had not spoken to in five years and could hear them wondering what I wanted.

The useful part arrived about three months in, once I had run out of things to tidy. With no restaurant to point at, I had to work out what I would actually do with a day if nobody was paying me for it. The answer was writing, which was inconvenient, as it pays considerably worse than a burger.

You can get lost for the price of a bus ticket

You do not need to sell a business or fly to Patagonia. Nowhere comes in small doses and most of them are free.

Pick a district of your own city you have no reason to visit and spend three hours there on foot. Not a famous one. A dull one, with hardware shops and a wet market and nothing on sale to anyone carrying a suitcase. I do this in Bangkok about once a month and I have never regretted it, though I have frequently regretted the shoes.

Go somewhere your phone cannot help you. Not switched off, just outgunned: the lanes are not on the map and the only language on offer is one you do not speak.

Be a beginner at something in public. Take a class where you are visibly the worst person in the room. It is physically uncomfortable for about twenty minutes. After that it stops mattering, and what is left is quite close to fun.

And if you do travel, leave one day entirely unplanned. No booking, no list, no reservation you have to walk fast to reach. Most people schedule a trip so tightly that they never get further than a warmer version of their normal week.

What actually turns up

Let me manage expectations. You do not come back from a petrol station with a revelation.

What you come back with is a shorter list. Two or three things you thought you cared about turn out to belong to somebody else. One or two things you have never mentioned to anyone are suddenly all you think about when there is nothing else to think about. That is it. It looks like very little on paper. It does not feel that way at thirty-eight, when you are still doing a job you picked at twenty-two to impress someone who stopped watching years ago.

There is a trap in this, though. Some people use the middle of nowhere as somewhere to hide, and the giveaway is that they keep having to go back. If every trip is an escape from the same unaddressed thing at home, the scenery is doing the work of a conversation you have been avoiding. Distance is excellent for seeing a problem clearly. It has never once solved one for me.

The dog at the petrol station, for the record, took no interest in any of this. He sat under the ice cabinet, moved twice in four hours, and had evidently worked something out about Wednesdays that I am still catching up on.

I used to think of a certain kind of person as a weather system. You know the type. You ask how the traffic was and somehow you have insulted their driving, their neighbourhood and their late mother. Everything lands as a slight. Everything requires a correction.

For years my take on this was simple and a bit smug. Attention seekers. People who enjoy the theatre of being wronged.

Then I started reading the actual psychology, and it turns out I had the story backwards. The people who seem offended by everything are rarely shopping for a fight. Most of them are running a security detail, and they have been running it since they were small.

When insults were the weather, everything looks like an insult

Here is the mechanism. If you grow up somewhere that regularly treats you as a target, your brain gets very good at spotting incoming fire. That is not a flaw. In the original environment it was survival. The problem is that the skill does not switch off when you move somewhere safer.

Psychologists call this hostile attribution bias, and it shows up early. Researchers followed around 1,300 children across nine countries and gave them scenarios where someone’s behaviour could be read as an accident or as deliberate. A shove in a corridor. A joke that could go either way. The children who consistently read hostile intent went on to show higher rates of persistent aggressive behaviour, even after accounting for how aggressive they had already been.

Two children see the same shove. One files it under accident, one files it under attack. Twenty years later, one of them is the adult who somehow takes offence at the weather report.

Being told you are too much is its own training

The other route in is quieter and I suspect more common.

Some people are not knocked around. They are simply corrected, constantly, about their own inner life. You are not upset. You are not tired. That did not hurt. Stop being dramatic. Clinicians call this an invalidating environment, a setting that consistently dismisses or punishes someone for expressing what they feel or need.

The theory behind that term was built to explain a specific clinical picture, so I would not go throwing it at your touchy colleague as a diagnosis. But the underlying logic travels. If your read on your own experience gets overruled a thousand times, you learn something ugly. You learn that your sense of things will not be taken seriously unless you make it loud.

And making it loud is exactly what the rest of us punish. We call it oversensitivity. We are reading the receipt and ignoring the purchase.

The tax the sensitive person pays

None of this is a free pass, and here is where it stops being sympathetic.

Researchers describe a disposition they call rejection sensitivity, meaning a tendency to anxiously expect rejection, spot it readily, and react hard when you think you have found it. People high in it tend to be less satisfied in their close relationships, and their partners report the same.

The trap is that the vigilance manufactures the thing it fears. You brace for the cold shoulder, so you go cold first. Your partner feels the chill and pulls back. Now you have evidence. Now the system that was built to protect your dignity has quietly started demolishing it.

I have watched this happen up close, over what I promise you was a genuinely neutral text message. There was no villain in that story. There was a very old alarm and a very ordinary Tuesday.

What actually helps when you are on the receiving end

Arguing about whether the offence was reasonable is a losing game. The alarm is not calibrated to this conversation. It was calibrated years ago, by somebody else.

Try naming the feeling without conceding the facts. Something like: I can see that landed badly, and I did not mean it that way. That costs you nothing on the question of intent, and it grants them something rare, which is agreement that their reaction was real. It does more work than an hour of you proving your innocence.

Be boringly consistent. Vigilance responds to evidence, not reassurance, and that takes months. You cannot talk someone out of a threat detector. You can only give it a long run of days where nothing bad happens.

And hold your line anyway. Understanding why someone snaps is not the same as accepting being snapped at. You can say plainly that you will not be shouted at and still mean everything above.

And if the thin skin is yours

Then start somewhere other than whether you were right. You often are. Slights are real, and some of the people telling you to calm down are exactly the ones worth watching.

The more useful question is what the alertness is costing you. Running security is expensive. It eats your Sundays. It makes you rehearse conversations that never happen and re-read messages for tone that was never there. My grandmother had a version of this. It made her formidable company. I think it also made her lonely.

So build a delay. When something lands wrong, wait a day before you respond. Graciousness has nothing to do with it. You are checking whether the feeling survives a night’s sleep. Usually it does not. The ones that do are worth taking seriously, and now you can take them seriously without the static.

]]>

The Robot Report https://www.therobotreport.com/ Robotics news, research and analysis Mon, 26 Oct 2026 14:10:21 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 https://www.therobotreport.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/cropped-robot-report-site-32x32.png The Robot Report https://www.therobotreport.com/ 32 32 Agility and GXO Logistics plan expanded deployment of Digit humanoid https://www.therobotreport.com/agility-gxo-logistics-plan-expanded-deployment-digit-humanoid/ https://www.therobotreport.com/agility-gxo-logistics-plan-expanded-deployment-digit-humanoid/#respond Mon, 26 Oct 2026 14:05:21 +0000 https://www.therobotreport.com/?p=590002 GXO Logistics, which has tested humanoid robots from multiple companies, will deploy Agility's Digit at two more sites.

The post Agility and GXO Logistics plan expanded deployment of Digit humanoid appeared first on The Robot Report.

]]>

Agility and GXO have been collaborating since 2023. Source: GXO Logistics

Agility Robotics and GXO Logistics today said they are expanding their partnership to deploy Agility’s Digit humanoid robot in GXO sites in North Carolina and Tennessee.

“GXO was the first customer to put Digit to work in live operations under a commercial agreement, and expanding to additional sites is the clearest signal that the value is real,” stated Peggy Johnson, CEO of Agility. “Customers are moving beyond asking whether humanoid robots can work to deciding where they can scale them. Years of experience performing real work in GXO’s operations have shaped how we build, deploy and support Digit, and we’re focused on disciplined execution as we grow this partnership.”

Founded in 2015, Agility Robotics said it has more than 65,000 hours of real-world operation working with industry safety standards. The Salem, Ore.-based company recently got U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission approval for its planned merger with special-purpose acquisition company (SPAC) Churchill Capital Corp. XI as it prepares to go public.

In 2024, Digit earned Agility the inaugural RBR50 Robot of the Year award for being one of the first humanoids to enter commercial trials. It received 2026 honors for moving more than 100,000 totes for GXO last year. This month, the company chose Nyobolt for fast charging, expanded its partnership with NVIDIA, and said it plans to deploy Digit at an AGCO factory for agricultural equipment in 2027.

GXO and Agility continue collaboration

Spun out of XPO Inc. in 2021, GXO Logistics claimed that it is “the world’s largest pure-play contract logistics provider.” The third-party logistics provider (3PL) has more than 150,000 employees across over 1,000 facilities, totaling more than 200 million sq. ft. (18.5 million sq. m). The Greenwich, Conn.-based company last month partnered with Exotec to automate fulfillment for Guess in the Netherlands, and like Agility, its executives participated in keynote panels last week’s RoboBusiness event.

GXO and Agility first deployed Digit in late 2023 in at a facility in Flowery Branch, Ga. The companies asserted that it was the industry’s first commercial deployment of humanoid robots in live operations and the first robotics-as-a-service (RaaS) agreement for humanoid robots.

Since then, Digit has moved more than 100,000 totes at the Flowery Branch facility, demonstrating its ability to perform repetitive material handling tasks reliably in an active logistics environment. The robot uses the Agility Arc cloud-based fleet management and integration platform. It has worked alongside existing automation to move totes and place them onto conveyors.

“Innovation is most powerful when it delivers practical solutions that create value for our customers and our people,” said GXO CEO Patrick Kelleher. “Our partnership with Agility Robotics has been defined by a shared commitment to turning emerging technologies into real-world operational advantage. Together, we’ve helped pioneer the use of humanoid robotics in the warehouse and this expansion reflects our confidence in the technology’s ability to create measurable value for our customers and a better working environment for our teams.”

Digit will move from handling bins to more applications. Source: Agility

GXO Logistics has tested other humanoids

GXO has also tested humanoid robots including Apollo from Apptronik and Reflex from Reflex Robotics. In the company’s second-quarter earnings call in August, Kelleher acknowledged that it had not yet deployed humanoids in production, nor had they produced a return on investment (ROI).

“We’ve done 45 pilots on humanoids so far. We have an additional pilot launching in Europe very shortly,” he said at the time. “We have not achieved ROI on humanoids yet. I think we are a couple of years away from that, but we’re seeing such great progress with our partners around the efficacy of that technology and the application opportunities that it has in the warehouse environment.”

GXO did not say how much it is investing in the Digit expansion or when and if it expects ROI. The Robot Report has reached out and will share any additional comment or clarification.

Partners plan to deploy Digit to more U.S. sites

Under the expanded agreement, Digit will support e-commerce fulfillment at GXO sites in Statesville, Tenn., and Lebanon, Ind. The companies said they expect to begin deployments of Digit 4 in in early 2027.

Digit 5, which Agility unveiled last month, is designed with new legs, to operate safely near people, and to address a wider range of industrial workflows. GXO said it will migrate to Digit 5 when it becomes commercially available.

“The expansion reflects GXO’s long-standing approach to advancing warehouse automation through practical implementation at scale,” said GXO. “As an industry leader in advanced automation and physical AI, GXO partners with leading technology developers to test, refine and deploy emerging solutions in live operating environments. The expanded partnership underscores GXO’s and Agility’s shared commitment to accelerating innovation through real-world application and continuous learning.”

Agility also noted that it has invested in infrastructure to manufacture, deploy, and support humanoid robots at scale, including its 70,000 sq. ft. (6,503.2 sq. m) RoboFab facility to manufacture up to 10,000 robots per year. The company has also expanded software and service capabilities, as well as announced plans for a new 50,000 sq. ft. (4,645 sq. m) facility in Pittsburgh to support commercial deployments.

The post Teradyne Robotics partners with Sereact to scale physical AI in retail and logistics appeared first on The Robot Report.

]]>

At Zalando’s fulfillment centers in Germany and Poland, Sereact and Universal Robots now autonomously processes returned fashion items. | Source: Teradyne Robotics

Teradyne Robotics, the company behind Universal Robots and Mobile Industrial Robots, last week partnered with Sereact. The companies aim to accelerate industrial AI solutions in retail, logistics and manufacturing.

Through this partnership, Sereact’s Cortex physical AI platform runs robot arms from Universal Robots to give retailers and logistics providers a proven way to automate unstructured tasks such as returns handling and piece picking. Together, the companies have already shipped hundreds of UR robots in dual-arm systems to live customer sites across Europe.

“Physical AI only matters when it performs in real-world operations, and that is where Universal Robots has always been at home,” said Jacob Pascual Pape, the chief commercial officer of Teradyne Robotics. “Our robots are built for the AI era: open, connected, and proven through more than 100,000 industrial deployments. That is why Sereact has chosen our platform.”

“When combined with Sereact’s Cortex, the joint solution handles mixed goods, unknown items, and varied packaging,” he added. “This has moved well beyond the demo or pilot stage with the technology now usefully deployed at real customer sites. Our technologies are a natural fit and through our partnership we will scale these AI-powered solutions fast across applications, industries and markets.”

To serve the rapidly growing demand and bring the joint solution to North America, Sereact this summer opened U.S. headquarters in Charlestown, Mass. The company develops physical AI software that enables robots to grasp, identify, and handle objects they have never seen before. The companies made the announcement at NVIDIA GTC Berlin 2026.

Teradyne and Sereact already have deployments running

Teradyne Robotics and Sereact said their joint offering can help a variety of critical logistics and manufacturing use cases. These include piece picking and sortation, order induction, machine tending, bin consolidation, kitting, packing, and goods handling.

“Returns, replenishment, kitting — with Cortex, every one of these applications runs on the same production model. One brain serves every robot, with no retraining for each new item or task. And what one robot learns, every robot benefits from,” said Dr. Ralf Gulde, co-founder and CEO of Sereact. “Partnering with Teradyne Robotics and its global distribution and integrator network helps us bring that one brain to their customers around the world, accelerating the abilities of retailers and logistics providers to adopt AI-powered automation across their operations.”

The company is already deploying the system with CEVA Logistics for Zalando, a European technology platform for fashion and lifestyle. At Zalando’s fulfillment centers in Greven, Germany, and Świebodzin, Poland, the robots now autonomously process returned fashion items. This is the first phase of a broader initiative to scale returns automation across Europe.

“Returns are one of the hardest jobs in logistics,” said Gulde. “Returned products almost never arrive in a robot-friendly sequence. Items differ in shape, orientation and packaging, and the mix changes continuously.”

“That is exactly what Cortex is built to handle on the Universal Robots platform,” he said. ”By rapidly reconditioning returned goods for resale, the solution also helps retailers comply with European Union regulations prohibiting the destruction or landfill disposal of returned merchandise.”

NVIDIA plays a role in the collaboration

NVIDIA’s technologies are a key part of the Sereact and Universal Robots demonstration at GTC Berlin. Cortex is trained in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, an open simulation framework, using NVIDIA Cosmos open world models.

It is post-trained with reinforcement learning using NVIDIA Isaac Lab framework and benchmarked on Teradyne Robotics hardware before any model is deployed. In deployment, Cortex runs on NVIDIA Jetson Thor at the cell where inference must happen at line speed and on NVIDIA DGX Spark for site-level development, validation and model updates.

Teradyne Robotics also uses NVIDIA computing in its Universal Robots cobots and Mobile Industrial Robot platforms. The company said it is contributing SimReady OpenUSD robot assets to SimReady Central Library on Hugging Face for both UR and MiR products, helping developers discover and reuse robot models in simulation with less asset preparation.

The post Eka Robotics raises $150M to scale its vision-force-action model for robots appeared first on The Robot Report.

]]>

Eka says its model can generalize across objects, tasks, and environments. | Source: Eka Robotics

Eka Robotics this week said it has raised $150 million in Series A funding. The startup said the new funding will help it scale its technology and customer deployments.

Founded in 2024, Eka is building a vision-force-action (VFA) model to develop an intuition of physics through reinforcement learning at scale. The Cambridge, Mass.-based company said that robots using its AI can pick a wide variety of objects outside the training distribution at a speed of roughly 1,500 operations per hour.

The same robots can screw in a light bulb and insert wires, Eka asserted.

Robots shouldn’t just mimic humans, says Eka Robotics

Eka Robotics said it is targeting dexterous manipulation. The company said that for robots to handle complicated work, they need the versatility to handle changing conditions and the performance to deliver useful work every day.

Eka also said it believes that robots should master physics, not mimic human data, to be truly general-purpose. This would allow the robot to build “intuition” for tasks the same way a human can by jointly reasoning about vision and forces.

The company uses simulation learning, and it said its VFA model is demonstrating that the typical sim-to-real barrier is falling. In simulation, the company can generate thousands of hours of robot experience in minutes, varying objects, environments, and physical conditions.

Eka claimed that transferring this learning to the real world unlocks a scalable, performant, and capital-efficient path to a foundation model for manipulation. “Reinforcement learning at scale buys performance, and breadth of experience buys generality,” it said.

Investors seek to level up dexterous manipulation

Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) and F-Prime, a venture capital fund affiliated with FMR LLC, the parent company of Fidelity Investments, led the round.

“Eka’s Vision-Force-Action model is the first approach I’ve seen that truly solves manipulation with the generality and throughput needed for deployments,” stated Raghu Raghuram, a general partner at a16z. “This team has the ideal DNA to push the frontier of robotics research while scaling commercial operations.”

Eka Robotics’ Series A included continued support from the lead investors in its seed round, Obvious Ventures and E14 Fund. Other funding came from MFV Partners, Bison Ventures, Glasswing Ventures, Samsung Next, and several Fortune 500 strategics.

“From the factory floor, a robot’s value comes down to two things: its success rate and its speed over thousands of repetitions,” said Shyam Kamadolli, a managing director at Fine Structure Ventures. “Early on, I recognized that current approaches to generalization simply won’t get us there. Achieving the next level of performance requires a deep understanding of physics and, crucially, breaking free from our dependence on human demonstrations.”

“Eka’s VFA model, trained through simulation and reinforcement learning, achieves this for the hardest problem in robotics, dexterous manipulation, in a way no other company has,” he added. “I truly believe Eka’s approach is the only one that will hold up in real-world deployments of complex tasks.”

]]>

Vecna Robotics makes its systems in the U.S. and is not directly affected by the FCC ruling. Credit: Eugene Demaitre

In July, the Federal Communications Commission, or FCC, said it had determined that certain foreign-made advanced robots pose a cybersecurity and competitive risk to the U.S. It has restricted imports of new models of advanced robotic devices, including mobile robots and legged robots.

What should companies considering purchases of such robots do? What are some of the concerns around design, deployment, and ongoing support?

Leaders from Vecna Robotics, Locus Robotics, and the Association for Advancing Automation (A3) will discuss the practical implications of the commission‘s determination in a free webinar at 2:00 p.m. ET on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. The panelists will examine how connected systems differ from traditional automation.

Webinar attendees can also learn how companies can evaluate the long-term supportability of their robotics investments. They will hear perspectives on strengthening supply chains, questions buyers should be asking their technology providers, and what the changing landscape could mean for the U.S. robotics industry.

Register now to learn about FCC policy implications

The webinar will also help attendees:

  • Identify what types of robots and companies are affected by the FCC action
  • Understand the intent behind the restriction and other U.S. policies under consideration, such as tariffs
  • Build acquisition, implementation, and service strategies for resilience
  • Track how the robotics ecosystem is reacting to U.S. and competitive challenges
  • Be aware of standards efforts in addition to regulatory changes
  • Look at long-term trends in automation

Register now to attend this webinar, which is sponsored by Vecna Robotics. The panelists will answer questions during the live broadcast, which will be available on demand afterwards to registrants.

About the webinar panelists

Karl Iagnemma is CEO of material handling systems provider Vecna Robotics Inc. He holds a Ph.D. from MIT and was director of the MIT Robotic Mobility Group.

Iagnemma previously founded nuTonomy, the world’s first venture-backed driverless car software business, which was acquired by Aptiv for $450 million. Under his leadership, nuTonomy was spun out into Motional, a $4 billion joint venture with Hyundai Motor Co.

Karl brings a wealth of experience in scaling robotics companies from research through commercialization to Vecna.

Rick Faulk is CEO of warehouse automation supplier Locus Robotics Corp. He leads its executive team with more than 30 years of experience in executive management, sales, and marketing for some of the world’s most successful technology companies, such as Cisco, Intronis, j2 Global, WebEx, Intranets.com, Barracuda Networks, Lotus Development, Mzinga, and PictureTel.

Faulk leads Locus Robotics’ executive team and is responsible for the overall strategy and execution at the company. Generative Bionics this week announced plans to build a proprietary, multi-site “Physical AI Data Factory” in Italy. The company said the new 5,000-sq.-m (53,819.5-sq.-ft.) hub will help move humanoid robotics from laboratory demonstrations to reliable industrial deployment.

In addition, Generative Bionics said it hopes to advance European humanoid sovereignty, ensuring that the data, models, and know-how behind Europe’s industrial humanoids are generated, trained and validated on the continent.

“The value that Europe has right now is within its industry, and we have to extract physical AI data in order to train our own models,” Daniele Pucci, the CEO of Generative Bionics, told The Robot Report. “This is a competitive advantage that Europe right now has, because of the automation that we have been putting in place over the last 40 years.”

Generative Bionics said the new facility will be operational by the fourth quarter of 2027. The Genoa, Italy-based company plans to eventually open a second facility elsewhere in Europe and a third serving global markets. Together, the three facilities will reproduce real industrial environments, generate high-fidelity physical data, and connect that data with large-scale simulation.

Building on their strategic technology collaboration, Advanced Micro Devices Inc. will be Generative Bionics’ AI infrastructure partner, and the Physical AI Data Factory network will be powered by AMD Helios. Its rack-scale architecture will provide the compute foundation to process physical and synthetic data, train physical AI models, and run thousands of digital-twin scenario variations in parallel.

Data Factory to test GENE.01 in a range of industries

The Physical AI Data Factory will connect real-world robot operations, simulation and AI development in a continuous real-to-sim-to-real cycle, said Generative Bionics. The company said this will allow it to configure and validate its GENE.01 humanoid robot for specific industrial environments before customer deployment, then feed data from deployed fleets into future training cycles.

Industrial humanoids must learn from the conditions they will encounter at work, noted the Generative Bionics. This requires data that captures contact, force, motion, proximity, temperature, task constraints, and human interaction in realistic operating settings. For GENE.01, the dataset will include vision and motion data as well as signals captured through its full-body multimodal skin.

“A robot is not only vision and is not only language,” said Pucci. “It is position, velocity, acceleration, temperature, and contact forces, so there is a large variety of data that you have to take into account.”

The Data Factory will reproduce environments selected with industrial partners and allow fleets of GENE.01 robots to perform tasks continuously in real-world conditions. These operations will generate high-fidelity physical data for training world action models (WAM) and validating the complete robot system, including perception, control, safety behavior, and task execution, before deployment at customer sites.

Each physical environment and robot configuration will also be recreated as a digital twin. The same tasks can then be repeated across thousands of variations in layout, objects, materials, operating conditions, and failure modes that would be impractical to reproduce physically. Models trained and tested in simulation will be deployed back to the robots for validation, while data from physical operations will feed the next training cycle.

Generative Bionics wants to help find robot ‘ChatGPT moment’

Large language models (LLMs) learn from vast amounts of information available online, noted Generative Bionics. Humanoid robots have no comparable source of data on how to act in the physical world.

The Physical AI Data Factory will create such a source by collecting data as GENE.01 performs industrial tasks and expanding those experiences through digital-twins running on AMD compute.

“We have the ambition of being the European champion in physical AI, and even robotics, designed to scale globally,” said Pucci. “That’s our clear positioning, and for this, we are taking a close look at the supply chain that can supply our future manufacturing.”

“Manufacturing here is divided into three levels: the manufacturing of data, the manufacturing of robots, and the manufacturing of models,” she continued. Pucci said if Europe wants to achieve sovereignty in this area, it needs to invest in all three.

Right now, humanoid robots from China have been garnering a lot of attention with flashy demos and large funding rounds. But, Pucci, notes that this doesn’t mean the country is necessarily ahead of Europe.

“I want to be crystal clear about this. Many of the Chinese robots that are out there are simply not certified to enter industrial settings,” Pucci said. “The narrative that the Chinese solved as the issues is very far from reality.”

“Right now, we believe that many of the existing solutions are basically for entertainment, and this is a market segment that we respect,” she added. “But, Generative Bionics is taking the issue of safety and certification very seriously because we want to go B2B first.”

GENE.01 can be customized for specific applications

Generative Bionics claimed that a few things separate its platform from the average humanoid robot. To start, GENE.01 features full-body tactile sensing.

“It comes naturally to give the humanoid robots the sense of touch, because humanoid robots have to perceive people not only while talking, but also while interacting with them physically,” Pucci said. “That’s why GENE was given this unique multimodal scheme, which can perceive not only the sense of touch but also the sense of proximity.”

Generative Bionics also plans to offer GENE.01 as a base platform that can be customized for different industries.

“We have a clear view that humanoid robots cannot be used for anything that comes to your mind, because a humanoid robot welding in a shipyard cannot be the same as a humanoid robot in healthcare,” noted Pucci. “There is a fundamental difference in the development cycle.”

The company has three levels of customization. “The first one is the AI, because a robot moving boxes does not need the same AI of a robot in healthcare,” said Pucci. “The second is the exterior design. In the shipyard, you have to be resistant against high temperatures, sparks, and powders. The third is the hands and the feet.”

“This is really scalable at the manufacturing level, because you have a common platform, and then you can customize at the end the so-called end of lines at these three levels,” she continued. “This is basically the same approach that you have in automotive.”

Generative Bionics is building on more than 20 years of research, development, and prototyping of humanoids at the Italian Institute of Technology (IIT). The company spun out of IIT in 2024, and IIT has granted it exclusive licenses to key technologies.

“Dream-1 approaches a new robot the same way, so a new robot can do useful work in minutes, not months,” he added. “And instead of edited demos, we’re giving people a working model they can test themselves, mistakes included.”

B Capital and Kindred Ventures led the round. It also included participation from A.Capital, Unusual Ventures, SV Angel, Wing VC, Scribble VC, and Adrian Aoun, among others.

Developers and robot enthusiasts can start using Dream Labs’ AI products today. The company said Dream API translates visual inputs and natural language prompts directly into robot actions.

The company also offers fine-tuning as a service. For unsupported hardware or new capabilities, developers and robot makers can submit a small batch of demonstration data to receive a tailored model within hours.

Developers also have access to Dream Labs’ robot playground. Anyone with a browser can type commands to a robot in Dream Labs’ San Francisco office and watch it respond live and unedited, no robot purchase required.

Dream Labs supports robots today that cost between about $2,000 and $10,000. Dream-1 needs no extra data to control a two-armed robot with parallel grippers.

Arrowfly, an award-winning B2B media and marketing company, today announced that RoboBusiness, the leading robotics industry event for the past 20 years, is being rebranded as Robotics Summit & Expo West, a conference and expo dedicated to the design, deployment, and scaling of commercial robots and businesses. The first event under the new name will be in October 2027 in Santa Clara, Calif.

The timing reflects how the industry has matured. Many robotics companies have moved past the prototype stage, shipping real products into factories, warehouses, and other sites. The questions that define their work are no longer only technical. They are about design for manufacturing, bringing products to market, implementation, managing growing fleets, and providing service and support. Robotics Summit & Expo West will help industry professionals meet increasing demand for intelligent systems across sectors.

“The robotics industry has matured, and the hardest problems have grown with it,” said Steve Crowe, executive editor of The Robot Report and chair of the Robotics Summit. “For 20 years, RoboBusiness brought this community together. Robotics Summit & Expo West will serve that community by sharing lessons from industry leaders on how to move from a pilot that works to a product deployed across multiple sites and building a business that can support it.”

Robotics Summit & Expo West is organized around the questions that define the post-prototype stage of a robotics company:

Deployment at scale: What changes when a robot moves from a controlled pilot to multiple live sites, including integration, fleet management, remote monitoring, and autonomous operations in increasingly unstructured environments.

Go-to-market and commercial strategy: How robotics companies are responding to market demand and structuring pricing, sales, and channel strategies for products that combine hardware, software, and services.

Field data and product decisions: How real-world performance data flows back into product iteration and AI model evolution. Ongoing service and support, whether directly or through partners, is also key to demonstrating a return on investment.

Investment and growth: How investors evaluate robotics companies, and how founding teams can build businesses that last.

Avenda Health bases Surgery Mode on research

Avenda Health said it designed Surgery Mode to enhance how surgeons use 3D AI mapping during non-robotic and robotic surgeries, alongside new tools to simplify patient case management and physician workflows.

In the study, the system outperformed MRI and other modalities in assessing whether cancer had spread beyond the prostate, assisting surgeons in making nerve-sparing decisions.

The suite of improved workflow tools also gives physicians and staff greater visibility into the status of each patient case.

Gecko said its AI and robotic technology can save the U.S. Navy up to $8 million in repair costs per ship and return vessels to sea quicker. It does this by identifying structural issues up to 50 times faster than traditional methods, reducing inspections from months to days.

Komodo scans through deck coating without stripping them

Central to the expansion is Komodo, a proprietary Gecko robotic technology system. Komodo scans through thick, non-skid deck coatings without stripping or damaging them, giving the Navy the ability to see the health of assets without taking it apart.

It produces a full-deck heatmap of corrosion and material thickness, enabling repair teams to pinpoint damage and plan work before a ship enters drydock, which was previously possible only after maintenance had begun.

The ceiling increase comes as the Department of the Navy places greater emphasis on fleet readiness as a national security priority. Each additional day a warship spends in maintenance reduces its ability to deter adversaries, respond to crises, and project power around the world, said the Navy. The chief of naval operations has set a target of 80% fleet readiness, which Gecko will have a crucial role in helping to meet.

Gecko’s wall-climbing robots, drones, and fixed-sensors collect an unprecedented amount of data on the health of U.S. Navy ships and submarines, including components, hulls, decks and welds, with AI being used to create accurate models to identify any current and future structural issues, even ones that cannot be seen by the human eye.

]]> Part one was about strategy: the “why” behind PR, which stakeholders to chase, how to move them, and which media channels to pursue. You have the map, but now you need to understand the territory and how to move effectively inside of it.

Three practical considerations remain before you are ready to pitch: what actually earns a journalist’s attention, which activities are worth the effort, and how to conduct yourself effectively and ethically.

Newsworthiness

So what makes it to the media? Can you pitch anything you want? Not really. To determine what gets covered and what doesn’t, it helps to understand the concept of newsworthiness. If something is newsworthy, it is important and interesting enough to be covered in the media (whether it’s a news announcement or not).

The “gatekeepers” mentioned in the last piece all have their own perceptions of what is and isn’t newsworthy. Newsworthiness varies by outlet, by person, and changes with time. We can break it down into five main components.

Timeliness comes first and can be determined in two ways: short-term and long-term. Short-term timeliness is controllable, as the source decides when newsworthy information, such as funding announcements, is released to the media and typically covered that same day. Long-term timeliness, however, depends on external developments beyond the source’s control, such as breaking news, regulatory changes, or cultural trends that align with the current zeitgeist.

The second factor is impact. And when we say impact, we mean scale. Some stories make it based on sheer size because they involve staggering revenue, eye-watering funding rounds, or skyrocketing headcount. Bigger numbers make bigger stories, which explains why funding rounds remain such reliable triggers. They arrive with a figure and a set of backers that together signal validation. To be clear, a non-funding-related action that has an outsize effect on the industry, society or a human life, is equally newsworthy. A case study of new technology that saved a person’s life, which would have not been otherwise possible, is also a good example of impact.

Geography matters more than founders expect. A national desk may wave aside what a local or regional outlet would treat as a genuine event, and trade titles care about their own patch above all else. Starting close to home is usually the easiest way in, and it is the lever most startups overlook. Wanting US or UK hits as a small startup in mainland Europe is usually wishful thinking, but European startup outlets may have better openings.

Name recognition goes a long way. A well-known investor, a notable advisor, or a marquee client can elevate an entire story by lending credibility. A journalist who would pass on an unknown startup will often look twice when a familiar name is involved. “Celebrity” counts, especially if you have a real celebrity, like when the legal AI platform Legora hired the aptly-named Jude Law as a spokesperson.

Conflict is the most volatile of the five factors. Newsrooms are drawn to tension and disagreement, but picking fights can backfire on young companies trying to build goodwill. There are exceptions, mostly in the form of a clear, defensible stance on the trajectory of your industry. (Mudslinging at competitors is not something wise for early stage startups to do.) Even so, this is a rare exception, not a strategy.

Before pitching anything, look hard at your own company, technology, product and people, and be objective about genuine newsworthiness versus merely interesting to you. Study your target channels, and what they cover. What do they find newsworthy? That will show you what is newsworthy, to whom, and where.

Activity tracks

Across those channels, think in terms of sustained activities rather than one-off hits. Three tracks are worth knowing.

News is the obvious and easiest one. For an early startup, a funding announcement is usually the most valuable of all. It carries a number and a set of named backers, which together read as validation you cannot otherwise claim alone. Milestones such as a new product launch, a marquee customer, a new market, a hire senior enough to signal intent work similarly, but may be newsworthy only in trade and smaller media. For news, journalists tend to appreciate a well-written, factual press release. Don’t believe those that say the press release is dead!

Thought leadership is the second track, and the most misunderstood. It’s not shameless self-promotion, just like PR isn’t. It’s a contribution to the industry and community by sharing a point of view, insight or constructive criticism about your field. It’s your contribution to a larger conversation. In PR, the value of that contribution needs to be substantial enough to warrant a third-party media platform, which in turn lends you a higher level of credibility. Thought leadership comes in many forms, but op-eds, podcasts and speaking slots are the most common. 

Profiling is the third. It can take the form of Q&As, features and company or executive profiles that give a face and human identity to a business. Sometimes labelled “slots” or “series“, these are out there for the taking once you have traction, so understand which outlets and journalists do them, what truly interests them, and pitch them.

Not everyone has frequent newsworthy items or time for thought leadership. But ideally, you’ll have a good enough mix. Once you’re solid in your PR journey, more activity tracks become available, but that’s for another time.

Keep it human

A last word, because this is where the whole thing can come undone. Everything rests on real people trusting real people. The temptation to automate the human away is strong and growing. A PR agency was recently caught pitching journalists using a roster of fake, AI-generated PR pros, all without telling clients. Journalists notice, and they do not forgive it.

A similar logic applies to a number of other lazy shortcuts: blasting emails without checking relevance, fully AI-written pitches, etc. It wastes journalists’ time and weakens your credibility, and it is the quickest way to undo months of careful work. Use AI the way good journalists do. Follow them and see what they think about AI, you’ll find they appreciate it for research, analysing notes and internal documents and a number of other secondary tasks. This is a very fluid area, so stay up to date.

Your PR methodology

PR is not rocket science, but few take the time to learn it. This article aims to be less a set of tactics than a practical framework to help founders think about PR without overcomplicating it.

A reputation doesn’t rest on one headline but many trusted sources over time that tell a consistent story about who you are. Build that, and the big title you always wanted might eventually come to you. But never mistake the foundation for the cherry on top.

The post EU Inc. survives Council negotiations, but are Europe’s founders getting what they asked for? appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> On Friday, 23 October 2026, the Council of the European Union adopted its negotiating position on the proposed 28th corporate regime (EU Inc.), retaining the ambition of allowing companies to incorporate online within 48 hours for no more than €100 and operate across the EU single market.

The agreement comes just over a week after the EU–INC campaign, backed by more than 26,000 founders, investors and startup operators from across Europe, warned that the legislation was being stripped of its most important provisions.

But the questions remains: Are Europe’s founders getting what they asked for? Or the watered down version?

A win, with strings attached

One of the most significant developments is the survival of the proposed European Employee Stock Option Plan (EU-ESO), a mechanism designed to help startups attract and retain talent.

In its earlier warning, the EU–INC campaign argued that removing harmonised stock-option rules would undermine one of the framework’s central advantages. Startups often depend on equity incentives to compete for employees against larger companies offering higher salaries.

The Council has now retained the scheme, including provisions intended to defer taxation until shares are sold, rather than when options are granted, vested or exercised.

However, eligibility has been tightened. The Council’s position restricts the relevant tax provisions to companies with fewer than 750 employees and annual turnover not exceeding €150 million, compared with an earlier compromise proposing thresholds of 1,000 employees and €450 million.

Dr. Peter Möllmann, founding partner of German law firm PXR, shares with EU-Startups: “The Council has preserved the original idea of EU Inc. as an optional, digital and Europe-wide regime. But the more restrictions and national safeguards are added, the greater the risk that Europe creates a politically acceptable framework that founders and investors will simply not use.”

The missing pieces

Other concerns raised by the startup community appear less resolved.

The Council’s full negotiating mandate confirms that plans for a central European company register have been removed, alongside the requirement for real-time tracking of registrations.

Although digital registration and a simplified digital share register remain part of the framework, these are not equivalent to a single centralised European company register.

For founders and investors, the distinction matters. A shared registration infrastructure could have helped simplify due diligence, company verification and cross-border financing. Without it, businesses may still need to navigate different national administrative systems.

The Council has also removed the dedicated insolvency chapter from the Commission’s original proposal. This means EU Inc. companies would continue to face applicable national insolvency rules rather than benefiting from the proposed simplified European procedures.

Another unresolved issue concerns freedom of incorporation. The Council maintains the optional nature of EU Inc., allowing companies to choose the new framework instead of existing national corporate forms. However, the structure will still operate within national legal systems, which will govern matters not harmonised by the regulation.

This leaves open the concern that the regime could develop into 27 national variations rather than becoming the recognisable, predictable European standard sought by its supporters.

Despite this, Micheál Martin, Taoiseach of Ireland (the country currently holding the presidency of the Council of the European Union), was positive in his comment shared to the press.

“I warmly welcome the agreement on ‘EU Inc.’ reached in the Council today. As Presidency, Ireland has placed strong emphasis on improving Europe’s competitiveness. This is a measure that will make a real and practical difference to startups and SMEs looking to scale up across the EU. It will be easier to establish, easier to attract and retain talented staff, easier to take advantage of the Single Market, one of Europe’s greatest strengths.”

Workers’ rights in focus

The Council’s position also attempts to address concerns raised by European trade unions, which have warned that the new structure could allow businesses to take advantage of differences between national employment and corporate governance rules.

Under the negotiating mandate, EU Inc. companies would generally remain subject to the employee participation rules of the member state where they have their registered office.

However, the Council has introduced an optional mechanism allowing member states to address situations where a company incorporated elsewhere exceeds employee participation thresholds in their territory.

The agreement also strengthens safeguards against abuse, permitting national authorities to delay or refuse registration on grounds relating to money laundering, terrorist financing or other criminal activity.

These provisions are aimed at calming concerns about regulatory arbitrage and employee representation – although the optional nature of the participation mechanism leaves questions about consistency across the EU.

This introduces a potential trade-off. Additional national checks may offer stronger protections, but could make implementation more complex and weaken the simplicity that entrepreneurs originally sought.

Taxation remains another limitation. Beyond the specific provisions for employee stock options, EU Inc. does not create a unified European tax regime. Companies would continue to comply with applicable national corporate tax, VAT and employment obligations.

What’s next?

Friday’s agreement represents a political milestone, but EU Inc. has not yet become law. The Council has adopted its negotiating mandate, establishing the position that member states will defend in discussions with the European Parliament.

The Parliament still has to establish its own position on the proposal, which could seek to restore, add or remove elements of EU Inc. As of 26 October 2026, the status of the legislative file remains at “Awaiting committee decision“.

Once Parliament agrees its negotiating position, representatives of the Parliament, Council and Commission can begin interinstitutional negotiations, commonly known as trilogues, to establish a final legislative text.

The Council is also proposing a 21-month implementation period. Meaning even if EU institutions reach an agreement before the end of 2026, companies would not immediately be able to register under the new regime.

But there are reasons for cautious optimism. The proposed framework remains alive, its principal incorporation commitments have survived and the employee stock-option scheme has been retained, albeit in a more restricted form.

The next stage will determine whether the European institutions can reconcile the competing demands for simplicity, investor confidence and regulatory protection without compromising the framework’s usefulness.

Editor’s Note: EU–INC is an independent, founder-led advocacy campaign pushing for a common European startup standard, while EU Inc. is the European Commission’s proposed corporate legal framework, introduced on 18 March 2026. The campaign helped build momentum behind the reform but does not control the legislative process.

]]> Z_One Fund, the Italian venture capital fund managed by Eureka! Venture has announced the first close at more than €35 million, with a total fundraising target of €60 million.

The fund’s investor base includes some of Italy’s most prominent institutional investors. CDP Venture Capital SGR has committed capital through its newly launched Fondo Acceleratori 2. Other investors include Euronext Milan-listed Zest, Lazio Innova through a parallel fund focused on the Lazio region, Fondazione Compagnia di San Paolo, and a number of private investors.

“The development of an increasingly mature innovation ecosystem comes from the ability to value specialised operators capable of supporting startups from the earliest stages of growth. It is with this vision that we chose to invest in Z_One Fund, the first investment of the Fondo Acceleratori 2, the cornerstone of our new acceleration strategy, designed to leverage the skills of specialised managers and operators, while maintaining the Rete Nazionale Acceleratori’s ability to combine investment with operational and mentorship support to help companies with go-to-market and the validation of their business model,” said Stefano Molino, Head of the Fondo Acceleratori at CDP Venture Capital.

Luigi Capello, a pioneer of the Italian innovation ecosystem, leads the fund alongside partner Giulio Montoli and junior partner Giulia Fazzini. Montoli has built his career in acceleration and pre-Seed investing, including leading the management of one of the country’s largest startup portfolios, while Fazzini is one of the youngest women to hold a partner-level role at an Italian VC firm.

Collectively, they bring experience of over 340 investments, more than 25 exits, and over €80 million under management, with notable deals including FitPrime, Robot.com, JetHR, Vikey and 2Hire. The fund targets pre-Seed and Seed stage startups across two focus areas: AI Applications and UrbanTech and Smart Cities.

In AI Applications, the fund will back startups embedding artificial intelligence into corporate and public administration workflows, covering verticals from financial services and retail to digital security and the development of new AI models. In UrbanTech and Smart Cities, the fund is focusing on technologies transforming cities, including smart buildings, electric mobility, water and waste management, and the regeneration of public spaces.

“Italian venture capital needs a financial supply chain to help high-potential startups grow. This requires institutional capital willing to invest from the very beginning and the ability to support founders in developing their business. With Z_One Fund we put to use the experience gained over years of investing and acceleration,” said Capello, Partner at Z_One Fund.

He added, “We want to give more teams the opportunity to test themselves against the market and to progressively concentrate resources on the companies that show the greatest potential, in segments that open up important opportunities for a new generation of tech companies. Our ambition is to help them be born in Italy with a European outlook.”

Z_One Fund is managed by Eureka! Venture, an independent Milan-based asset management company founded in 2019 and supervised by the Bank of Italy and Consob. The firm is focused exclusively on DeepTech investments and recently launched Eureka! Fund II – Deep Tech Lazio, a €20 million early-stage fund. To date, the firm has raised over €190 million across a multi-strategy platform spanning technology transfer, software, DeepTech, AI, UrbanTech, and SME-focused vehicles.

The Z-One Fund aims to be the first institutional cheque to startups with initial tickets up to €250k, with selective follow-on investments of up to €1 million. The fund is also part of CDP Venture Capital’s Rete Nazionale Acceleratori, which means portfolio companies will receive not just funding but also access to a structured acceleration programme delivered in partnership with Zest.

“With Z_One Fund we take a further step in Eureka!’s growth path as a multi-strategy platform dedicated to alternative investments. We believe venture capital needs increasingly specialised and vertical models, capable of combining entrepreneurial talent, capital, expertise and operational support,” said Stefano Peroncini, CEO of Eureka! Venture SGR, manager of Z_One Fund.

Alongside the main vehicle sits Z_One Fund Lazio, a parallel fund created through the Lazio Venture 2 initiative under the PR FESR 2021-2027 programme and managed by Lazio Innova.

The parallel fund applies the same investment strategy as Z_One Fund while directing capital specifically toward startups connected to the Lazio region, aiming to strengthen the availability of pre-Seed and Seed financing locally and bridge innovation with regional universities and industry.

]]> In response to recent reports of Russian advancement in drone and missile production, German military AI startup Helsing has unveiled Contra; an AI-controlled autonomous air defence system against scaled drone and missile attacks.

The company also introduced two advanced interceptor missiles, AD-1 Inferno and AD-2 Ambush, designed to outmatch and outrun even the fastest jet-powered drone and cruise missile threats.

Niklas Köhler, co-founder and President of Helsing, says: “Contra ends the air defence dilemma: slow fair-weather drones, or million-euro missiles fired at cheap, mass-produced targets. Our AI links existing sensors and effectors in real time and adds our interceptors, AD-1 and AD-2. With jet and rocket propulsion, a low-cost all-weather radar seeker, and two independent European supply chains, they deliver autonomous fire superiority up to ten kilometres high–affordable and at industrial scale.”

This enter a competitive landscape for European DefenceTech spending and activity.

EU-Startups has reported approximately €511 million in financing across European startups developing interceptor systems, counter-drone technologies and related autonomous capabilities in 2026.

Among the closest comparisons, UK-based Cambridge Aerospace secured €173.1 million in April and a further €259.7 million in August to scale affordable air-defence interceptors, while Estonia’s Frankenburg Technologies raised €30 million to expand missile manufacturing.

In Germany, Hannover-based INLEAP Photonics secured €20 million for laser-based drone defence, alongside smaller investments in Denmark’s Shotling (€700k) and Sweden’s Freya Industries (€533k).

Related autonomy investments included €12 million for Norway’s Six Robotics and €15 million for Finland’s Kelluu. Separately, German unmanned-systems developer Quantum Systems raised €1 billion in July. Helsing itself previously secured a €600 million Series D in June 2025, as documented by EU-Startups.

Founded in 2021 in Munich, Helsing is a Military AI company that designs new types of AI-defined and autonomous systems across multiple domains.

According to the company, recent intelligence indicates that Russia has systematically increased its jet-powered drone and cruise missile production, with Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet drone output alone rising to 4,000 units per month. At the same time, Russia is constructing numerous additional launch sites for such drones.

This reportedly brings parts of the EU within range of potential Russian attacks.

Contra is designed to counter this threat. Autonomous AI-based operation allows the detection and engagement of hundreds or thousands of drone and missile threats at the same time by fusing sensors and effectors into a single air picture. With Helsing’s Altra C2 platform as the foundation, users allegedly retain full control over decision making and prioritisation.

To effectively engage large numbers of fast aerial targets, Helsing is also developing two missile interceptors with advanced radar seekers:

  • AD-1 Inferno is a jet-powered interceptor capable of aerial loitering, swarming, and repeated re-engagements.
  • AD-2 Ambush is a solid-rocket – motor (SRM) missile for rapid intercepts, reaching Mach 2.5 and a range of 20km+.

Both systems receive mid-course guidance from Contra radar ground stations and feature an advanced onboard radar-seeker for all-weather terminal guidance. Both interceptors are container-launched.

Mass production will take place at Helsing’s Resilience Factories, with unit prices reportedly undercutting those of existing missile interceptors.

While AD-1 and AD-2 form an essential part of the Contra offering, the system is natively set up to integrate third-party hardware, such as other interceptors, cUAV lasers, cUAV guns or net-based systems.

The compant says that Contra reflects their cross-domain approach: using AI and software to draw high capability from affordable, mass-producible hardware. The result is autonomous fire dominance at scale that remains under human control.

The funding came from Springvest, with backing from both new and existing investors, including venture capital firm Maki.vc. “Volare 01 proves that our […]

The post Finland’s Volare raises €7.1 million and opens 5,000-tonne insect protein factory appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> Volare, a Finnish DeepTech company turning food-industry side streams into high-quality insect protein, has inaugurated its first industrial-scale facility called Volare 01 in Pori, Finland, and raised €7.1 million in fresh funding.

The funding came from Springvest, with backing from both new and existing investors, including venture capital firm Maki.vc.

“Volare 01 proves that our technology and production model work at industrial scale. We delivered the factory on schedule and on budget, demonstrating our ability to build production capacity cost-effectively and laying a strong foundation for further growth,” said Jarna Hyvönen, CEO and co-founder of Volare.

Founded in 2021 by Tuure Parviainen, Matti Tähtinen, and Hyvönen as a spin-off from VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland, Volare began working on its technology way back in 2014. The company has successfully brought its technology from lab to industrial production, which relies on the Black soldier fly, described by the company as nature’s own bioreactor.

The insect is fed food-industry side streams, and within roughly a week of active growth, converts them into protein and oil. Volare has built a proprietary, highly automated production process that covers the full chain, from rearing larvae to finished ingredients. It says the result is a facility that generates no process wastewater, runs entirely on non-fossil fuel energy, and operates with just four people per shift.

Volare 01, its new 10,000-square-metre plant, targets annual production of up to 5,000 tonnes of insect protein and 2,000 tonnes of insect oil, converting food-industry side streams into high-value ingredients for aquafeed, pet food, and poultry feed markets. Instead of building the factory from scratch, the company built the facility inside a former newspaper printing hall, an approach that reduces construction requirements and costs.

The company says the facility was delivered on schedule and within its €15 million budget. Volare 01 represents a thousandfold expansion from the company’s demonstration plant, yet relies on the same production process that has been commercially validated over four years.

Compared with other insect-based producers, Volare claims its factory requires four to ten times less capital expenditure, around 50% fewer full-time employees, and 30% less energy for end-product processing. Its protein meal delivers over 90% digestibility.

A significant share of Volare 01’s production capacity has already been sold with offtake agreements in place with Skretting, one of the world’s largest aqua feed companies and a leading global chemical company.

Volare says its protein has been commercially used since 2022, featuring in insect-based dog treats developed with Alvar Pet, cat food under Dagsmark’s (Vafo Group brand), and rainbow trout feed through a collaboration with Alltech Fennoaqua.

The €7.1 million in fresh funding will be used to finance a second factory and a broader push across and beyond Europe. With Volare 01 now operational and financing secured for a second facility, the Finnish company is preparing itself for a roadmap that spans multiple plants across Europe, built in partnership with food industry players who generate the side streams it processes.

“Europe needs significantly more locally produced protein, and we have built a model that can deliver it efficiently and competitively. Our next step is to replicate our model from Finland and bring more local, efficient protein production capacity to Europe and beyond,” Hyvönen added.
