]]> Sonexos, a Lausanne-based DeepTech company, has raised approximately €5.4 million (CHF 5 million/USD 6.1 million) in new equity financing to take its solid-state noise control from working prototypes to industrial production.

The round was led by Valquest Partners, with participation from Robert Bosch Venture Capital GmbH (Bosch Ventures) and industry angels and private investors. Fadi Noureddine, founder and Managing Partner of Valquest Partners, has joined the Sonexos Board of Directors.

“Engineers have always had to trade space and weight for silence. Plasmacoustics removes that compromise. This financing carries it from working prototypes into our customers’ products, at scale,” said Mark Donaldson, founder and CEO of Sonexos. 

Sonexos was founded in 2022 by Donaldson, who has built companies in active noise control, including SoundChip, which developed noise-cancelling smart audio codecs for headphones and earbuds from leading consumer electronics brands and was acquired by DSP Group, now part of Synaptics.

Sonexos develops solid-state acoustic technology that solves low-frequency noise where passive materials and speaker-based ANC (active noise cancellation) fall short.

It claims to be developing a new way to address low-frequency noise from fans, compressors and motors. According to the company, this persistent hum carries through walls and windows and is the hardest noise to eliminate. 

It argues that conventional acoustic treatments become increasingly bulky at lower frequencies and can restrict airflow. It further notes that while loudspeaker-based active noise control works well in the confined space of a headphone, it struggles with the complex, three-dimensional sound fields of real-world applications.

The company claims that its patented Plasmacoustic Metalayer uses a software-controlled plasma layer to absorb sound at a surface. The system is thin, lightweight and has no moving parts. 

The Plasmacoustic Metalayer platform enables electronically programmable sound control, allowing compact, lightweight, energy-efficient management of low-frequency noise in domestic appliances, HVAC, and industrial, infrastructure, automotive, and specialised acoustic applications.

The Swiss startup reported that prototype systems have achieved up to 20 dB of low-frequency noise reduction in ventilation systems and 16 dB in domestic appliances under application-specific test conditions.

The company’s Plasmapanel and Plasmadrive technologies are designed to overcome the practical limitations of conventional passive acoustic materials and traditional active noise control systems. 

Sonexos’s Plasmapanel packages the actively controlled plasma metalayer into a sealed, inert-gas-filled module driven by proprietary low-power, high-voltage electronics. The company explains that, depending on the installation, Plasmapanel-enabled systems absorb sound from 30 Hz to 1,500 Hz and, compared with passive silencers with similar low-frequency performance, require less than a fifth of the space and weight. It highlighted that for OEMs, this frees room for more compact products or for features that bulky acoustic treatment would otherwise displace.

Sonexos states that it is developing an industrial ecosystem rather than manufacturing every component in-house. STMicroelectronics is supporting development of low-power, low-cost electronics. A strategic collaboration with Vandewiele Group, through its subsidiary Roj, provides a route toward series manufacturing for European OEM programmes, including electronics production, box-build and cabling.

Sonexos plans to offer turnkey panels with integration support, as well as an enterprise model in which larger OEMs build the technology into their own products and production lines using Sonexos components, such as Plasmadrive, and software.

The company is also planning expansion into AI data-centre cooling, where reduced fan noise could ease community concerns and help sustain cooling capacity under night-time noise limits. It is developing the Plasmapanel Radial Active Silencer to mount around a fan discharge and attenuate low-frequency sound without obstructing the airflow path. 

In July 2026, the company announced a collaboration with Euronext Milan-listed SIT to integrate the technology with fan platforms for data centres, battery energy storage and industrial cooling. ]]> Finnish SpaceTech unicorn ICEYE has announced two new partnerships aimed at expanding its satellite intelligence capabilities across defence and environmental monitoring.

The company signed a Letter of Intent alongside Nokia and Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence to explore sovereign satellite communications, while also announcing a collaboration with German startup OroraTech to develop an integrated wildfire intelligence solution.

This follows a period of notable growth for the Espoo-based scale-up. In June 2026, ICEYE secured €450 million in primary Series F funding, valuing the company at more than €10 billion, with a further €300 million revolving credit facility secured in May.

This funding activity can be placed alongside adjacent 2026 European SpaceTech funding announcements, including €51 million for Luxembourg and US-based Hydrosat to expand thermal satellite intelligence, €34 million for the UK’s SatVu to scale its thermal observation constellation, and €61 million for Switzerland’s SWISSto12 to develop satellite and communications infrastructure.

In Finland, Helsinki-based Kelluu also raised €15 million to expand its autonomous aerial intelligence capabilities.

Together with funding for France’s UNIVITY (€27 million) and Germany’s AIRMO (€5 million), these 2026 rounds account for approximately €643 million in the general SpaceTech sector, including ICEYE’s primary financing.

Founded in 2014 by Rafal Modrzewski and Pekka Laurila, ICEYE specialises in synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellite technology, providing Earth observation data and intelligence to governments, defence organisations, insurers and emergency management agencies.

The company originated from research at Aalto University and launched its first SAR satellite in 2018, becoming an early pioneer in miniaturised radar satellites.

The first of the two announcements centres on a Letter of Intent signed by ICEYE, Nokia and Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence to explore cooperation on secure satellite communications. Announced during the Finnish Prime Minister’s visit to Ukraine, the initiative aims to strengthen the country’s defence capabilities by developing communications infrastructure that Ukraine can independently own and control.

The agreement builds on an earlier partnership between ICEYE and Nokia, announced on October 1st 2026, to develop secure, high-performance broadband communications systems using low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites. Designed for governments, these systems would support defence, border security, emergency services and disaster response, while giving participating countries control over their satellites, ground infrastructure and terminals.

Rafal Modrzewski, CEO and Co-founder of ICEYE, said: “Ukraine needs secure, sovereign and high-performance satellite communications systems that it controls. We have a proven track record of delivering sovereign missions at speed to help build that capability. ICEYE has proudly supported Ukraine since 2022, and we remain committed to continuing that support today.”

ICEYE has supported Ukraine with satellite intelligence since 2022, making the proposed communications collaboration a potential extension of an existing relationship. The latest agreement remains exploratory, with no deployment timetable or financial commitments disclosed.

Alongside its defence-related developments, ICEYE has also partnered with Munich-based OroraTech to expand its wildfire intelligence services. The collaboration will combine OroraTech’s thermal satellite data with ICEYE’s SAR observations, creating a platform intended to help organisations monitor wildfires from their earliest stages through to damage assessment and recovery.

Founded in 2018 by Thomas Grübler, Rupert Amann, Florian Mauracher and Björn Stoffers, OroraTech develops space-based thermal intelligence for wildfire detection and monitoring. The startup has expanded its satellite network and provides information to governments and organisations managing wildfire risks worldwide.

As per our coverage, OroraTech secured a €37 million Series B extension in 2025.

Until now, ICEYE’s wildfire intelligence capabilities have primarily focused on assessing building-level damage during active fires. By incorporating OroraTech’s thermal observations, the company aims to extend its services to include identifying initial hotspots, tracking fire progression and assessing threats to communities and critical infrastructure.

The combination brings together two complementary technologies. OroraTech’s thermal satellites can detect heat anomalies and monitor active fires, while ICEYE’s SAR satellites can capture observations through clouds, smoke and darkness, helping assess damage to buildings and infrastructure even while a wildfire is ongoing.

Dr. Ignacio Zuleta, Chief Technology and Product Officer at OroraTech, commented: “Our thermal satellite intelligence provides that critical visibility from the earliest stages of an event, detecting hotspots and tracking fire activity as it develops. By bringing that intelligence together with ICEYE’s SAR capabilities, we can help decision-makers maintain a more continuous understanding of a wildfire, from first detection through its impact on communities, infrastructure and the surrounding environment.”

The integrated solution targets several sectors, including government emergency management, utilities and insurance. Emergency services could use the intelligence to inform evacuations and coordinate firefighting resources, while energy providers could monitor threats to electricity networks and other infrastructure. Insurers could also use the data to identify exposed properties, assess damage and prioritise claims.

According to ICEYE, the technology could help accelerate disaster response by providing more timely information on wildfire progression and its consequences. The company says its integrated approach could support damage assessments for disaster declarations within 24 hours, compared with processes that can otherwise take weeks.

Taken together, the two announcements are one of many examples of how ICEYE is expanding its satellite capabilities beyond Earth observation imagery into a broader range of intelligence and communications services.

]]> Phononic Vibes, a Milan-based noise management company that designs and manufactures noise and vibration products for rail, energy, industry, construction and mobility, has secured a €25 million financing round. The company has also launched its new identity and website today. 

The round was led by Jolt Capital, a Paris-based private equity firm specialising in DeepTech growth companies, through Jolt Capital V, a fund targeting €1 billion and nearing final close. Eureka! Venture SGR, CDP Venture Capital SGR, and Simest SpA also participated in this round. The transaction includes the acquisition of 360 Capital’s stake, which it has held since the company’s Seed round. In 2020, the company announced the closing of a €2.3 million funding round.

Andrea Traversone, Managing Partner at Jolt Capital, said, “Noise control is reaching a turning point. Conventional products have hit their physical limit, and infrastructure needs quieter assets with less weight and space. Phononic Vibes is a company combining breakthrough science, a patented design engine and manufacturing at scale. We are excited to back the team in building a global leader in noise and vibration control. This is Jolt Capital V’s first investment in Italy, a country with an increasingly dynamic and vibrant deeptech ecosystem.”

Founded in 2018 by Luca D’Alessandro, Giovanni Capellari, and Stefano Caverni as a spin-off of Politecnico di Milano, the company manufactures in Italy and leads a group of established European manufacturers, including Matis, founded in 1979.

The company designs and manufactures noise and vibration products that do the same job with less material. According to the company, every noise barrier, enclosure, and silencer on the market obeys the mass law: more quiet means more material. Phononic Vibes claims to break it.

It designs metamaterials, structures whose shape does the work mass used to do. Its products weigh up to 30% less while delivering the same acoustic performance, or they perform better at the same weight.

At the core of the company is a proprietary design engine, protected by 18 patent families. “It turns the physics of metamaterials into certified products, drawing on application libraries that grow with every project, so each new market starts from proven designs rather than a blank sheet,” the company mentioned in the press release 

The company highlighted that Deutsche Bahn certified its transparent noise barrier for the German rail network, the first see-through panel it rates as highly absorbing. Phononic Vibes. It also reports that Mercedes-Benz uses its technology in series production, which the company says is the first metamaterial in a series-production car. Contractors such as Webuild and Eteria choose its barriers because they install faster. Its revenue has doubled every year since 2018, reaching break-even in 2025.

Luca D’Alessandro, CEO and co-founder of Phononic Vibes, said, “Weight has always been the price of quiet. We have shown it is a design choice, with two of Europe’s most demanding customers. With Jolt Capital by our side in this new chapter, and the continued support of our existing investors Eureka! Venture SGR, CDP Venture Capital and Simest, we can accelerate our international growth, expand into new applications and make lighter noise control the standard across data centres, rail, energy and industry. I would also like to thank 360 Capital for believing in us from the early days, when we were still working at the desks of Politecnico di Milano, and for being part of the journey that brought us here.”

The company plans to use this capital to scale its proprietary design engine internationally, expand its technology into new applications and strengthen its delivery capabilities.  Phononic Vibes also notes that targeted acquisitions will complement this strategy by extending the reach of its technology and bringing additional industrial capabilities to the group.

AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ Aerospace Global News Mon, 26 Oct 2026 13:23:13 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/cropped-AGN_Icon_Jet-32x32.png AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ 32 32 Retired KC-10A rises from US desert boneyard to fly again in commercial sector https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/retired-usaf-kc10-extender-omega-flight-refuelling/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 14:27:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54511 The former USAF aircraft will continue to operate on the civilian register for Texas-based Omega Air Refuelling.

The post Retired KC-10A rises from US desert boneyard to fly again in commercial sector appeared first on AGN.

]]> A retired US Air Force (USAF) KC-10A Extender has returned to the skies after spending years in storage at an aircraft boneyard in Arizona. The tanker, formerly designated 86-0034, departed Davis-Monthan Air Force Base on 20 October, beginning a new chapter under private ownership with Omega Air Refuelling.

The aircraft, now registered as N82247, flew to San Antonio International Airport (SAT) in Texas, marking a significant milestone for the company and the retired military tanker fleet.

Its return to flight demonstrates how aircraft once considered destined for museums or spare parts can still have valuable roles in commercial aviation and military support operations.

According to the aviation publication MiGFlug, Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) records identify Omega Air Inc., based in Selma, Texas, as the aircraft’s registered owner. Its registration as a McDonnell Douglas DC-10-30F was issued on 6 October 2026, just over two years after the USAF completed the retirement of its KC-10 fleet.

From military service to the aircraft boneyard

The KC-10 Extender was developed from the civilian DC-10 airliner and adapted to provide aerial refuelling capabilities for the US military. Its combination of three engines, substantial fuel capacity, and versatile refuelling equipment made it an important asset for supporting aircraft on long-distance missions.

The USAF received 60 KC-10s, with deliveries beginning in 1981. One aircraft was destroyed in a ground fire at Barksdale Air Force Base in 1987, leaving 59 to continue serving the fleet.

Retirement began in July 2020, when aircraft 86-0036 became the first KC-10 to leave operational service and fly to the 309th Aerospace Maintenance and Regeneration Group (AMARC) at Davis-Monthan.

The process concluded on 26 September 2024, when the final operational Extender departed Travis Air Force Base in California for storage.

The fleet was retired as the USAF transitioned towards newer tanker capabilities, including the KC-46A Pegasus. However, the departure of the last KC-10 did not necessarily mean the end of the aircraft’s usefulness.

In 2025, ten retired KC-10s were offered for auction through the US General Services Administration. They were sold in non-flyable condition and without their refuelling booms. The aircraft also lacked one wing-mounted engine, meaning buyers faced substantial work before any could return to the air. For N82247, that restoration effort has now resulted in a successful departure from the Arizona storage facility.

Omega Air Refuelling expands its fleet

The aircraft’s new owner, Omega Air Refuelling, is an established contractor providing aerial refuelling services to the US military.

Rather than replacing military tankers in combat operations, companies such as Omega support training, testing and ferry flights, allowing military aircraft to concentrate on operational duties.

Omega already operates former Royal Netherlands Air Force KDC-10 tankers, acquired in 2019, alongside other tanker aircraft.

Adding a former US Air Force KC-10 gives the company another airframe derived from the DC-10 family, an aircraft type with which it has considerable experience.

One particularly important feature of the KC-10 is its original ability to refuel aircraft using both a central boom and a hose-and-drogue system. This combination allows it to support different types of receiver aircraft, including those associated with the US Air Force, Navy and Marine Corps.

Omega has demonstrated the value of its boom-equipped tankers in recent years. In March 2024, one of its KC-10s refuelled a B-52 bomber and an MC-130J aircraft over the Pacific.

n April 2025, another refuelled a C-17 Globemaster III over California. These missions highlight the potential value of the KC-10 platform in contractor-operated refuelling services.

A challenging return to flight

The return of N82247 is particularly noteworthy because the aircraft was not simply waiting in storage in an immediately flyable condition. The ten KC-10s auctioned in 2025 were offered without their refuelling booms and with one wing-mounted engine missing from each aircraft.

Restoring an aircraft to flight under these circumstances requires significant technical work, inspections and coordination to ensure it meets the necessary airworthiness requirements.

The aircraft’s departure from Davis-Monthan therefore represents more than a change of ownership: it demonstrates that at least one retired Extender has successfully completed the work required to fly again.

However, the aircraft’s return should not be confused with a full restoration of its original military capabilities. N82247 departed without its refuelling boom, and Omega has not publicly outlined its complete plans for the aircraft. A boom could potentially be installed again if future contracts require it.

Reports have also indicated that Omega acquired a group of retired KC-10 airframes, although the company’s precise intentions for the remaining aircraft have not been publicly confirmed.

A future beyond military retirement

The KC-10’s story may extend beyond Omega’s commercial operations. In October 2026, reports also indicated that the USAF was seeking industry interest in reactivating up to four stored KC-10s for an unidentified North African partner through the foreign military sales programme.

This possibility highlights the continuing relevance of older tanker aircraft in a world where aerial refuelling remains essential to military aviation.

Reactivating stored aircraft can present substantial challenges, but established designs may still offer useful capabilities when the cost and technical requirements make restoration practical.

For Omega Air Refuelling, N82247 provides an opportunity to expand a fleet built around supporting military aviation. Its existing experience with DC-10-derived tankers gives the company a foundation for operating the aircraft, although its eventual mission profile will depend on its configuration and contractual requirements.

The departure of N82247 from Davis-Monthan Air Force Base is therefore a striking example of an aircraft finding a second life after military retirement.

Once part of a fleet that supported USAF operations around the world, the former 86-0034 has left the Arizona desert under a new registration and a new owner.

]]> Airbus explores role in GCAP sixth-generation fighter programme https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/airbus-bae-gcap-germany/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 13:48:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54432 Airbus is expected to hold exploratory talks with BAE Systems on joining the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP), as Germany considers involvement in the UK, Italy and Japan-led project.

The post Airbus explores role in GCAP sixth-generation fighter programme appeared first on AGN.

]]> Following Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s comments that the UK is open to Germany joining GCAP, representatives from Airbus are expected to meet with BAE Systems to discuss possible participation in the GCAP/Tempest fighter jet programme.

According to the Financial Times, Airbus executives will meet their counterparts at BAE Systems to explore how it could contribute to the GCAP/Tempest next-generation fighter jet programme.

The Financial Times cited four people familiar with the matter, while BAE described the meeting as “routine.”

The report comes a fortnight after Prime Minister Andy Burnham invited Germany to join the programme. Germany is not expected to make a final decision at this stage.

Germany exploring future combat-air options

Germany is looking for how to move forward after the breakdown of the FCAS programme with France and Spain earlier this year. France is pursuing its own next-generation fighter, potentially in partnership with India.

The Financial Times writes, “An initial plan for a German-led alternative by Airbus, its Spanish partner Indra and other industrial groups has been dropped.”

Any German participation would likely involve discussions over industrial workshare, as the programme’s existing partners have already agreed major responsibilities.

The UK is already building a separate Combat Air Flying Demonstrator intended to inform GCAP, with flight testing planned around 2027–28.

Mike Schoellhorn, head of Airbus’s Germany-based Defence and Space business, recently said he expects Germany’s Airbus to have a “key role” in GCAP. Other major German companies, like MTU Aero Engines, also expect “fair” workshares.

And an Airbus spokesperson told Reuters: “Airbus is fundamentally open to partnerships, ​provided they grant the German, Spanish and European industry substantial ​and equal participation in development, production, and operational use.”

Airbus’ uncrewed Valkyrie completes first European flight as combat drone programme targets 2029 Airbus’ uncrewed Valkyrie completes first European flight as combat drone programme targets 2029

More than just the core fighter jet

The flagship GCAP/Tempest fighter jet is one important component of a larger 6th-generation system. In the UK, this wider capability has been referred to as the Future Combat Air System (FCAS), while Germany and France used FCAS/SCAF for their separate (now collapsed) programme.

In the upcoming talks, Airbus and BAE are expected to discuss alternative areas for co-operation such as collaborative combat aircraft (CCAs) and the combat cloud. The combat cloud is a networked architecture to connect aircraft with drones, satellites, radars, and sensors.

Germany is investing in collaborative combat aircraft programmes through companies including Airbus and Helsing.

Other potential areas for German participation could include CCA mission autonomy, electronic warfare, weapons integration, selected engine work, mission computing and AI.

Military cooperation can be complex and include industrial offsets and agreements on other programmes.

It remains unclear what level of industrial participation Germany could secure in GCAP and whether any arrangement would be acceptable to all parties.

The post easyJet turns to Starlink as airlines race to improve in-flight connectivity appeared first on AGN.

]]> easyJet is set to introduce onboard internet for the first time after signing a deal with Starlink, the satellite broadband service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.

The move will allow passengers to browse, stream and stay connected from take-off to landing, something that has become increasingly expected by travellers who are used to being online almost everywhere else.

It’s also another win for Starlink, which has emerged as one of the aviation industry’s hottest technologies, with airlines around the world racing to upgrade ageing inflight connectivity systems.

What is Starlink?

SpaceX‘s low-Earth-orbit satellite network was created by Elon Musk to deliver high-speed broadband using thousands of low-Earth orbit satellites.

Unlike traditional inflight WiFi systems, Starlink’s low-latency network can support streaming, cloud-based work, online gaming and even video calls, making it one of the most sought-after connectivity solutions in commercial aviation.

Fleet-wide rollout planned

The airline plans to install Starlink technology across its A320, A320neo and A321neo fleets, with the rollout expected to begin in 2027.

It’s expected to be completed in early 2028, making internet access a standard feature on many easyJet flights.

Change of heart for easyJet

The announcement marks a change in direction for easyJet.

Earlier this year, Chief executive Kenton Jarvis suggested the airline was unlikely to adopt Starlink’s connectivity technology.

However in a statement today, Jarvis said: “In an increasingly digital world, staying connected matters more than ever to many of our customers, whether that’s holidaymakers looking to unwind with in-flight entertainment, or our business customers keeping up to speed with what’s happening on the ground.

Boeing 777F production halted by supplier dispute

Boeing’s 777 Freighter (777F) production line has been halted for nearly two months following a dispute with Florida-based supplier Vaero, according to a Reuters report published on 23 October.

Despite reaching a settlement with Vaero in late September, Boeing had not resumed production as of 23 October, according to three company workers cited by Reuters. The dispute also affected production of the Boeing 767, including its freighter variant and the KC-46 Pegasus aerial refuelling tanker.

At the centre of the dispute is a fixed trailing-edge rib kit used in the wings of the 777F and 767. Boeing identified Vaero as its sole supplier and alleged in a legal complaint filed in August that the company had stopped delivering the kits.

Without the parts, Boeing could not complete the relevant wing sections, preventing aircraft assembly from progressing at its Everett, Washington, facility.

According to court filings cited by Reuters, Boeing estimated that the disruption was costing it as much as $6.5 million per day. The manufacturer has reportedly begun efforts to bring production of the component in-house, reducing its dependence on a single external supplier.

The effects have already reached the assembly line. Two partially assembled 777Fs were removed because of the shortage. One was identified as destined for FedEx, although the courier did not respond to a request for comment.

Boeing had delivered 21 777Fs during 2026 by the time of the Reuters report. Some further deliveries may still be possible using aircraft whose wings were assembled before the disruption.

Which airlines have Boeing 777F aircraft on order?

The production halt comes as several major cargo operators await new aircraft. Boeing’s order book at the end of September 2026 listed 38 unfilled orders for the current-generation 777F, although some are associated with Russian operators and may not be deliverable under present circumstances.

The outstanding orders include:

  • FedEx Express: Seven aircraft remain on order, making the US cargo giant one of the customers most exposed to potential delays.
  • Saudia: Four 777Fs are listed as outstanding.
  • Emirates: Three aircraft remain on order, following its decision in October 2024 to purchase five additional 777Fs.
  • China Airlines: Two aircraft are listed as outstanding.
  • China Southern Cargo: Two aircraft remain on order.
  • Silk Way West Airlines: Two aircraft are listed in the backlog.
  • Ethiopian Airlines Cargo: Two additional 777Fs were ordered in September 2026.

Another 10 aircraft were attributed to unidentified customers in Boeing’s September order figures, while six remained associated with Russia-linked Volga-Dnepr. Their eventual delivery remains uncertain.

The figures reflect the published order position at the end of September, rather than a confirmed schedule of future deliveries. Boeing has not publicly specified revised delivery dates for customers affected by the production interruption.

Recent deliveries underline continuing demand

Despite the production difficulties, Boeing continued delivering 777Fs during 2026. FedEx and Air China Cargo each received a 777F in September, bringing Boeing’s deliveries of the type to 20 by the end of that month.

Air China Cargo subsequently received another aircraft, its 14th 777F, on 1 October.

Air China Cargo operates its 777Fs alongside Airbus A330 freighters and Boeing 747s, providing capacity across its international cargo network. Ethiopian Airlines, meanwhile, operates 12 777Fs and continues to expand its long-haul freight operations.

Ethiopian Airlines placed a significant order on 30 September, purchasing two additional 777Fs alongside eight next-generation 777-8 Freighters.

The agreement makes Ethiopian the first African airline to order the 777-8F and demonstrates continuing demand for Boeing’s large freighters.

The 777-8 Freighter offers a longer-term solution

Boeing’s production difficulties come amid a transition towards the 777-8 Freighter, the next-generation aircraft intended to succeed the current 777F.

The 777-8F belongs to the 777X family and features a different wing design. Consequently, the supplier dispute affecting the current 777F and 767 does not directly affect the 777X programme.

The new freighter has attracted substantial interest from cargo operators. In July 2026, MSC Air Cargo ordered five 777-8Fs, while Ethiopian Airlines added eight to its order book in September.

Other customers include Qatar Airways Cargo, Cargolux, Korean Air and China Airlines. Cirium’s analysis identifies Qatar Airways as the largest customer, with 34 777-8Fs on order, followed by Cargolux with 10.

However, the new aircraft is not expected to enter service until around 2029, leaving the current-generation 777F important to airlines seeking additional capacity in the intervening years.

The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has also granted Boeing an exemption allowing up to 35 additional current-generation 777Fs to receive their first airworthiness certificates between 2028 and 2030.

The decision is intended to help bridge the gap before the 777-8F becomes available, although it does not mean all 35 aircraft have been ordered.

Supply chain resilience remains the immediate challenge

For Boeing, the priority is to restore production and establish a reliable supply of the wing components needed to complete outstanding aircraft.

The dispute demonstrates how a shortage involving a single specialist component can disrupt multiple aircraft programmes, even when demand remains strong and a commercial settlement has been reached.

For FedEx, Saudia, Emirates and other operators awaiting new aircraft, the timing of production recovery will be crucial. The longer the interruption continues, the greater the risk of delivery schedules being pushed back.

With the 777-8F still several years from entering service, Boeing’s ability to resolve the dispute and deliver the remaining 777F backlog will remain a key factor in the availability of new long-haul cargo capacity worldwide.

]]> Airbus is bringing military-grade navigation technology to its A220 passenger jet to help aircraft maintain accurate navigation when GPS signals are jammed, disrupted or deliberately falsified.

The European aircraft manufacturer has selected SkyNaute, an inertial navigation system developed by Safran Electronics & Defense and already used on military platforms. The system is expected to enter service on the A220 around 2030, according to Aviation Week, which reported the timetable following an announcement by Safran executive Benjamin Declety on 21 October.

The decision comes as interference with satellite navigation becomes a growing problem for commercial airlines, particularly on routes passing near military conflicts. Aircraft may suddenly lose reliable GPS information or receive false position data, leaving crews to rely on other navigation systems.

SkyNaute is designed to address that problem by combining satellite navigation with sensors that can independently calculate an aircraft’s movement. When satellite signals become unreliable, the system can continue providing navigation information without depending on GPS.

For Safran, the A220 will be SkyNaute’s first application on a commercial airliner.

Why GPS jamming and GNSS spoofing are growing threats for airlines

Commercial aircraft use satellite navigation to establish their position and support flight management systems. GPS is the best-known service, but it is part of a wider group of satellite navigation networks collectively called Global Navigation Satellite Systems, or GNSS.

These systems have become important to modern airline operations because they provide accurate positioning across long distances, including over oceans and remote regions where ground-based navigation aids may be limited.

The problem arises when satellite signals are deliberately interfered with.

GPS jamming involves transmitting radio signals that overwhelm or block the genuine satellite signals received by an aircraft. The result can be a loss of reliable satellite positioning.

Spoofing is more deceptive. Instead of simply blocking the signal, it involves transmitting false navigation information that can mislead a receiver about the aircraft’s location or time.

The distinction matters. A crew may recognise that GPS has become unavailable, but false position information can be harder to identify, particularly if different aircraft systems begin showing conflicting information.

Interference has become a recurring concern around conflict-affected regions, where military forces use electronic warfare equipment to disrupt satellite-guided weapons, drones and other systems. Civilian aircraft operating in or near these areas can also be affected.

The eastern Mediterranean, the Middle East and areas around the Black Sea and Baltic region have all experienced reports of satellite navigation interference.

Such incidents do not mean an aircraft immediately loses the ability to navigate. Airliners already carry other navigation equipment, and crews have procedures for dealing with unreliable satellite information. However, interference can increase cockpit workload, affect navigation accuracy and complicate operations that depend on satellite positioning.

It is against this background that Airbus is introducing SkyNaute on the A220.

How Safran’s SkyNaute works without GPS

SkyNaute uses a different method of navigation when satellite signals cannot be trusted.

At the centre of the system are three hemispherical resonator gyroscopes, or HRGs, developed by Safran. These sensors measure changes in the aircraft’s orientation using vibrations inside a small, precisely engineered component.

Working with other inertial measurements, the system calculates how the aircraft is moving and estimates its position from a known starting point. It does not need to receive a continuous signal from satellites to do this.

Under normal conditions, SkyNaute combines inertial information with GNSS data to maintain an accurate position. Satellite updates help correct the small errors that gradually accumulate in inertial navigation.

When GNSS information appears unreliable, SkyNaute can identify the discrepancy and rely on its inertial measurements instead.

“We created it for our defense applications, and it brings us the capability to find spoofing situations with a high level of certainty,” Declety told Aviation Week. “Then, the system switches to inertial.”

That does not mean an aircraft can navigate indefinitely without any loss of accuracy. All inertial systems accumulate some error over time. The advantage is that the aircraft retains an independent source of navigation information when satellite signals are lost or manipulated.

Safran says the HRG technology also offers reliability benefits because the gyroscope has no mechanical parts subject to wear.

SkyNaute weighs approximately 3kg, occupies three litres of space and consumes 20 watts of electrical power, according to Safran’s published specifications. Its relatively small size and low power requirements make it easier to integrate into an aircraft without adding substantial weight.

Military technology moves into commercial aviation

SkyNaute was developed for military applications, where aircraft and other platforms must continue operating despite electronic warfare.

Safran says the technology has already been selected for military aircraft, helicopters and drones operated by European armed forces.

These platforms face different operating conditions. Helicopters must cope with strong vibrations, while combat aircraft can experience high manoeuvring loads and deliberate attempts to interfere with their navigation. Uncrewed aircraft may also need to navigate accurately when radio signals are disrupted.

The underlying requirement is the same: a reliable way to establish position and movement without depending entirely on external signals.

The A220 will be the first civil aircraft equipped with SkyNaute. Before introduction, Airbus will need to complete integration testing and the necessary certification work.

Safran also intends to offer the system for retrofit installation, although no airline customers or retrofit timetable have been disclosed.

Safran expands production in France

The move into commercial aviation comes as Safran increases production of the gyroscopes used in SkyNaute.

The technology is developed and manufactured at Montluçon in central France, where the company announced a €120 million ($135 million) investment in June 2026 to expand and modernise its facilities.

Safran plans to increase annual HRG production from 10,000 units to 30,000 by 2032, supporting demand across military and civilian applications.

“Seeing SkyNaute take its place on board the Airbus A220 is a source of immense pride for our teams: for the first time, our inertial navigation system will fly on an airliner. This is a strong signal for French industrial expertise. We sincerely thank Airbus for its trust,” Declety said in Safran’s announcement.

The A220 selection comes as aviation authorities are pressing airlines and manufacturers to prepare for more frequent satellite navigation disruptions.

In March 2026, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) and EUROCONTROL published a joint action plan to improve aviation safety during GNSS interference. EASA followed in July with updated guidance addressing the growing severity and sophistication of jamming and spoofing.

The guidance covers crew training, alternative navigation methods, reporting procedures and better coordination between pilots and air traffic controllers.

]]> Sydney’s new Western Sydney International Airport has welcomed its first international passenger flights, marking the opening of Australia’s first major new airport in more than 50 years.

Air New Zealand flight NZ165 from Auckland landed at Western Sydney International (Nancy-Bird Walton) Airport on Monday, 26 October, becoming the first international passenger service to arrive at the new airport.

The aircraft later departed for Auckland as flight NZ166, inaugurating a three-times-weekly international connection operating on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays.

The milestone follows the airport’s opening to domestic passengers on Sunday, 25 October, when Jetstar operated the first scheduled passenger departure to the Gold Coast.

The A$5.6 billion airport is located at Badgerys Creek, about 60 kilometres west of central Sydney. It was designed to relieve pressure on the city’s existing Kingsford Smith Airport and provide additional capacity for domestic and international aviation.

Sydney’s second airport opens after decades of planning

Western Sydney International has been under development for decades. The Australian government identified Badgerys Creek as the location for Sydney’s second major airport in 1986.

Construction took seven years, with more than 13,000 workers involved in delivering the airport and its associated infrastructure.

The airport’s opening gives Sydney a second major passenger gateway, with facilities designed to accommodate up to 10 million passengers annually in its initial configuration.

The terminal incorporates more than 40 check-in kiosks and 34 automated baggage-drop kiosks, with domestic and international services operating under the same roof.

Its 3.7 km runway can accommodate large long-haul aircraft, allowing the airport to expand its international network as airline demand develops.

The Australian government marked the first passenger departures on 25 October, describing the opening as a milestone for Western Sydney and Australia’s aviation network.

Which airlines will fly from Western Sydney International Airport?

Air New Zealand is the first international airline to operate passenger services from Western Sydney, but several other carriers have confirmed plans to use the airport.

Singapore Airlines is scheduled to begin daily nonstop flights to Singapore Changi Airport on 23 November 2026.

International services are expected to expand further in 2027, with Vietjet planning flights to Ho Chi Minh City in January and Fiji Airways expected to introduce flights to Nadi in March.

Qatar Airways has also announced plans to serve Western Sydney, adding another potential long-haul connection through its Doha hub.

Domestic operations began with Jetstar, which is introducing services to Melbourne, Brisbane and the Gold Coast. The airline’s initial schedule includes up to 14 weekly flights to Melbourne, four to the Gold Coast and three to Brisbane.

Qantas is scheduled to begin operating from the airport on 28 March 2027, using QantasLink Embraer E190 aircraft on services to Melbourne and Brisbane. The airline plans four weekly flights on each route.

Facilities at Western Sydney International Airport

WSI’s terminal was designed for seamless, stress-free and intuitive passenger journeys. The airport will offer several passenger facilities, including retail, food and beverage and lounges.

WSI will open with a selection of cafes and food outlets, with additional venues opening as flight services and passenger numbers grow.

The terminal’s retail offering includes two duty-free shopping areas, various speciality retail outlets, including EyeLove and Tech2Go, and three RELAY stores that offer fresh food, drinks, travel essentials and convenience products.

WSI’s first international lounge—The Rayleigh Lounge—will open in November and be operated by dnata. Eligible Singapore Airlines passengers will enjoy a premium dining and lounge experience, with expansive views of the airfield, fast WiFi, ready access to power outlets to charge their devices, and three private showers.

The terminal was also designed for accessibility and inclusivity, including dedicated sensory spaces for travellers experiencing anxiety or sensory stress, designed by specialist firm Creative Sensory Spaces. 

There are also pet relief rooms for arriving and departing passengers with accredited assistance animals. These rooms are wheelchair accessible and include artificial grassed relief areas, water bowls, waste bags and handwashing facilities.   

Hearing Loop Technology lets travellers with hearing aids or implants hear live announcements and PA messages. People can use the AFILS system by switching their hearing aid or cochlear implants to T switch or telecoil position.  

Dedicated family rooms let parents and carers feed, change and care for infants. Changing places support travellers with complex disability and high support needs beyond the accessible toilets located throughout the airport terminal.  

The airport also has multi-faith, quiet rooms, and ablution rooms available. 

Sydney’s new airport can operate 24 hours a day

One of Western Sydney International’s main operational advantages is its ability to accommodate aircraft movements around the clock.

Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport operates under an overnight curfew restricting most aircraft movements between 11 pm and 6 am.

Western Sydney International does not have the same curfew restrictions, giving airlines greater flexibility to schedule international flights, particularly services connecting Australia with Asia, the Middle East and other long-haul markets.

The airport also has a dedicated 24-hour cargo precinct, which began operations in July 2026.

According to the Australian government’s 26 October announcement, the facility increases Sydney’s air cargo capacity by approximately 33%.

The additional freight capacity is expected to support importers, exporters and logistics operators across Western Sydney.

Western Sydney Airport designed for future growth

The airport forms part of a wider A$18 billion government investment programme in Western Sydney, including road improvements and a new rail connection.

Road access was improved through the M12 motorway. The planned Sydney Metro–Western Sydney Airport line will provide a direct rail connection to the terminal. However, the metro service is not expected to open until late 2027, so passengers will initially have to use road transport, buses and connections to existing rail services.

The airport has been designed for phased expansion beyond its initial annual capacity of 10 million passengers.

For airlines, the new gateway offers additional opportunities to serve Sydney’s western suburbs without relying entirely on Kingsford Smith Airport.

Its location could also make it more convenient for residents and businesses in Western Sydney. Passengers travelling to central Sydney will need to consider the distance and available ground transport.

According to the Australian Government, the “WSI project created over 12,800 jobs,” with around half of those going to local workers.

Construction contributed $500 million to over 360 Western Sydney-based businesses, “including local tradies and construction companies, caterers, and security guards.”

Who was Nancy-Bird Walton and why is Sydney’s new airport named in her honour?

The airport is named after pioneering Australian aviator Nancy-Bird Walton (1915–2009), who became one of the country’s first female commercial pilots.

Born in New South Wales, she learned to fly under Sir Charles Kingsford Smith, whose name is carried by Sydney’s first international airport. She gained her pilot’s licence in 1933 and her commercial licence the following year, becoming the youngest female commercial pilot in the British Commonwealth.

Walton earned the nickname “Angel of the Outback” for flying medical personnel to remote communities in New South Wales during the 1930s. She later trained women during the Second World War and founded the Australian Women Pilots’ Association in 1950.

The Australian government announced the airport’s name in March 2019, recognising her achievements and contribution to Australian aviation.

The airport also celebrates her legacy through artwork and installations in its passenger terminal.

“It is fitting that having recognised Charles Kingsford Smith at Sydney Airport that we now recognise Australia’s greatest female aviation pioneer, Nancy-Bird Walton, in the naming of Western Sydney Airport,” then Prime Minister Scott Morrison said when the airport’s name was announced. 

First international flights mark new chapter for Australian aviation

The Australian government expects Western Sydney International to support tourism, trade and employment as additional airlines begin services.

In the official statement welcoming the first international flights, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said: “Western Sydney is now connected directly to the world, bringing more jobs, more visitors and more opportunities for local businesses.”

The airport’s next major international connection will launch on 23 November, when Singapore Airlines begins its daily Singapore service. 

“It can’t be overstated how big a moment this is for Western Sydney, for its people, for its economy and its industries,” said Catherine King, Minister for Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development and Local Government, during the launch of Jetstar’s domestic services on Sunday. “Today is a real milestone in our country’s travel history, and with tomorrow seeing the first international flight leave the tarmac for Auckland—the sky is the limit.”

For long-haul travellers, those few extra inches can make a noticeable difference, especially on overnight flights. To help, we’ve compared economy class seat pitch across major international airlines to find which carriers offer the most legroom.

Japan Airlines and All Nippon Airways top the list of most generous legroom in economy class, with seat pitches reaching 34” (86 cm) on selected aircraft. 

Here’s how the leading carriers compare, and how to identify the roomiest seats before you book.

Seat pitch varies around the world

Economy seat pitch varies widely between airlines and aircraft. The comparison below shows the maximum reported standard economy seat pitch on selected long-haul aircraft operated by 20 major international airlines.

These are main-cabin economy seats, excluding extra-legroom seats which often cost extra.

Which airlines offer 34 inches of economy seat pitch?

Japan Airlines

Japan Airlines (JAL) is a top choice for passengers who want extra space without paying for premium economy.

Its JAL SKY WIDER economy seats, installed on selected international Boeing 787, Boeing 777 and Boeing 767 aircraft, provide more space than more densely configured economy cabins.

The airline has also introduced new economy seating on its Airbus A350-1000 long-haul aircraft.

JAL’s published international economy seat guide distinguishes between aircraft and seat products. Check the aircraft type assigned to your flight.

Passengers can also compare individual configurations using AeroLOPA’s Japan Airlines seat maps.

All Nippon Airways (ANA)

ANA offers up to 34” (86 cm) of economy seat pitch on selected Boeing 787-9 aircraft.

The airline says its redesigned slimline seats provide this spacing while preserving passenger comfort. Their construction also improves knee clearance without requiring additional cabin space.

ANA’s official international economy seat specifications confirm the 34” measurement for its 206-seat Boeing 787-9 configuration.

However, not every ANA aircraft has the same economy cabin. Travellers should check the aircraft configuration and not assume the maximum seat pitch applies to the whole fleet.

Other airlines offering generous economy legroom

Korean Air

Korean Air also offers comparatively generous economy seating on selected long-haul aircraft.

Many of its economy cabins provide about 33” (84 cm) of seat pitch, well above the 30–31 inches commonly found on more densely configured aircraft.

As with other international airlines, dimensions depend on the aircraft type and seating configuration.

Emirates

Emirates is another airline worth considering, particularly for long-haul passengers travelling on its Airbus A380.

Most Emirates economy configurations have 32” (81 cm) seat pitch. The airline operates several aircraft configurations, each with different seating arrangements.

Passengers should check the seat map for the aircraft operating their flight to confirm legroom.

JetBlue

Among US airlines, JetBlue stands out for its spacious economy seating, even on domestic flights. Its standard economy product, branded Core, offers 32” of pitch on many aircraft. 

The airline also sells EvenMore seats with additional legroom, which often costs extra.

Singapore Airlines

Singapore Airlines offers approximately 32” (81 cm) of economy seat pitch on most of its long-haul aircraft and no less than 79 cm.

Like others on our list, Singapore Airlines has different cabin layouts on the same aircraft type. Passengers should check which version operates their flight.

Cathay Pacific

Cathay Pacific is another long-haul airline that offers economy seating with 32” pitch on selected aircraft.

Its Airbus A350 and Boeing 777 aircraft have different cabin configurations, and available space depends on the installed seating product.

Passengers travelling through Hong Kong can compare the aircraft assigned to competing flights before selecting their seats.

Qantas

Qantas offers approximately 31”–32” of economy seat pitch across selected long-haul aircraft, including its Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners and Airbus A380s.

Seat pitch can vary by aircraft and row, so passengers should check the individual seat map when booking.

Does seat pitch really measure legroom? 

Seat pitch measures the distance between a fixed point on one seat and the same point on the seat directly ahead or behind it. While it is a useful metric for comparing cabin configurations, it doesn’t measure the actual clearance available for passengers’ knees. 

Seat design, cushion thickness, recline and the position of the seatback pocket can all affect comfort. Two economy seats with identical pitch may feel different because of their construction.

Slimline seats can provide extra knee clearance by reducing seatback thickness. Conversely, a bulky seatback, entertainment equipment or a poorly positioned literature pocket can reduce usable space.

Seat width also matters, particularly on long flights. An aircraft with 32” pitch and wider seats may feel more comfortable than one with 34” pitch but narrower seating.

Passengers should also consider whether the seat reclines, the position of the armrests and the amount of space beneath the seat ahead.

How to find the economy seats with the most legroom

The best way to find a spacious economy seat is to check the aircraft configuration before booking.

Independent aircraft seating guides provide detailed cabin maps showing seat positions, window alignment, lavatories, galleys and other features. AeroLOPA lets you identify the specific cabin of the aircraft that typically operates your flight with a flight number search, making your booking decision easier. 

Travellers can use these maps, along with the airline’s seat map in the booking platform, to compare cabin products and the onboard passenger experience before booking flights and selecting seats.

Exit-row and bulkhead seats may offer additional legroom, although they can come with restrictions. Some have fixed armrests, reduced storage or limitations on reclining. Passengers should also check whether additional-legroom seats are priced differently, as many airlines sell these as a pricier economy plus product.

For those travelling long distances in standard economy, choosing a flight operated by the right aircraft type can make as much difference as choosing the airline. Remember that airlines sometimes make last-minute aircraft changes when maintenance or other operational issues arise.

]]> Why the race back to the Moon is heating up https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/race-back-to-moon/ Sun, 25 Oct 2026 12:04:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=53931 The Moon is back at the centre of a new space race. Here's why the US, China, India and private companies are investing in lunar exploration.

The post Why the race back to the Moon is heating up appeared first on AGN.

]]> The Moon has never stopped capturing imaginations, but for decades it seemed largely absent from humanity’s plans. That is changing fast.

Governments are preparing new crewed lunar missions, private companies are building hardware capable of reaching deep space, and a new race is emerging over who will shape the next era of exploration.

NASA is aiming to return astronauts to the lunar surface in 2028, having completed the crewed flyby in 2026. China is planning to land its astronauts on the lunar surface before 2030, and India says it will follow suit around a decade later.

For the first time, private space companies are developing to the point where they can discuss their own missions to the Moon or even Mars.

Here’s why nations and companies are racing back to the Moon

Why they went to the Moon in the first place

Before answering the question of why “everyone wants to go back to the Moon,” it’s useful to answer why they went there in the first place.

In the 1960s, the Cold War, geopolitical competition, and Kennedy’s internal politics were central.

Although the Apollo missions conducted important scientific experiments and returned invaluable lunar samples, public attention focused overwhelmingly on the symbolism of humanity’s first steps on another world.

That said, developing the entire Apollo ecosystem was in itself a major scientific windfall.

In 1957, the USSR’s Sputnik shocked the US. In 1961, the Soviet Union sent Yuri Gagarin into orbit before the United States could launch its first astronaut, securing another major propaganda victory in the Space Race, a feat that remains central to Russia’s national narrative.

Today’s context has substantially changed

Now, there are two credible missions to return to the Moon, and while the world has changed, it continues to bear many striking parallels to the 1960s.

Some actors are familiar, such as the United States and its NASA, while others are gone (the USSR).

Russia inherited the Soviet space programme, but it no longer possesses the resources or momentum that once enabled direct rivalry with NASA and currently has no clear independent pathway to a crewed lunar landing.

Russia’s greatest likely contribution is that of a major junior partner to China’s missions. Europe and Japan have major space programmes, but they contribute to the US-led Artemis mission.

India is perhaps the country worth watching the most after the US and China. Like China, it has powerful motivations to one day send a crewed mission independently to the Moon.

At the same time, there are powerful and capable private companies like SpaceX and Blue Origin that can contemplate their own self-funded or privately funded missions.

The canceled SpaceX dearMoon (Yusaku Maezawa’s privately funded project) lunar flyby and SpaceX’s long-term plans to visit Mars are examples.

All this means that the motivations of each of these countries and major companies should be discussed separately as they have different motives.

Why the US wants to return to the Moon

The US accomplished what it wanted with the Apollo programme; it established that it was the pre-eminent spacefaring nation. The inability of the USSR to challenge that, followed by its collapse, meant its position was secure without another expensive new programme.

But China is now challenging the US for that mantle. If the US does nothing and lets China go to the Moon, then it will always be able to claim it was the first, but the conversation becomes past tense. This could reinforce notions of the US as a country in decline.

Many analysts argue that returning astronauts to the Moon before China would help the US reinforce its position as the world’s leading space power.

It should also be stressed that the US has other motivations that include science and industrial base, but China still looms large.

Japan is enormously important, perhaps the third most important after the US and China. However, it has chosen to support the US effort instead of going it alone.

Unlike in the 1960s, mining and other commercial interests are becoming increasingly important. In 2023, Reuters reported, “NASA is looking to develop resources on the moon that initially include oxygen and water, and eventually may expand to iron and rare earths, and has already taken steps toward excavating moon soil in 2032.”

Japan prepares world-first mission to bring back samples from Mars moon Phobos Japan prepares world-first mission to bring back samples from Mars moon Phobos

Why China and India want to go to the Moon

For many observers, putting astronauts on the Moon would be highly symbolic for China. It fits into broader narratives of national rejuvenation and the country’s ambition to establish itself as a leading technological and geopolitical power.

China plans to put astronauts on the Moon before 2030; delays to the Artemis mission mean the missions are now likely to be very close.

Russia currently appears unlikely to mount an independent crewed lunar programme, making cooperation with China its most realistic route to returning cosmonauts to the Moon.

Working as a junior partner with China allows Russia to claim it remains an important actor in space.

Perhaps the most overlooked major space power is India.

India has said it will put astronauts on the Moon by 2040, making it the third major power with a declared crewed lunar ambition.

India’s motivations differ from China’s but similarly include national prestige, technological development and the desire to demonstrate its emergence as a major global power.

The big two companies: SpaceX and Blue Origin

Private companies, especially US-based ones, change the narrative significantly. These companies are essential to national efforts like Artemis, but they are also forces in their own right.

SpaceX has a goal of long-term expansion of human spaceflight, Elon Musk’s dreams of colonizing Mars, and sees commercial opportunities (e.g., mining, tourism). Blue Origin is similar and is guided by Jeff Bezos’s vision, tourism, and plans for long-term space industrialization.

Other notable companies include Intuitive Machines, Firefly, and Astrolab, although SpaceX and Blue Origin are the two companies with (or developing) the needed hardware.

These companies do not yet have confirmed self-funded programmes to land people on the Moon. However, as the canceled dearMoon mission shows, once SpaceX has its Starship fully operational, it can start chartering lunar flybys within a short time.

 DESTINATIONS PANEL  — overlay + grid
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
 /* Outer layer: covers full viewport */
 .sie-dest-panel {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 2147483000;
 display: flex;
 align-items: stretch;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .25s ease, visibility .25s;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open {
 opacity: 1;
 visibility: visible;
 pointer-events: auto;
 }
 /* Backdrop */
 .sie-dest-panel__backdrop {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 background: rgba(11, 55, 112, .52);
 backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 cursor: pointer;
 }
 /* Sheet — right-panel on desktop */
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1;
 width: min(800px, 100%);
 height: 100%;
 background: #fff;
 overflow-y: auto;
 -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch;
 padding: 26px 26px 40px;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 gap: 0;
 transform: translateX(28px);
 opacity: 0;
 transition: transform .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1), opacity .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1);
 box-shadow: -20px 0 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateX(0);
 opacity: 1;
 }
 /* Mobile: bottom-sheet */
 @media (max-width: 767px) {
 .sie-dest-panel {
 align-items: flex-end;
 justify-content: stretch;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 width: 100%;
 height: 92vh;
 border-top-left-radius: 22px;
 border-top-right-radius: 22px;
 padding: 20px 16px 40px;
 transform: translateY(28px);
 box-shadow: 0 -16px 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateY(0);
 }
 }
 /* ── Header ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__header {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 justify-content: space-between;
 margin-bottom: 6px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__titlewrap {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 10px;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__globe {
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #1e66f5;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__title {
 font-size: 1.5rem;
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #0b3770;
 margin: 0;
 line-height: 1.2;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close {
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #0b3770;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 6px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 line-height: 1;
 opacity: .75;
 transition: opacity .15s, background .15s;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close:hover {
 opacity: 1;
 background: #f0f4ff;
 }
 /* Subheading */
 .sie-dest-panel__sub {
 color: #466087;
 font-size: .94rem;
 margin: 0 0 20px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 /* ── Country grid ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 display: grid;
 grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);
 gap: 14px;
 /* allow this to grow and scroll */
 flex: 1;
 align-content: start;
 }
 @media (max-width: 620px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr);
 gap: 10px;
 }
 }
 @media (min-width: 621px) and (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
 }
 }
 /* ── Country card ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__card {
 position: relative;
 display: block;
 aspect-ratio: 3 / 2;
 border-radius: 12px;
 overflow: hidden;
 text-decoration: none;
 background: #1d3557;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card--no-img .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 background: linear-gradient(135deg, #1d3557 0%, #1e66f5 100%);
 }
 /* Hero image layer — scales on hover */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 transition: transform .4s ease;
 will-change: transform;
 }
 /* <img> fills the card exactly like background-size:cover did.
 loading="lazy" means the browser only fetches each image when the
 panel opens and the card enters the viewport — saving ~30 MB of
 upfront image requests on every page that includes this panel. */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-img {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center;
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-bg,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 transform: scale(1.07);
 }
 /* Gradient overlay + text */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-body {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 padding: 10px 12px 10px;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .72) 0%,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .30) 55%,
 transparent 100%
 );
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card-name {
 color: #fff;
 font-weight: 700;
 font-size: .92rem;
 line-height: 1.2;
 text-shadow: 0 1px 5px rgba(0,0,0,.55);
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {
 display: block;
 color: rgba(255,255,255,0);
 font-size: .75rem;
 margin-top: 2px;
 transition: color .2s ease, transform .2s ease;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {
 color: rgba(255,255,255,.9);
 transform: translateX(4px);
 }
 /* ── Body-scroll lock ── */
 body.sie-dest-panel-open {
 overflow: hidden;
 }
 /* ── Country interest heart ── */
 .sie-country-heart {
 position: absolute;
 top: 8px;
 right: 8px;
 z-index: 10;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 border: none;
 border-radius: 20px;
 padding: 4px 8px 4px 7px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 cursor: pointer;
 font-size: 13px;
 color: #94a3b8;
 box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.22);
 backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
 transition: color .18s, transform .18s, background .18s;
 line-height: 1;
 min-width: 28px;
 justify-content: center;
 }
 .sie-country-heart:hover {
 transform: scale(1.12);
 background: #fff;
 color: #ef4444;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.voted {
 color: #ef4444;
 background: #fff;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.voted i {
 animation: sie-heart-pop .35s cubic-bezier(.36,.07,.19,.97);
 }
 @keyframes sie-heart-pop {
 0%   { transform: scale(1); }
 40%  { transform: scale(1.45); }
 70%  { transform: scale(.88); }
 100% { transform: scale(1); }
 }
 .sie-country-heart__count {
 font-size: 11px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: inherit;
 display: none;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.has-votes .sie-country-heart__count {
 display: inline;
 }
 /* ── Trigger button styles (for use in any menu) ── */
 /* Desktop globe icon */

 .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover {
 transform: scale(1.15);

 /* Tooltip on desktop */
 @media (min-width: 1024px) {
 .se-dest-desktop-btn::after {

 white-space: nowrap;
 }
 .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover::after {
 opacity: 1;
 }
 }

 .se-dest-btn {
 background: #0b3770 !important;

 }

<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">There are specific provisions e.g. in the general policies, rules and regulations of the institution</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>In signing the Erasmus Charter for Higher Education, the institution agrees to respect <strong>in full</strong> the principles of non-discrimination as set out in the Programme. The institution must clearly demonstrate through its policies, rules and regulations that equal access and opportunities to mobile participants from all backgrounds. Which means that all individuals or groups will be treated equally, irrespective of their characteristics. In accordance with Article 21 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, there should be no discrimination "based on sex, race, colour, ethnic or social origin, genetic features, language, religion or belief, political or any other opinion, membership of a national minority, property, birth, disability, age or sexual orientation". For more information, see: <a href="http://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf">http://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf</a></p>                      </div>

                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The receiving institution must <strong>not </strong>charge any type of fees to incoming mobility students for the tuition, registration or examination of these students or for their access to laboratory, library and other facilities offered to local students.<br>In certain cases, however, mobile students may be required to pay small fees for insurance, student unions, use of miscellaneous materials (e.g. photocopies, laboratory products) on the same basis as these are charged to local students.                         <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>In accordance with equal access and opportunities, all students and staff should be treated equally in all academic and service matters.                         <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is vital to ensure that incoming mobility participants have full access to the same services and facilities as local students and staff. For example, mobility participants with special needs can benefit from the support services that the receiving institution offers to its local students and staff.</p>                      </div>

                         <p>To ensure fair and equitable opportunities to all potential participants, including those from groups which are usually under-represented in mobility programmes (students or staff with special needs, students from lower socio-economic backgrounds, with family responsibilities or with part-time jobs, etc.), it is important for institutions to devise and publicise a system that actively promotes mobility opportunities to students from these groups and ensures that their needs can be supported and their privacy respected.</p><p>This may be supported by inviting all those applying to the mobility programme to disclose whether they belong to an under-represented group, so that appropriate support can be provided at the receiving organisation.</p><p>Targeted support services may include, but are not limited to:</p><ul><li>Appointing a counsellor or officer for these under-represented groups,</li><li>Developing and delivering courses and exams through specific learning and teaching approaches</li><li>Developing specific support services, e.g. for people with special needs.                                                 <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Ensuring that the mobile participant, sending and receiving HEI/organisation/enterprise (i.e. all three parties) sign the Learning Agreement before the start of the mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The purpose of the Learning Agreement is to provide a transparent and efficient preparation of the study period abroad and to ensure that the student will receive recognition in his/her degree for the educational components or traineeship successfully completed abroad. The Learning Agreement:</p><ul><li>Sets out the learning outcomes for the mobility, including both the educational components or traineeship activities to be carried out by the student at the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise, which will be recognised by the sending institution upon successful completion of the study programme abroad and counted towards his/her degree.</li><li>Ensures full recognition for satisfactorily completed activities of study mobility and traineeships in terms of credits awarded, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams, and documents these credits in the student records, so that they can be identified in a transparent way.</li></ul><p>The Learning Agreement is binding for all parties and constitutes the cornerstone of successful student mobility (for studies, traineeships, and combinations thereof), including quality assurances and the process for transparent transfer of credits. Therefore, it is essential to conduct mobility based on an agreed and signed Learning Agreement. The Learning Agreement should be agreed and signed by all parties (the student, the sending institution and the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise) before the start of the mobility. It is not compulsory to circulate papers with original signatures; scanned copies of signatures or digital signatures may be accepted, depending on the national legislation.</p><p>The EU official templates for Learning Agreements for studies and traineeships are available online: <a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm&nbsp;&nbsp;</a></p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Including allocation of responsibility to an academic who has the authority to approve, amend and recognise the Learning Agreements on behalf of the responsible academic body</span>
